rows.basis: as sold, ug of element per kg of the emitting material (product as tested)
rows.rationale: No government anywhere sets a lead content maximum for an air freshener, plug-in evaporator, puff releaser, candle body, wax melt, oil or nebula diffuser, gel or reed diffuser, incense stick, potpourri, vacuum-cleaner fragrance additive or fragrance refill. The only sovereign heavy-metal instrument in any jurisdiction that names a product in this category is the United States CPSC prohibition on lead-cored candlewicks, 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13), mirrored by Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956; it restricts lead in the metal of a wick core and covers no other analyte and no other product form. The cell is therefore a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS, and it is taken on the axis the regulators themselves used: route of administration. Colorado's 2022 heavy-metal table and Maryland's Technical Authority Rev. 6.0 both publish a route LADDER over the same underlying matrices, with the inhalation row strictest, the oral row looser and the topical or cutaneous row looser still. The value is therefore a function of the route, not of the source matrix's chemistry, and Colorado scopes its strictest row in the instrument's own words to "inhaled product or audited product administered by metered-dose nasal spray", which describes a delivery mechanism this category shares. Maryland's own route gap is the sharpest available evidence for that reading: its inhalation-route total-chromium value is 600 ug/kg while its oral and cutaneous values for the same products are 1,100,000 ug/kg. Selected value 500 ug/kg, from Colorado (co2022 inhaled/nasal row). California DCC section 15723 independently sets the identical 0.5 ug/g for inhalable products (us_ca_dcc_2026_pb_inhalable_cannabis_0_5ugg), so two sub-national regulators converge on this value. The looser or route-unspecific values on the register are recorded and NOT selected: Maryland inhalation route 1000 ug/kg, Massachusetts all-uses protocol 500 ug/kg (equal but route-unspecific), Nevada 1200 ug/kg, Israel IMC-GMP Procedure 152 5000 ug/kg. The basis is identical to this row's native basis, micrograms of element per kilogram of product as tested, so no basis conversion, no reconstitution and no dry-to-wet adjustment is performed. The read-across is published as `read-across` and never as `regulatory-alignment`, because no instrument regulates this exact cell. Adopting it tightens rather than relaxes the applicable regulatory position: it is three to four orders of magnitude stricter than every article-content instrument that actually binds these products (RoHS lead at 1,000,000 ug/kg of homogeneous material, the candlewick-core prohibition threshold at 600,000 ug/kg of wick-core metal, REACH cadmium in polymers at 100,000 ug/kg). No occurrence, percentile, feasibility or precautionary input touched the number in either direction. Determined on the refill charge as supplied, in the physical state in which it is sold by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS with collision/reaction-cell control of the interfered masses, with the article's non-emitting components digested and screened separately per this row's component plan. DISPOSITION OF THE ADDITIONAL ANALYSES THIS CELL MANDATES. This cell requires one analysis beyond the published test, and it carries a criterion and a lot consequence, so that no mandatory analysis on this row is an obligation without an outcome. COMPONENT RESULTS, THE FIRST ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS THIS CELL MANDATES. The published ceiling of 500 ug/kg governs the emitting material and is NOT transferred to a component's bulk content: a metal crimp, seal or foil, a metallised cartridge or cup, or a pigmented closure is or may be substantially metal, metal-plated, metal-glazed or metal-pigmented by construction, and reading an emitting-material value against a structural component's bulk content would be exactly the basis conflation this row's basis guard exists to prevent, failing every compliant article for a metal that never enters the air. Every component result is instead dispositioned in three ordered branches, and no component result is left outside them. (a) WHERE A SOVEREIGN INSTRUMENT REACHES THE COMPONENT AND THIS ANALYTE, that instrument is the criterion. For lead and this row's components, branch (a) is EMPTY, and the instruments checked before saying so are named rather than waved at: EU RoHS 2011/65/EU is scoped to the homogeneous materials of electrical and electronic equipment and this row carries no powered sub-assembly; Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 on batteries is scoped to batteries and this row contains none; REACH Annex XVII entry 63 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2015/628 (eu_2015_628_pb_mouthable_general_public_articles_0_05pct) reaches only articles supplied to the general public that may be placed in the mouth by children; Regulation (EU) 2018/1513 reaches consumer clothing and skin-contact textiles and does not reach a packaging, sachet or decorative textile that is not worn; the EU Toy Safety Directive 2009/48/EC with EN 71-3, the CPSIA surface-coating limit and the Canadian and Australian toy-coating limits reach accessible toy material and toy surface coatings, and none of these articles is a toy; 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13) reaches only the metal of a candlewick core and this row has no wick core; the food-contact ceramic, glassware and enamelware instruments reach only articles intended to come into contact with food. Every component result on this row therefore falls to branch (b) or branch (c), and neither leaves a result without a criterion or without a lot consequence. (b) WHERE THE COMPONENT IS IN THE EMISSION PATH (the wick, reed or pad where supplied, the vial, cartridge or cup, and the closure, gasket, liner and any metal crimp, seal or foil the charge contacts), the criterion is the published ceiling itself, applied where its basis makes it meaningful: the test is performed on emitting material sampled from the finished, filled and assembled article rather than from a pre-fill bulk batch, at the end of the declared shelf life at the declared storage conditions, in the physical state in which the refill is sold, so that any lead transferred out of an emission-path component into the emitting material is carried into the published result rather than escaping it. An emitting-material result at or above 500 ug/kg fails the lot. A rising component result while the emitting material stays below the ceiling does not by itself fail the lot and falls to branch (c). (c) OTHERWISE, for a component outside the emission path that no sovereign instrument reaches for lead, the component result is dispositioned under the HMTc control-and-escalation rule, in the same terms this row's control cells already use: the result is held to ALARA against the manufacturer's demonstrated process capability for that formulation and component set; a result outside that capability band, or an unexplained step change between lots, triggers CAPA and raw-material traceback to the fragrance house, the carrier-solvent or gel-matrix supplier, the propellant supplier, the wick, reed or pad supplier and the vial, cartridge and closure converter; a confirmed uncontrolled source blocks certification until it is removed or substituted; and the analyte goes onto priority surveillance for this row. No component ceiling is invented in branch (c), because no credible sovereign government publishes a lead content maximum for these components in this product form, and an occupational exposure limit, an indoor-air guideline and an ambient-air standard are none of them converted into one.

rows.rationale: Program-wide consistency ruling (2026-08-17): the German BVL 2017 orientation values are treated as SELECTABLE anchors across HMTc. rows.basis: total nickel content of the product as placed on the market (consumer-chemical product-content basis; disclosed read-across)
rows.rationale: Nickel is the analyte this category's exposure pathway is built around: nickel is a confirmed dermal sensitiser, and a residue deposited on fabric that is then worn is prolonged, repeated dermal contact. No sovereign sets a nickel maximum for a laundry or fabric-care product. Instruments checked: China GB 14930.1-2022 (the only sovereign detergent contaminant standard in the register; scope is Type A detergents used directly for food cleaning and Type B detergents for tableware and food-contact tools, equipment, packaging and containers, and it sets a total-arsenic ceiling only); China NMPA 2015 Safety and Technical Standards for Cosmetics Table 2 (lead, arsenic, mercury, cadmium); Korea MFDS Notice 2025-63 and its predecessor Notice 2024-9 (lead, cadmium, nickel, antimony, arsenic, mercury); Germany BVL 2017 technically-avoidable heavy metals in cosmetics (lead, cadmium, mercury, arsenic, antimony); Health Canada cosmetic heavy-metal impurity limits; the ASEAN Cosmetic Directive Annex (2019) and the Malaysia NPRA, Singapore HSA, Indonesia BPOM, Taiwan MoHW and New Zealand cosmetic group-standard equivalents; EAEU TR CU 009/2011; EU REACH Annex XVII entry 20 (organotin), entry 23 (cadmium in listed polymers and paints), entry 47 as amended by Regulation (EU) 301/2014 (Cr(VI) in skin-contact leather), entry 72 with Appendix 12 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2018/1513 (lead, cadmium, arsenic and Cr(VI) in consumer clothing and skin-contact textiles) and entry 75 under Regulation (EU) 2020/2081 (tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures); EU Directive 2009/48/EC toy-safety migration limits; EU RoHS 2011/65/EU; and the dietary contaminant regimes (EU 2023/915, EU 2024/1987, Codex CXS 193, US FDA, FSANZ, Health Canada, UK, Hong Kong Cap. 132V), which are inapplicable both on scope and on basis. China NMPA 2015 Table 2 — the instrument that anchors lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury on this row — sets no nickel limit at all, so for nickel the nearest applicable sovereign consumer-chemical value is the Korean statutory limit, which is the only regime in the register that sets one. The Korean instrument writes a product-form split (eye make-up 35, colour make-up 30, all other cosmetic products 10 mg/kg); the split is preserved and the "all other products" tier is the applicable one, because a fabric-care product is not a decorative make-up. rows.rationale: Program-wide consistency ruling (2026-08-17): the German BVL 2017 orientation values are treated as SELECTABLE anchors across HMTc. Whether a national enforcement orientation value ranks as a sovereign maximum level is a genuine governance question, recorded for ratification as OI-20260817-bvl-selectability-ruling; until it is ruled on, every category states the same rule. A lot in which every component is inside the ceiling, but in which any component sits outside the running per-row control band, is escalated to ALARA review with raw-material trace-back to the specific component that moved.

rows.basis: Finished cosmetic total content as placed on market (ug/kg of product as sold); technically-unavoidable-impurity basis. Not migration, not leachate, not dietary, not an ingredient purity specification.
rows.rationale: Applicable sovereign maxima surveyed for this exact form: Germany BVL 2017 general cosmetic orientation value, 2000 ug/kg; China NMPA 2015, 10000; Health Canada, 10000; Taiwan MOHW 2024, 10000; Korea MFDS Notice 2025-63, 20000; Singapore HSA 2024 and the ASEAN directive with its Indonesian and Malaysian transpositions, 20000; Kenya KS 2937:2021, 20000. Looser and therefore non-binding: the EAEU natural-raw-material tier (5000), the Korean clay-powder tier (50000), the India IS 3959:2004 skin-powder rows (20000 and 10000) and the Australian customs value (250000). The German value binds. Its own scope excludes the make-up categories the same table lists at 5000 ug/kg (make-up powder, rouge, eye shadow, eyeliner, kajal and theatrical make-up); none of those forms falls in this row, so the general branch is the applicable cell. The US FDA draft lead guidance for lip and externally applied cosmetics (10000) carries draft status in the register, is gated out by the compiler, and is looser in any case. No colour-additive or ingredient purity specification is used as an anchor: the US 21 CFR 73/74 cosmetic-use specifications (10000-20000 ug/kg), the India permitted-colour specification (20000), the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant specification (20000) and the New Zealand / Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles (10000) bound one raw material's purity rather than the finished product, they are refused by this row's basis guard, and every one of them is looser than the binding value in any event.

rows.rationale: Korea MFDS is the ONLY authority in the register that publishes a nickel maximum for a finished cosmetic, and the instrument tiers it by product class: eye makeup 35000 ug/kg, colour makeup 30000, all other cosmetics 10000. Method step 4 requires the government's own product-form split to be preserved, so the applicable branch is selected rather than the strictest branch overall. Both register transpositions of the instrument (MFDS Notice 2024-9 and Notice 2025-63) are named and carry identical values, which is the cross-edition check. No other credible authority publishes a cosmetic nickel ceiling: the EU prohibits nickel compounds as intentional cosmetic ingredients under Regulation 1223/2009 Annex II without setting a numeric trace maximum, and Germany's BVL 2017 table covers only lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury and antimony. This row is neither an eye-makeup nor a colour-makeup product, so the 10000 ug/kg branch is the applicable cell and it binds. Where the mapping of an HMTc row onto the Korean product classes is not unambiguous, or where a row's forms straddle two branches, HMTc takes the stricter branch rather than claiming the looser one.

rows.basis: finished leave-on cosmetic as placed on market — total heavy-metal content per unit mass of the product as sold (ug/kg). Total content, not a migration or leachate value, and not a dietary basis. No reconstitution, dilution, or in-use concentration conversion is applied: the ceiling is compared to the product in the form the consumer buys it.
rows.rationale: Aluminium is the PERMITTED ACTIVE INGREDIENT of an antiperspirant, not a contaminant of it. Aluminium chlorohydrate, aluminium chloride, aluminium sesquichlorohydrate and aluminium zirconium tetrachlorohydrex glycine are the astringent actives that make the product work; the US over-the-counter antiperspirant monograph at 21 CFR 350 lists them as permitted actives and regulates their concentration as an active-ingredient specification expressed in percent of the anhydrous salt, and the EU restricts the aluminium zirconium complexes as ingredients under Regulation 1223/2009 Annex III. Neither is an impurity ceiling. Publishing a total-aluminium contaminant maximum for this form would be a category error: every compliant product would exceed any contaminant-scale value by three to four orders of magnitude, so the number would police the label claim rather than any contamination, and a brand could satisfy it only by removing the active. No credible sovereign publishes an aluminium contaminant maximum for an antiperspirant or for any other cosmetic form.

rows.rationale: Both named ids share the migration/soluble basis, so the strictest-selection is basis-clean. Total-lead CONTENT law runs in parallel on a different basis and is a companion obligation, not this cell's ceiling: CPSIA s.101 caps total lead at 100 mg/kg in any accessible children's-product substrate (cpsia_pb_childrens_product_substrate_100ppm) and at 90 mg/kg in the dried paint film (cpsia_pb_surface_coating_90ppm); Canada SOR/2016-193 and SOR/2011-17 set 90 mg/kg total lead in surface coating material and in applied stickers and films; Canada SOR/2018-83 sets 90 mg/kg total lead in accessible parts. HMTc requires conformity with both the migration ceiling published here and those content ceilings; the two are different measured quantities and are never combined into one number. Craft-kit jewellery components carry parallel total-CONTENT ceilings: Canada SOR/2018-82 caps total lead at 90 mg/kg in children's jewellery, Canada SOR/2018-83 caps total lead at 90 mg/kg in accessible parts of consumer products, and CPSIA s.101 caps total lead at 100 mg/kg in children's-product substrate. Those are content ceilings on a different measured quantity, all of them far more permissive than the 0.5 mg/kg migration ceiling published here, and they are companion obligations rather than this cell's anchor. OVER-COMPLIANCE, DISCLOSED: this row's scope spans all three of the Directive's material categories and the strictest of them is published across the whole row, so for the row's Category I material (crayons, chalk, pastel and pencil cores, powder pigment, glitter, modelling clay and dough) and Category III material (craft-kit beads, jewellery findings, wire, cord and moulded plastic or wooden parts) the published value is stricter than the Directive's own value for those forms. It is a deliberate protective choice, not those forms' legal ceiling; the compiled record's candidate set names every applicable category row with its value so the tag regulatory-alignment is read against the full disclosed set rather than as an assertion that Category II is this material's legal category. THAT ARGUMENT IS WITHDRAWN AS UNSUBSTANTIATED. The only repository artifact cited for it, wiki/sources/iso2020-8124-3-toy-migration-elements.md, documents the Table 2 analytical correction for ISO 8124-3:2020 and says of ASTM only that F963 4.3 sits in the same lineage and used the legacy EN 71-3 limits unchanged through F963-07 — a limit-VALUE lineage statement that expressly ends before the F963-08 and later editions this cell relies on, and it attributes no analytical correction to ASTM at all. A previous revision of this config published the Directive's looser Category III figure instead, on the argument that ASTM states its soluble limits in the legacy EN 71-3 / ISO 8124-3 lineage, in which conformity is judged against an analytical-correction-adjusted result, so that ASTM's nominal figure is looser than the Directive's once both are put on a raw-result footing. THAT ARGUMENT IS WITHDRAWN AS UNSUBSTANTIATED. The only repository artifact cited for it, wiki/sources/iso2020-8124-3-toy-migration-elements.md, documents the Table 2 analytical correction for ISO 8124-3:2020 and says of ASTM only that F963 4.3 sits in the same lineage and used the legacy EN 71-3 limits unchanged through F963-07 — a limit-VALUE lineage statement that expressly ends before the F963-08 and later editions this cell relies on, and it attributes no analytical correction to ASTM at all. The register row's own notes record only that the values are unchanged across F963-08/-11/-16/-17/-23. HMTc does not publish a ceiling above a figure made mandatory by CPSIA s.106 / 16 CFR 1250 on an unsubstantiated reading of a conformity clause. If ASTM F963-17 4.3.5 / 8.3 is later ingested as a source page that quotes the conformity-decision rule and it does specify a correction, the question may be reopened on that record; until then the stricter figure binds, which is also the position already published on wiki/regulations/astm-f963-soluble-migration and wiki/regulations/eu-2009-48-toy-safety-migration-limits. On this row the ASTM and NOM-252 mercury figures (60 and 25 mg/kg) are looser than the binding Category II value of 1.9 mg/kg and do not change the ceiling. Canada SOR/2016-193 and SOR/2011-17 set 10 mg/kg TOTAL mercury in surface coating material; that is a content ceiling on a different measured quantity, carried as a companion obligation with which conformity is also required, and not substituted into this migration cell. OVER-COMPLIANCE, DISCLOSED: this row's scope spans all three of the Directive's material categories and the strictest of them is published across the whole row, so for the row's Category I material (crayons, chalk, pastel and pencil cores, powder pigment, glitter, modelling clay and dough) and Category III material (craft-kit beads, jewellery findings, wire, cord and moulded plastic or wooden parts) the published value is stricter than the Directive's own value for those forms. It is a deliberate protective choice, not those forms' legal ceiling; the compiled record's candidate set names every applicable category row with its value so the tag regulatory-alignment is read against the full disclosed set rather than as an assertion that Category II is this material's legal category. rows.rationale: Directive 2009/48/EC Annex II Part III point 13 is the only instrument in the register that sets a numeric tin ceiling for toy material: ASTM F963-17 and ISO 8124-3:2020 do not regulate tin, and NOM-252-SSA1-2011 Table 1 regulates antimony, arsenic, barium, cadmium, total chromium, lead, mercury and selenium and sets no tin limit, so admitting MX to the credible-regulator set does not add a candidate to this cell. The instrument itself sets TWO tin lines on the same migration basis: total tin (15 000 / 3 750 / 180 000 mg/kg for Categories I / II / III) and organic tin (0.9 / 0.2 / 12 mg/kg), the latter reproduced from the point 13 table on wiki/regulations/eu-2009-48-toy-safety-migration-limits. A prior revision of this cell asserted that the Directive is the only credible sovereign instrument setting a numeric tin ceiling and disclosed only the REACH Annex XVII entry 20 organotin CONTENT restriction; that statement was wrong by omission, because it left the reader unaware that the same instrument caps organic tin at 0.2 mg/kg for this row's liquid or sticky (Category II) material while this cell publishes 3 750 mg/kg. The organic-tin migration rows are a recorded REGISTER GAP returned for ingestion through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway; once ingested, this row should gain a published organotin cell beside the total-tin screen, exactly as chromium carries a published Cr(VI) cell beside its total-chromium screen. Organotin is additionally restricted by REACH Annex XVII entry 20 on a total-CONTENT basis (0.1 percent as tin for dibutyltin, and for skin-contact and childcare articles dioctyltin); that is a different measured quantity and is a further companion obligation, not this cell's anchor. This row's scope names modelling clay, dough and finger paint expressly (and, for school articles, crayons, chalk, pastels and pencil cores), so NOM-252-SSA1-2011's preschool, modelling-clay and finger-paint tier is directly applicable and binds at 25 mg/kg, below the 60 mg/kg set by both its general tier and ASTM F963-17. A PRIOR STATEMENT ON THIS CELL IS WITHDRAWN AS AFFIRMATIVELY WRONG: earlier revisions published 60 mg/kg here and recorded the 25 mg/kg modelling-clay and finger-paint chromium value as an un-ingested register gap traceable only to ISO 8124-3:2020 Table 1. The same 25 mg/kg value for the same two material forms was already in the register as a Mexican statutory row, and it is now named and binds. The ASTM analytical-correction reading previously offered on this cell is also withdrawn as unsubstantiated for the F963 editions relied on, for the reason recorded on the tAs cell. OVER-COMPLIANCE, DISCLOSED: this row's scope spans all three of the Directive's material categories and the strictest of them is published across the whole row, so for the row's Category I material (crayons, chalk, pastel and pencil cores, powder pigment, glitter, modelling clay and dough) and Category III material (craft-kit beads, jewellery findings, wire, cord and moulded plastic or wooden parts) the published value is stricter than the Directive's own value for those forms. That requires new Category 21 subcategory slugs in data/taxonomy/hmtc-v2.json, which is a Step 0 taxonomy lock and outside a remediation pass; it is recorded as an outstanding item rather than performed here. For the row's non-clay, non-finger-paint, non-school-article forms (adhesives, slime, glitter, craft-kit components) the 25 mg/kg figure is stricter than the 60 mg/kg those forms carry under the general NOM-252 tier and ASTM, which is disclosed here as over-compliance in the protective direction. rows.basis: as sold, ug of element per kg of the emitting material (product as tested)
rows.rationale: No government anywhere sets a lead content maximum for an air freshener, plug-in evaporator, puff releaser, candle body, wax melt, oil or nebula diffuser, gel or reed diffuser, incense stick, potpourri, vacuum-cleaner fragrance additive or fragrance refill. The only sovereign heavy-metal instrument in any jurisdiction that names a product in this category is the United States CPSC prohibition on lead-cored candlewicks, 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13), mirrored by Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956; it restricts lead in the metal of a wick core and covers no other analyte and no other product form. The cell is therefore a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS, and it is taken on the axis the regulators themselves used: route of administration. Colorado's 2022 heavy-metal table and Maryland's Technical Authority Rev. 6.0 both publish a route LADDER over the same underlying matrices, with the inhalation row strictest, the oral row looser and the topical or cutaneous row looser still. The value is therefore a function of the route, not of the source matrix's chemistry, and Colorado scopes its strictest row in the instrument's own words to "inhaled product or audited product administered by metered-dose nasal spray", which describes a delivery mechanism this category shares. Maryland's own route gap is the sharpest available evidence for that reading: its inhalation-route total-chromium value is 600 ug/kg while its oral and cutaneous values for the same products are 1,100,000 ug/kg. Selected value 500 ug/kg, from Colorado (co2022 inhaled/nasal row). California DCC section 15723 independently sets the identical 0.5 ug/g for inhalable products (us_ca_dcc_2026_pb_inhalable_cannabis_0_5ugg), so two sub-national regulators converge on this value. The looser or route-unspecific values on the register are recorded and NOT selected: Maryland inhalation route 1000 ug/kg, Massachusetts all-uses protocol 500 ug/kg (equal but route-unspecific), Nevada 1200 ug/kg, Israel IMC-GMP Procedure 152 5000 ug/kg. The basis is identical to this row's native basis, micrograms of element per kilogram of product as tested, so no basis conversion, no reconstitution and no dry-to-wet adjustment is performed. The read-across is published as `read-across` and never as `regulatory-alignment`, because no instrument regulates this exact cell. Adopting it tightens rather than relaxes the applicable regulatory position: it is three to four orders of magnitude stricter than every article-content instrument that actually binds these products (RoHS lead at 1,000,000 ug/kg of homogeneous material, the candlewick-core prohibition threshold at 600,000 ug/kg of wick-core metal, REACH cadmium in polymers at 100,000 ug/kg). No occurrence, percentile, feasibility or precautionary input touched the number in either direction. Determined on the metered cartridge formulation as dispensed, including propellant by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS with collision/reaction-cell control of the interfered masses, with the article's non-emitting components digested and screened separately per this row's component plan. DISPOSITION OF THE ADDITIONAL ANALYSES THIS CELL MANDATES. This cell requires one analysis beyond the published test, and it carries a criterion and a lot consequence, so that no mandatory analysis on this row is an obligation without an outcome. COMPONENT RESULTS, THE FIRST ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS THIS CELL MANDATES. The published ceiling of 500 ug/kg governs the emitting material and is NOT transferred to a component's bulk content: a metering valve, a timer motor or solenoid, a gear train, a solder joint, a cell contact or spring, or a pigmented moulded housing is or may be substantially metal, metal-plated, metal-glazed or metal-pigmented by construction, and reading an emitting-material value against a structural component's bulk content would be exactly the basis conflation this row's basis guard exists to prevent, failing every compliant article for a metal that never enters the air. Every component result is instead dispositioned in three ordered branches, and no component result is left outside them. (a) WHERE A SOVEREIGN INSTRUMENT REACHES THE COMPONENT AND THIS ANALYTE, that instrument is the criterion. The instruments that reach this row's components for lead are: EU Directive 2011/65/EU (RoHS) restricts lead to 1,000,000 ug/kg of any homogeneous material of electrical and electronic equipment (register row eu_rohs_2011_pb_homogeneous_materials_1000000), and this row's powered sub-assembly is such equipment, so its printed circuit assembly, solder joints, heater or drive element, plated contacts, pins and connectors, and moulded housing are each tested as separate homogeneous materials against that value. Further, Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 on batteries restricts lead to 100,000 ug/kg of a portable battery by weight (register row eu_batteries_2023_pb_portable_batteries_100000), and it governs any primary or rechargeable cell supplied with the article, tested on the cell as a whole. Each is applied in its own basis at its own threshold, on the component it actually governs, and an exceedance blocks certification of the lot outright irrespective of the emitting-material result. None of these article-and-component values is ever republished as this row's emitting-material limit, because each is three to four orders of magnitude looser and republishing one would misrepresent a component prohibition as a product permission. (b) WHERE THE COMPONENT IS IN THE EMISSION PATH (the cartridge's internal lacquer, the metering valve with its stem and gasket, and the actuator nozzle), the criterion is the published ceiling itself, applied where its basis makes it meaningful: the test is performed on emitting material sampled from the finished, filled and assembled article rather than from a pre-fill bulk batch, at the end of the declared shelf life or after the declared maximum number of metered actuations, whichever is the more demanding, so that any lead transferred out of an emission-path component into the emitting material is carried into the published result rather than escaping it. An emitting-material result at or above 500 ug/kg fails the lot. A rising component result while the emitting material stays below the ceiling does not by itself fail the lot and falls to branch (c). (c) OTHERWISE, for a component outside the emission path that no sovereign instrument reaches for lead, the component result is dispositioned under the HMTc control-and-escalation rule, in the same terms this row's control cells already use: the result is held to ALARA against the manufacturer's demonstrated process capability for that formulation and component set; a result outside that capability band, or an unexplained step change between lots, triggers CAPA and raw-material traceback to the fragrance house, the propellant and cartridge supplier, the metering-valve maker, the electronics contract manufacturer, the cell supplier and the housing moulder; a confirmed uncontrolled source blocks certification until it is removed or substituted; and the analyte goes onto priority surveillance for this row. No component ceiling is invented in branch (c), because no credible sovereign government publishes a lead content maximum for these components in this product form, and an occupational exposure limit, an indoor-air guideline and an ambient-air standard are none of them converted into one.

Further, Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 on batteries restricts mercury to 5,000 ug/kg of a battery by weight (register row eu_batteries_2023_thg_batteries_5000), and it governs any primary or rechargeable cell supplied with the article, tested on the cell as a whole. Each is applied in its own basis at its own threshold, on the component it actually governs, and an exceedance blocks certification of the lot outright irrespective of the emitting-material result. None of these article-and-component values is ever republished as this row's emitting-material limit, because each is three to four orders of magnitude looser and republishing one would misrepresent a component prohibition as a product permission. (b) WHERE THE COMPONENT IS IN THE EMISSION PATH (the cartridge's internal lacquer, the metering valve with its stem and gasket, and the actuator nozzle), the criterion is the published ceiling itself, applied where its basis makes it meaningful: the test is performed on emitting material sampled from the finished, filled and assembled article rather than from a pre-fill bulk batch, at the end of the declared shelf life or after the declared maximum number of metered actuations, whichever is the more demanding, so that any mercury transferred out of an emission-path component into the emitting material is carried into the published result rather than escaping it. An emitting-material result at or above 100 ug/kg fails the lot. A rising component result while the emitting material stays below the ceiling does not by itself fail the lot and falls to branch (c). (c) OTHERWISE, for a component outside the emission path that no sovereign instrument reaches for total mercury, the component result is dispositioned under the HMTc control-and-escalation rule, in the same terms this row's control cells already use: the result is held to ALARA against the manufacturer's demonstrated process capability for that formulation and component set; a result outside that capability band, or an unexplained step change between lots, triggers CAPA and raw-material traceback to the fragrance house, the propellant and cartridge supplier, the metering-valve maker, the electronics contract manufacturer, the cell supplier and the housing moulder; a confirmed uncontrolled source blocks certification until it is removed or substituted; and the analyte goes onto priority surveillance for this row. No component ceiling is invented in branch (c), because no credible sovereign government publishes a total-mercury content maximum for these components in this product form, and an occupational exposure limit, an indoor-air guideline and an ambient-air standard are none of them converted into one.

rows.basis: as sold, ug of element per kg of the emitting material (product as tested)
rows.rationale: No government anywhere sets a total chromium content maximum for an air freshener, plug-in evaporator, puff releaser, candle body, wax melt, oil or nebula diffuser, gel or reed diffuser, incense stick, potpourri, vacuum-cleaner fragrance additive or fragrance refill. The only sovereign heavy-metal instrument in any jurisdiction that names a product in this category is the United States CPSC prohibition on lead-cored candlewicks, 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13), mirrored by Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956; it restricts lead in the metal of a wick core and covers no other analyte and no other product form. The cell is therefore a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS, and it is taken on the axis the regulators themselves used: route of administration. Colorado's 2022 heavy-metal table and Maryland's Technical Authority Rev. 6.0 both publish a route LADDER over the same underlying matrices, with the inhalation row strictest, the oral row looser and the topical or cutaneous row looser still. The value is therefore a function of the route, not of the source matrix's chemistry, and Colorado scopes its strictest row in the instrument's own words to "inhaled product or audited product administered by metered-dose nasal spray", which describes a delivery mechanism this category shares. Maryland's own route gap is the sharpest available evidence for that reading: its inhalation-route total-chromium value is 600 ug/kg while its oral and cutaneous values for the same products are 1,100,000 ug/kg. Selected value 600 ug/kg, from Maryland (inhalation route). Maryland is the only regulator on the register that publishes a chromium value scoped to the inhalation route. The looser or route-unspecific values on the register are recorded and NOT selected: no other jurisdiction on the register publishes a chromium value for any inhaled product: California DCC section 15723, the Colorado route table, the Massachusetts protocol, the Nevada action levels and Israel IMC-GMP Procedure 152 all omit chromium entirely. Maryland's own oral-route and cutaneous-route chromium values for the same products, 1,100,000 ug/kg, are a different route scope and are deliberately not used. The basis is identical to this row's native basis, micrograms of element per kilogram of product as tested, so no basis conversion, no reconstitution and no dry-to-wet adjustment is performed. The read-across is published as `read-across` and never as `regulatory-alignment`, because no instrument regulates this exact cell. Adopting it tightens rather than relaxes the applicable regulatory position: it is three to four orders of magnitude stricter than every article-content instrument that actually binds these products (RoHS lead at 1,000,000 ug/kg of homogeneous material, the candlewick-core prohibition threshold at 600,000 ug/kg of wick-core metal, REACH cadmium in polymers at 100,000 ug/kg). No occurrence, percentile, feasibility or precautionary input touched the number in either direction. Determined on the metered cartridge formulation as dispensed, including propellant by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS with collision/reaction-cell control of the interfered masses, with the article's non-emitting components digested and screened separately per this row's component plan. DISPOSITION OF THE ADDITIONAL ANALYSES THIS CELL MANDATES. This cell requires one analysis beyond the published test, and it carries a criterion and a lot consequence, so that no mandatory analysis on this row is an obligation without an outcome. COMPONENT RESULTS, THE FIRST ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS THIS CELL MANDATES. The published total-chromium screen of 600 ug/kg governs the emitting material and is NOT transferred to a component's bulk content: a metering valve, a timer motor or solenoid, a gear train, a solder joint, a cell contact or spring, or a pigmented moulded housing is or may be substantially metal, metal-plated, metal-glazed or metal-pigmented by construction, and reading an emitting-material value against a structural component's bulk content would be exactly the basis conflation this row's basis guard exists to prevent, failing every compliant article for a metal that never enters the air. Every component result is instead dispositioned in three ordered branches, and no component result is left outside them. (a) WHERE A SOVEREIGN INSTRUMENT REACHES THE COMPONENT AND THIS ANALYTE, that instrument is the criterion. For total chromium and this row's components, branch (a) is EMPTY, and the instruments checked before saying so are named rather than waved at: EU RoHS 2011/65/EU restricts HEXAVALENT chromium in the homogeneous materials of electrical and electronic equipment (eu_rohs_2011_crvi_homogeneous_materials_1000000) and publishes no total-chromium value, so it reaches this row's hexavalent-chromium cell on the powered sub-assembly this row carries and never this total-chromium cell, because a species and its total-element parent are not interchangeable in either direction; Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 on batteries restricts mercury, cadmium and lead only and publishes no chromium value, so it does not reach this cell even on the primary or rechargeable cells this row carries; REACH Annex XVII entry 63 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2015/628 (eu_2015_628_pb_mouthable_general_public_articles_0_05pct) reaches only articles supplied to the general public that may be placed in the mouth by children; Regulation (EU) 2018/1513 reaches consumer clothing and skin-contact textiles and does not reach a packaging, sachet or decorative textile that is not worn; the EU Toy Safety Directive 2009/48/EC with EN 71-3, the CPSIA surface-coating limit and the Canadian and Australian toy-coating limits reach accessible toy material and toy surface coatings, and none of these articles is a toy; 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13) reaches only the metal of a candlewick core and this row has no wick core; the food-contact ceramic, glassware and enamelware instruments reach only articles intended to come into contact with food. Every component result on this row therefore falls to branch (b) or branch (c), and neither leaves a result without a criterion or without a lot consequence. (b) WHERE THE COMPONENT IS IN THE EMISSION PATH (the cartridge's internal lacquer, the metering valve with its stem and gasket, and the actuator nozzle), the criterion is the published total-chromium SCREEN of 600 ug/kg, applied where its basis makes it meaningful: the test is performed on emitting material sampled from the finished, filled and assembled article rather than from a pre-fill bulk batch, at the end of the declared shelf life or after the declared maximum number of metered actuations, whichever is the more demanding, so that any chromium transferred out of an emission-path component into the emitting material is carried into the published result rather than escaping it. The screen is a tripwire and never a pass/fail in its own right. An emitting-material total-chromium result reaching half the screen (300 ug/kg) orders reflex hexavalent-chromium speciation on that lot under the reference method published on this row's Cr-VI cell, and that cell's disposition then governs the lot: any hexavalent chromium quantifiable above the method limit of quantitation fails the lot. (c) OTHERWISE, for a component outside the emission path that no sovereign instrument reaches for total chromium, the component result is dispositioned under the HMTc control-and-escalation rule, in the same terms this row's control cells already use: the result is held to ALARA against the manufacturer's demonstrated process capability for that formulation and component set; a result outside that capability band, or an unexplained step change between lots, triggers CAPA and raw-material traceback to the fragrance house, the propellant and cartridge supplier, the metering-valve maker, the electronics contract manufacturer, the cell supplier and the housing moulder; a confirmed uncontrolled source blocks certification until it is removed or substituted; and the analyte goes onto priority surveillance for this row. This row is not a colour cosmetic, so the 10 ug/g tier applies directly. Both the 2024 Notice No. 9 row and the 2025 revision row are named; they carry the same value and naming both shows the limit survived a revision cycle. Nickel is a leading contact-sensitiser in children, which is why the cell is published as a firm ceiling rather than a control even though only one jurisdiction sets it.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market (total content, ug/kg of product as sold)

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market (total content, ug/kg of product as sold)
rows.rationale: Germany's BVL 2017 Table 1 is the strictest sovereign finished-cosmetic lead limit in the register at 2.0 mg/kg, roughly five times stricter than Health Canada (10 mg/kg), China NMPA 2015 (10 mg/kg) and Taiwan MOHW 2024 (10 mg/kg), which are named alongside it so the derivation shows the full sovereign spread rather than one convenient number. The US FDA draft cosmetic lead guidance (10 mg/kg) is gated as draft and is looser in any case.

Nickel is a leading contact-sensitiser in children, which is why the cell is published as a firm ceiling rather than a control even though only one jurisdiction sets it.

rows.rationale: Germany's BVL 2017 Table 1 is the strictest sovereign finished-cosmetic lead limit in the register at 2.0 mg/kg, roughly five times stricter than Health Canada (10 mg/kg), China NMPA 2015 (10 mg/kg) and Taiwan MOHW 2024 (10 mg/kg), which are named alongside it so the derivation shows the full sovereign spread rather than one convenient number. BVL is issued by a German federal authority and defines what counts as technically avoidable under Article 17 of EU Regulation 1223/2009, which is binding EU law; it is not a trade-association guideline. The US FDA draft cosmetic lead guidance (10 mg/kg) is gated as draft and is looser in any case. Health Canada's cosmetic impurity guidance is NOT named on this row: the guidance states on its face that products regulated in Canada as drugs or natural health products - it names sunscreens, zinc-oxide skin protectants and therapeutic toothpaste - fall outside its cosmetic scope. Naming it here would be a scope conflation.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market — total element content per unit mass of undiluted product as sold (µg/kg). Not a dietary basis, not a migration or leachate basis, and no use-pattern dilution credit.
rows.rationale: BVL 2017 Table 1 (German Federal Office of Consumer Protection and Food Safety, with the Länder cosmetics working group) publishes the technically avoidable heavy-metal content of cosmetic products in general; lead is 2.0 mg/kg, and a content above the table is treated as technically avoidable under good manufacturing practice. Its status is a federal-authority guidance value rather than a statute, and it is disclosed as such, but it is the strictest published sovereign finished-cosmetic lead maximum and Method v2.0 takes the strictest applicable value. The named comparator set shows how far the binding sits below the field: Health Canada, China NMPA 2015 and Taiwan MOHW 2024 are five times looser at 10 mg/kg; Korea, ASEAN and its Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia transpositions, and Kenya KS 2937:2021 are ten times looser at 20 mg/kg; Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations threshold is 125 times looser at 250 mg/kg. Two sovereign cosmetic lead values in the register are stricter than the binding — the BVL 2017 toothpaste tier at 500 µg/kg and Washington State's Toxics-Free Cosmetics Act toothpaste limit at 1000 µg/kg — and the compiler's stricter-unselected audit flags both on every row of this category. Neither is applicable. Both are scoped by their own instruments to toothpaste, a dentifrice that sits on the oral mucosa and is partly swallowed; that ingestion pathway is the stated reason the toothpaste tier is tighter. Categories 20 and 2 carry the dentifrice forms and use those instruments. A shampoo, body wash, scrub or depilatory has no ingestion pathway inside either instrument's scope, so reading a toothpaste tier onto a hair or body rinse-off product would have HMTc inventing a stricter number that no government set for this form. Method v2.0 forbids that as squarely as it forbids inventing a looser one: applicability is a real constraint, and the strictest APPLICABLE value governs. The compiler's audit also flags EU REACH Annex XVII entry 75, which sets 700 µg/kg for lead in mixtures placed on the market for tattooing and permanent make-up. That value is stricter than the binding and is deliberately not adopted: the instrument governs a mixture INJECTED INTO THE DERMIS, on a 'mixture for tattooing or permanent make-up by weight' basis, and a rinse-off shampoo or body wash is not such a mixture on any reading of the entry. The row is held out by this row's basis_guard as well as on scope. It is surfaced rather than filtered out of the scan so that the record shows it was found and disposed of, not missed. Colour-additive and colourant purity specifications (21 CFR 73 and 74, the New Zealand and Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles, the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 permitted-colours entries, the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant entries) are raw-material ingredient specifications, not finished-product maxima. They are held out of every cell by this row's basis_guard, and none of them is in any case stricter than the binding for this analyte. This row additionally names the two sovereign tiers written for mineral-bearing cosmetics, so that the record shows they were evaluated rather than passed over: EAEU TR CU 009/2011 sets 5 mg/kg for perfumery-cosmetic products containing more than 1 percent natural plant or natural mineral raw material, and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-9 carves powder products using clay as a raw material out of its 20 µg/g tier and gives them 50 µg/g. Both are LOOSER accommodations for the geogenic metal load of mineral raw materials, at 2.5 and 25 times the binding. Method v2.0 takes the strictest applicable value, so neither relaxes this row: a clay, pumice or salt scrub is certified at 2000 µg/kg like every other rinse-off form. Adopting the mineral accommodation would be selecting a number for convenience, which is the precise failure this method forbids.

rows.rationale: BVL 2017 Table 1 sets arsenic in cosmetic products in general (excepting theatre, fan and carnival make-up, which are not rinse-off forms) at 0.5 mg/kg. This is a TOTAL-arsenic cell: the register value is mapped to tAs and is never substituted onto the inorganic-arsenic cell, which is a separate control. rows.rationale: BVL 2017 Table 1 sets mercury in cosmetic products in general at 0.1 mg/kg, and BVL's toothpaste tier is the same value, so mercury carries no dentifrice split. The comparator set is deliberately wide here because mercury in cosmetics is the one contaminant with a hard, enforceable US rule and an active illegal-adulteration problem: 21 CFR 700.13(d)(2)(i) deems a cosmetic adulterated unless its mercury content is unavoidable under good manufacturing practice and below 1 ppm, and Hong Kong Cap. 640 sets the same 1 ppm expressly for unintentional trace mercury in cosmetics including skin-lightening products. Mercury used as an intentional skin-lightening active, and the eye-area thiomersal and phenylmercuric preservative allowances in the India, Hong Kong and South Africa instruments, are ingredient permissions rather than contaminant ceilings; HMTc does not adopt them, and a rinse-off product formulated with an intentional mercury ingredient is not certifiable at all. Colour-additive and colourant purity specifications (21 CFR 73 and 74, the New Zealand and Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles, the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 permitted-colours entries, the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant entries) are raw-material ingredient specifications, not finished-product maxima. rows.rationale: Korea is the only jurisdiction in the register that sets a nickel content limit for finished cosmetics, and it tiers it by form: 10 µg/g for cosmetic products other than eye makeup and colour cosmetics, 30 µg/g for colour makeup, 35 µg/g for eye makeup. Every Category 14 form is a cleansing, conditioning, shaving, depilatory or hair-colouring preparation and none is an eye-makeup or colour-makeup product in the MFDS product taxonomy, so the strictest of the three tiers — 10 µg/g — is the directly applicable one, not a read-across. Korea MFDS Notice 2025-63 carries the same 10 µg/g value for the same scope and corroborates it; it is not named as a candidate because its register note contradicts its own value (the note reads '1 microgram/g = 1000 ug/kg' against a stored value of 10000 µg/kg), and a litigation-facing citation should not carry that discrepancy forward. The EU REACH restriction on nickel in tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures (5000 µg/kg) is stricter but governs a mixture injected into the dermis, a different form on a different basis, and is held out by this row's basis_guard. Nickel is a leading contact sensitiser, so the programme additionally holds it under ALARA post-publication and treats the published ceiling as an outer bound rather than a target.

rows.basis: as sold, edible portion (wet weight)
rows.rationale: Two credible sovereign instruments regulate this exact cell and agree: FSANZ Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code Schedule 19 sets 0.1 mg/kg for meat of cattle, sheep, pig and poultry excluding offal, and Hong Kong Cap. 132V Part 2 sets 0.1 mg/kg for meat of cattle, pig, goat and sheep. The corresponding EU Regulation (EU) 2023/915 and Codex CXS 193-1995 muscle-meat lead rows are ABSENT from this register and are therefore not named and not assigned a value from memory; they are recorded as register gaps for ingestion through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. Because Method v2.0 selects the strictest applicable value, ingesting them can only lower this cell or leave it unchanged, never raise it, and this cell must be re-derived when they land. The looser edible-offal lead maximum levels (Hong Kong 0.15-0.20 mg/kg, FSANZ 0.5 mg/kg) are a DIFFERENT product scope and are deliberately not used to anchor this muscle-meat row: Bovine offal is a separately-tested sub-lot governed by the offal maximum levels of its own species. BASIS OF THE BINDING INSTRUMENT, DISCLOSED: the two concurring instruments are written on DIFFERENT bases. FSANZ Schedule 19 states its maximum level for the portion ordinarily consumed (an as-consumed basis); Hong Kong Cap. 132V states the identical 0.1 mg/kg as-sold, for the edible portion after removal of bones and fat (Cap. 132V Part 2 Note 1). Because this row publishes an as-sold ceiling, the Hong Kong as-sold row is named as the binding instrument and the FSANZ row is disclosed as an independent sovereign value concurring at the same number. The published ceiling therefore rests on an instrument written in this row's own basis, and no as-consumed value is relabelled as-sold. The number is unaffected: both instruments sit at 100 ug/kg, so the strictest-applicable selection is identical either way.

rows.basis: extractable element content of the homogeneous textile material after the REACH Annex XVII entry 72 Appendix 12 extraction (mg/kg of homogeneous material)
rows.rationale: Entry 72 is the on-point sovereign instrument for an infant or toddler bib: its scope in the register is consumer clothing, related accessories, textiles with skin contact similar to clothing, and footwear, and its basis is the homogeneous material after extraction. At 1 mg/kg it is ninety times stricter than the 90 mg/kg total-content children's-product limits — but it is a DIFFERENT MEASURED QUANTITY, not a stricter version of the same one, and the two are not interchangeable. The total-content obligations therefore run alongside as companions and are enforced, not replaced: US CPSIA s.101 (100 mg/kg total lead in any part of a children's product), 16 CFR 1303 (90 mg/kg in a surface coating, which reaches a print or applied film on the garment), Canada SOR/2018-83 s.2(1) (90 mg/kg in each accessible part of child clothing and accessories) and Canada SOR/2016-193 s.2(1) and s.6 (90 mg/kg in a dried surface coating material and in applied stickers, films and coatings on products for children). A garment must satisfy both the extractable ceiling published here and the content companions. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value.

Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value. COMPLIANCE OBLIGATION, in the content basis rather than this row's extraction basis: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act prohibits cadmium exceeding 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component (register row wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b); codified in RCW chapter 70A.430), and its definition of a children's product expressly reaches products worn as clothing by children and products designed to help a child sleep. That 40 mg/kg is a TOTAL-CONTENT figure and is therefore not a stricter version of the 1 mg/kg extractable ceiling published here; the two measure different quantities and both bind. A component returning total cadmium above 40 mg/kg is escalated as a jurisdiction-specific regulatory hard stop under the HMTc legal-violation rule even where the extractable result conforms, pending scope-resolved re-ingest of the Washington row. Where the article incorporates a battery or a battery-powered module — a vibration unit, a sound or music module, a night light, a powered mobile or a powered rocker — the battery is a distinct regulated article with its own instrument, and its limits are not this row's. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 restricts cadmium in a portable battery whether or not incorporated into an appliance (register row eu_batteries_2023_cd_portable_batteries_20000, 20 mg/kg) and mercury in a battery (register row eu_batteries_2023_thg_batteries_5000, 5 mg/kg), both expressed on the weight of the battery. Both are stricter than the values published here and both are recorded as companion obligations on the battery in a battery-by-weight basis; the battery is never homogenised into an accessible-component sample and its instrument is never merged into this row's extractable ceiling. Where the article carries no battery and no powered module the obligation does not arise.

rows.basis: extractable element content of the homogeneous textile material, determined after the extraction specified for REACH Annex XVII entry 72 Appendix 12 and expressed as mg/kg of the homogeneous material. This is an EXTRACTION basis. It is not a total-content basis (CPSIA substrate, Canadian surface-coating materials, REACH entry 23 cadmium, Australian coating content), and it is not the EN 71-3 / Directive 2009/48/EC 0.07 M HCl toy-migration basis.
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign publishes a TOTAL-chromium value for an infant or toddler bib in this row's extraction basis. REACH Annex XVII entry 72 Appendix 12 regulates chromium(VI) specifically and not total chromium, which is the correct regulatory choice: total chromium in a textile is dominated by benign trivalent chromium from chrome-tanned leather trim, chromium(III) mordants and chromium-complex dyes, while the health-relevant species is Cr(VI), and that species carries a firm published 1 mg/kg extractable ceiling on this same row. The Australian coating-content value (60 mg/kg) and the ASTM F963 soluble value (60 mg/kg) sit in other bases. Publishing a total-chromium ceiling would add no protection over the published Cr(VI) ceiling and would misrepresent a benign total as a hazard measure, so total chromium is held as a screening control.

rows.basis: extractable element content of the homogeneous textile material after the REACH Annex XVII entry 72 Appendix 12 extraction (mg/kg of homogeneous material)
rows.rationale: Entry 72 is the on-point sovereign instrument for an infant blanket, swaddle or wearable sleep sack: its scope in the register is consumer clothing, related accessories, textiles with skin contact similar to clothing, and footwear, and its basis is the homogeneous material after extraction. At 1 mg/kg it is ninety times stricter than the 90 mg/kg total-content children's-product limits — but it is a DIFFERENT MEASURED QUANTITY, not a stricter version of the same one, and the two are not interchangeable. The total-content obligations therefore run alongside as companions and are enforced, not replaced: US CPSIA s.101 (100 mg/kg total lead in any part of a children's product), 16 CFR 1303 (90 mg/kg in a surface coating, which reaches a print or applied film on the garment), Canada SOR/2018-83 s.2(1) (90 mg/kg in each accessible part of child clothing and accessories) and Canada SOR/2016-193 s.2(1) and s.6 (90 mg/kg in a dried surface coating material and in applied stickers, films and coatings on products for children). A garment must satisfy both the extractable ceiling published here and the content companions. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value.

rows.basis: extractable element content of the homogeneous textile material after the REACH Annex XVII entry 72 Appendix 12 extraction (mg/kg of homogeneous material)
rows.rationale: Entry 72 Appendix 12 binds an infant blanket, swaddle or wearable sleep sack directly at 1 mg/kg extractable cadmium. The total-content companion obligations are EU REACH Annex XVII entry 23 (100 mg/kg cadmium in articles produced from the listed synthetic organic polymers, which reaches printed plastisol, laminated and coated panels and moulded trims) and the Australian Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956 Schedule 2 coating value (75 mg/kg on the non-volatile content of a coating material, which reaches a print or applied film). Both are enforced as companions in the content basis and neither is published here. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value. COMPLIANCE OBLIGATION, in the content basis rather than this row's extraction basis: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act prohibits cadmium exceeding 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component (register row wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b); codified in RCW chapter 70A.430), and its definition of a children's product expressly reaches products worn as clothing by children and products designed to help a child sleep. That 40 mg/kg is a TOTAL-CONTENT figure and is therefore not a stricter version of the 1 mg/kg extractable ceiling published here; the two measure different quantities and both bind. A component returning total cadmium above 40 mg/kg is escalated as a jurisdiction-specific regulatory hard stop under the HMTc legal-violation rule even where the extractable result conforms, pending scope-resolved re-ingest of the Washington row. Where the article incorporates a battery or a battery-powered module — a vibration unit, a sound or music module, a night light, a powered mobile or a powered rocker — the battery is a distinct regulated article with its own instrument, and its limits are not this row's. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 restricts cadmium in a portable battery whether or not incorporated into an appliance (register row eu_batteries_2023_cd_portable_batteries_20000, 20 mg/kg) and mercury in a battery (register row eu_batteries_2023_thg_batteries_5000, 5 mg/kg), both expressed on the weight of the battery. Both are stricter than the values published here and both are recorded as companion obligations on the battery in a battery-by-weight basis; the battery is never homogenised into an accessible-component sample and its instrument is never merged into this row's extractable ceiling. Where the article carries no battery and no powered module the obligation does not arise.

rows.basis: total lead content of the product as placed on the market (consumer-chemical product-content basis; disclosed read-across)
rows.rationale: Program-wide consistency ruling (2026-08-17): the German BVL 2017 orientation values are treated as SELECTABLE anchors across HMTc. The live Category 15 standard tags three of these same register rows regulatory-alignment, and Categories 2, 13, 14 and 20 bind them directly, so the earlier Category 19 position that a register status of 'guidance impurity limit' makes them unselectable contradicted five sibling categories on the identical rows, and did so in the looser direction (5x on lead, 50x on cadmium, 4x on total arsenic, 10x on total mercury). BVL is a single coherent sovereign consumer-chemical regime covering all four toxics, so reading it across preserves this category's own rule of adopting one coherent regime per analyte rather than picking the lowest number across regimes. The China NMPA 2015 value previously published is retained as a named looser comparator. Whether a national enforcement orientation value ranks as a sovereign maximum level is a genuine governance question, recorded for ratification as OI-20260817-bvl-selectability-ruling; until it is ruled on, every category states the same rule. Previously bound: cn_nmpa2015_pb_cosmetics_10.

rows.basis: total nickel content of the product as placed on the market (consumer-chemical product-content basis; disclosed read-across)
rows.rationale: Nickel is the analyte this category's exposure pathway is built around: nickel is a confirmed dermal sensitiser, and a residue deposited on fabric that is then worn is prolonged, repeated dermal contact. No sovereign sets a nickel maximum for a laundry or fabric-care product. Instruments checked: China GB 14930.1-2022 (the only sovereign detergent contaminant standard in the register; scope is Type A detergents used directly for food cleaning and Type B detergents for tableware and food-contact tools, equipment, packaging and containers, and it sets a total-arsenic ceiling only); China NMPA 2015 Safety and Technical Standards for Cosmetics Table 2 (lead, arsenic, mercury, cadmium); Korea MFDS Notice 2025-63 and its predecessor Notice 2024-9 (lead, cadmium, nickel, antimony, arsenic, mercury); Germany BVL 2017 technically-avoidable heavy metals in cosmetics (lead, cadmium, mercury, arsenic, antimony); Health Canada cosmetic heavy-metal impurity limits; the ASEAN Cosmetic Directive Annex (2019) and the Malaysia NPRA, Singapore HSA, Indonesia BPOM, Taiwan MoHW and New Zealand cosmetic group-standard equivalents; EAEU TR CU 009/2011; EU REACH Annex XVII entry 20 (organotin), entry 23 (cadmium in listed polymers and paints), entry 47 as amended by Regulation (EU) 301/2014 (Cr(VI) in skin-contact leather), entry 72 with Appendix 12 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2018/1513 (lead, cadmium, arsenic and Cr(VI) in consumer clothing and skin-contact textiles) and entry 75 under Regulation (EU) 2020/2081 (tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures); EU Directive 2009/48/EC toy-safety migration limits; EU RoHS 2011/65/EU; and the dietary contaminant regimes (EU 2023/915, EU 2024/1987, Codex CXS 193, US FDA, FSANZ, Health Canada, UK, Hong Kong Cap. 132V), which are inapplicable both on scope and on basis. China NMPA 2015 Table 2 — the instrument that anchors lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury on this row — sets no nickel limit at all, so for nickel the nearest applicable sovereign consumer-chemical value is the Korean statutory limit, which is the only regime in the register that sets one. The Korean instrument writes a product-form split (eye make-up 35, colour make-up 30, all other cosmetic products 10 mg/kg); the split is preserved and the "all other products" tier is the applicable one, because a fabric-care product is not a decorative make-up. A single coherent sovereign regime is read across per analyte rather than the lowest number picked across regimes, which would build a ceiling no sovereign enforces. China NMPA 2015 Table 2 is the strictest coherent STATUTORY consumer-chemical regime for lead, cadmium, total arsenic and total mercury (Korea MFDS is looser on lead at 20 and on total arsenic at 10 mg/kg; the ASEAN, Health Canada and Germany BVL values are cosmetics-scoped administrative or technical-avoidability findings rather than statutory maximum levels, and are on-scope-only under governance ruling GR-2026-08-17-BVL), and the same instrument is already the published read-across anchor of the live Category 12 (Household Cleaning and Dishwashing) standard for the identical logical move, verified 2026-08-17 against the live page https://heavymetalcertified.com/standards/all-purpose-cleaners (Category 12 standard version 1.0, dated 2026-08-13), which publishes lead 10, cadmium 5, total arsenic 2 and total mercury 1 mg/kg with provenance read-across and binding source China Safety and Technical Standards for Cosmetics (2015, NMPA), the values carried by register rows cn_nmpa2015_pb_cosmetics_10, cn_nmpa2015_cd_cosmetics_5, cn_nmpa2015_tas_cosmetics_2 and cn_nmpa2015_thg_cosmetics_1, and which states the same single-coherent-regime rule; the Category 12 records were rendered by a dedicated certification-repository builder rather than through this repository's compiled-standards manifest, so the live page and not an in-repo artifact is the citation a reader checks. Nickel is not regulated by the Chinese instrument at all, so for nickel the nearest applicable sovereign consumer-chemical value is the Korean statutory limit; that is the only regime in the register that sets one, and no number in this row was chosen by comparing outcomes. EU REACH Annex XVII entry 27 restricts nickel RELEASE from articles in prolonged skin contact rather than nickel content in a mixture and is not carried in the register as a content limit, so it is not read across; EU REACH Annex XVII entry 72 Appendix 12 sets no nickel row for consumer textiles, so no downstream fabric content ceiling is available for this analyte. EU REACH Annex XVII entry 75 (Regulation (EU) 2020/2081) sets the strictest sovereign consumer-mixture metal limits in the register (lead 0.7, cadmium 0.5, total arsenic 0.5, mercury 0.5, Cr(VI) 0.5 and nickel 5 mg/kg), but its scope is mixtures for tattooing and permanent make-up, an intradermal-injection route. Reading an injected-mixture ceiling across to a rinse-off or fabric-deposited topical product would conflate exposure routes, and its register basis is a tattoo/permanent-make-up mixture basis that this row's basis_guard excludes. Nickel is measured in soaps, detergents and household hygienic products in the routed corpus and is named for laundry care by greenseal2020-gs51-laundry-care-products, nydec2020-cleansing-product-disclosure-bmp and ecetoc1992-tr045-ni-co-cr-consumer-products, so a not-material determination is unavailable on the facts. Complete disposition of the stricter rows the compiler's audit safety-net surfaces for this row, none of which is adopted. (1) de_bvl2017_pb_cosmetics_general_2000 (2 mg/kg), de_bvl2017_cd_cosmetics_general_100 (0.1), de_bvl2017_tas_cosmetics_general_500 (0.5) and de_bvl2017_thg_cosmetics_general_100 (0.1): Germany BVL 2017 technical-avoidability findings for cosmetic manufacture, register status 'guidance impurity limit', dispositioned under HMTc governance ruling GR-2026-08-17-BVL as on-scope-only and therefore unavailable as a read-across anchor for a non-cosmetic product class. The ruling is stated in full in this configuration's credible_note and is the single programme-wide rule the live Category 15 (Feminine Care) standard and this category both now state; Category 15 binds these same four BVL rows because its rows ARE cosmetics, and every number Category 15 publishes is unaffected by the ruling. (2) hc_cosmetic_cd_3ppm (3 mg/kg): a Health Canada cosmetic impurity guidance limit, excluded for the same reason, and adopting it for cadmium alone would additionally mix regimes. (3) eu_2018_1513_pb_consumer_textiles_1mgkg, eu_2018_1513_cd_consumer_textiles_1mgkg and eu_2018_1513_tas_consumer_textiles_1mgkg (1 mg/kg each): the EU consumer-textile restriction, which governs the FABRIC and not the product applied to it, on a homogeneous-material-after-extraction basis rather than this row's product-content basis; carried as a downstream constraint and companion limit, and blocked from anchoring by the row's basis_guard. The audit_exclude_scope on this row removes only the oral/mucosal toothpaste tier, tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures, and colour-additive and colourant specifications; against the register as built it suppresses no row that the audit scope would otherwise surface, so nothing was excluded to make this list shorter. (4) Two further stricter rows exist that the compiler's audit safety-net structurally CANNOT surface, because it filters to the credible-regulator set, and they are therefore recorded by hand rather than left invisible. asean2019_th_cd_cosmetic_products_3000 (Thailand, cadmium 3 mg/kg) is a guidance impurity limit and falls to the same reasoning as the Health Canada value. eaeu_trcu009_2011_pb_natural_raw_material_cosmetics_5mgkg (EAEU, lead 5 mg/kg) is the only STATUTORY row anywhere in the consumer-chemical product-content basis family that is stricter than an anchor adopted here, and it is not adopted for three reasons: the EAEU is not in the HMTc credible-regulator set and admitting it is a governance ruling outside this derivation; its scope is formulation-conditioned (perfumery-cosmetic products containing more than 1 per cent natural plant or natural mineral raw material) rather than the general product tier, and that condition would be satisfied by some but not all rows in this category, which would fracture the category on a formulation test no sovereign wrote for laundry products; and the EAEU instrument does not dominate the adopted regime, since it is stricter on lead (5 against 10 mg/kg) but LOOSER on total arsenic (5 against 2 mg/kg), identical on mercury and silent on cadmium, so taking its lead value while keeping the Chinese arsenic value would compose a ceiling no sovereign enforces, which is precisely what the single-coherent-regime discipline exists to prevent. This enumeration is the output of a credible-set-blind sweep of every one of the 80 register rows the basis_guard admits, not of the automated scan alone, and it is complete as of this build. Verification method: total nickel by microwave-assisted closed-vessel acid digestion (HNO3/H2O2, with a hydrofluoric-acid or lithium-metaborate fusion step where an aluminosilicate, silicate or clay mineral phase is present) followed by ICP-MS quantification against matrix-matched calibration standards, with a certified reference material and a reagent blank in every run. The sampling unit is one composite sample per production lot, drawn from the product as placed on the market, with component-level sampling of the bleaching concentrate and, for unit-dose or tablet formats, the film, coating or wrapper, each sampled and tested as a distinct component. Disposition rule, stated identically in every cell and every row of this category: the published ceiling applies to EACH sampled component independently, and the lot fails if ANY single component result is at or above the ceiling. The whole-article composite is additionally measured and reported on the lot record, but the composite is never the basis of the pass or fail determination, because diluting a contaminated component in the mass of the rest of the article does not reduce the exposure that component delivers to the skin it contacts. A lot in which every component is inside the ceiling, but in which any component sits outside the running per-row control band, is escalated to ALARA review with raw-material trace-back to the specific component that moved.
