rows.basis: Finished cosmetic total content as placed on market (ug/kg of product as sold); technically-unavoidable-impurity basis. Not migration, not leachate, not dietary, not an ingredient purity specification.
rows.rationale: Korea MFDS is the ONLY authority in the register that publishes a nickel maximum for a finished cosmetic, and the instrument tiers it by product class: eye makeup 35000 ug/kg, colour makeup 30000, all other cosmetics 10000. Method step 4 requires the government's own product-form split to be preserved, so the applicable branch is selected rather than the strictest branch overall. Both register transpositions of the instrument (MFDS Notice 2024-9 and Notice 2025-63) are named and carry identical values, which is the cross-edition check. No other credible authority publishes a cosmetic nickel ceiling: the EU prohibits nickel compounds as intentional cosmetic ingredients under Regulation 1223/2009 Annex II without setting a numeric trace maximum, and Germany's BVL 2017 table covers only lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury and antimony. This row is neither an eye-makeup nor a colour-makeup product, so the 10000 ug/kg branch is the applicable cell and it binds. Where the mapping of an HMTc row onto the Korean product classes is not unambiguous, or where a row's forms straddle two branches, HMTc takes the stricter branch rather than claiming the looser one.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market — total element content per unit mass of undiluted product as sold (µg/kg). Not a dietary basis, not a migration or leachate basis, and no use-pattern dilution credit.
rows.rationale: BVL 2017 Table 1 (German Federal Office of Consumer Protection and Food Safety, with the Länder cosmetics working group) publishes the technically avoidable heavy-metal content of cosmetic products in general; lead is 2.0 mg/kg, and a content above the table is treated as technically avoidable under good manufacturing practice. Its status is a federal-authority guidance value rather than a statute, and it is disclosed as such, but it is the strictest published sovereign finished-cosmetic lead maximum and Method v2.0 takes the strictest applicable value. The named comparator set shows how far the binding sits below the field: Health Canada, China NMPA 2015 and Taiwan MOHW 2024 are five times looser at 10 mg/kg; Korea, ASEAN and its Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia transpositions, and Kenya KS 2937:2021 are ten times looser at 20 mg/kg; Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations threshold is 125 times looser at 250 mg/kg. Two sovereign cosmetic lead values in the register are stricter than the binding — the BVL 2017 toothpaste tier at 500 µg/kg and Washington State's Toxics-Free Cosmetics Act toothpaste limit at 1000 µg/kg — and the compiler's stricter-unselected audit flags both on every row of this category. Neither is applicable. Both are scoped by their own instruments to toothpaste, a dentifrice that sits on the oral mucosa and is partly swallowed; that ingestion pathway is the stated reason the toothpaste tier is tighter. Categories 20 and 2 carry the dentifrice forms and use those instruments. A shampoo, body wash, scrub or depilatory has no ingestion pathway inside either instrument's scope, so reading a toothpaste tier onto a hair or body rinse-off product would have HMTc inventing a stricter number that no government set for this form. Method v2.0 forbids that as squarely as it forbids inventing a looser one: applicability is a real constraint, and the strictest APPLICABLE value governs. The compiler's audit also flags EU REACH Annex XVII entry 75, which sets 700 µg/kg for lead in mixtures placed on the market for tattooing and permanent make-up. That value is stricter than the binding and is deliberately not adopted: the instrument governs a mixture INJECTED INTO THE DERMIS, on a 'mixture for tattooing or permanent make-up by weight' basis, and a rinse-off shampoo or body wash is not such a mixture on any reading of the entry. The row is held out by this row's basis_guard as well as on scope. It is surfaced rather than filtered out of the scan so that the record shows it was found and disposed of, not missed. Colour-additive and colourant purity specifications (21 CFR 73 and 74, the New Zealand and Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles, the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 permitted-colours entries, the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant entries) are raw-material ingredient specifications, not finished-product maxima. They are held out of every cell by this row's basis_guard, and none of them is in any case stricter than the binding for this analyte.

Mercury used as an intentional skin-lightening active, and the eye-area thiomersal and phenylmercuric preservative allowances in the India, Hong Kong and South Africa instruments, are ingredient permissions rather than contaminant ceilings; HMTc does not adopt them, and a rinse-off product formulated with an intentional mercury ingredient is not certifiable at all. Colour-additive and colourant purity specifications (21 CFR 73 and 74, the New Zealand and Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles, the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 permitted-colours entries, the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant entries) are raw-material ingredient specifications, not finished-product maxima. rows.rationale: Korea is the only jurisdiction in the register that sets a nickel content limit for finished cosmetics, and it tiers it by form: 10 µg/g for cosmetic products other than eye makeup and colour cosmetics, 30 µg/g for colour makeup, 35 µg/g for eye makeup. Every Category 14 form is a cleansing, conditioning, shaving, depilatory or hair-colouring preparation and none is an eye-makeup or colour-makeup product in the MFDS product taxonomy, so the strictest of the three tiers — 10 µg/g — is the directly applicable one, not a read-across. Korea MFDS Notice 2025-63 carries the same 10 µg/g value for the same scope and corroborates it; it is not named as a candidate because its register note contradicts its own value (the note reads '1 microgram/g = 1000 ug/kg' against a stored value of 10000 µg/kg), and a litigation-facing citation should not carry that discrepancy forward. The EU REACH restriction on nickel in tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures (5000 µg/kg) is stricter but governs a mixture injected into the dermis, a different form on a different basis, and is held out by this row's basis_guard. Nickel is a leading contact sensitiser, so the programme additionally holds it under ALARA post-publication and treats the published ceiling as an outer bound rather than a target.

rows.basis: read-across from the strictest credible animal-derived lead ML (as consumed)
rows.rationale: Lead is the priority analyte and a NOT-MATERIAL determination is REJECTED on the bone-leaching evidence. Bone is the body's principal lead reservoir (the skeleton holds the large majority of an animal's lifetime lead burden), and published analyses have reported measurably elevated lead in bone broth relative to the water it is made from, consistent with lead partitioning from bone into the broth during prolonged (and frequently vinegar-acidulated) simmering. No credible regulator sets a maximum level for bone broth, bone, gelatin or collagen (the only gelatin and meat-extract MLs on record are non-credible-tier and far looser, 2000 to 7000 ug/kg, so they are not used), so the nearest credible animal-derived anchor is adopted by read-across at 100 ug/kg. v1.2 CORRECTS THE AUDIT-TRAIL ARGUMENT. v1.1 stated the accumulating-tissue analog as a single figure, 'the looser edible-offal ML (500 ug/kg)', and framed the choice as passing over 500 in favour of 100. That overstated the gap by up to fivefold and is not true in every credible jurisdiction. The offal ladder is hk_cap132v_pb_edible-offal-of-poultry_100 at 100, hk_cap132v_pb_edible-offal-of-pig_150 at 150, hk_cap132v_pb_edible-offal-of-cattle_200 at 200 and aunz_sch19_pb_offal_500 at 500, so under Cap. 132V the poultry offal value EQUALS the adopted binding and there is no gap at all for a chicken bone broth. Nothing stricter is applicable: the by-hand scan of every credible live non-infant lead row below 100 ug/kg returns only drinking-water and bottled-water parametric values (5 to 10 ug/kg), the EU 10/2011 plastics specific migration limit (10), and the Cap. 132V Milk and Secondary milk products rows (20 each), none of which is an animal-tissue component of a bone broth. The Cap. 132V packaged-drinking-water and natural-mineral-water rows sit in the SAME basis string as Cap. 132V's food rows ('food as listed in Cap 132V Part 2 Schedule'), so this row's basis_guard does NOT filter them out even though it does filter the EU 2020/2184, US EPA, US 21 CFR 165.110 and Health Canada water instruments, whose basis strings are distinct. v1.2 corrects the earlier claim that the guard stops packaged-water values generally: the Cap. 132V water rows are excluded by DETERMINATION, not by the guard, and they are now named by id on every cell they could otherwise be read as binding. The determination: packaged drinking water and natural mineral water are a distinct beverage commodity, regulated as the sole daily hydration source and consumed by the litre, and formulation water is an INPUT SPECIFICATION rather than a principal component of the finished product. Certified lines are required to use potable water meeting the applicable national drinking-water standard, verified on the ingredient-water specification, rather than by re-deriving the composite ceiling from a water instrument. Applying a water parametric value as a food-content ceiling would hold a soup or a broth to a limit set for a product with a completely different daily intake, which no sovereign has done. NON-COMPONENT DISPOSITION, run by hand across the whole register rather than through the row's scope regex, because a scope regex can only hide what it does not match. Every credible, live, non-infant, same-basis register row STRICTER than this cell's published value that is not an animal-tissue component is named in this cell's companion set and declined here, by class. (d) RENDERED FATS: the Cap. 132V edible-fats-and-oils and fat-spread rows (lead 80, total arsenic 100). Adhering and rendered fat is skimmed rather than sold, and edible fats and oils certify under HMTc Category 30 in their own basis. Instruments checked: Commission Regulation (EU) 2024/1987 amending 2023/915, whose nickel maximum levels are plant-matrix only (fruiting vegetables 400, brassica 500, leafy vegetables 500, fruit/vegetable juices and nectars 250, cereals 800, root/tuber/bulb vegetables 900, legume vegetables 1000, pulses 4000, chocolate and cocoa products 2500 to 7000 ug/kg) plus infant-scoped rows that are Category 1 scope; EU 2023/915 itself (no nickel entry before the 2024/1987 amendment); Codex CXS 193 (no nickel entry); FSANZ Schedule 19 (no nickel entry); Hong Kong Cap. 132V Part 2 Schedule, whose only nickel rows are packaged-drinking-water and natural-mineral-water parametric values (70 and 20 ug/kg) in a different basis family that this row's basis_guard refuses; US FDA (bottled-water parametric value 100 ug/kg only); Health Canada and UK dietary instruments (no nickel ML). v1.2 CORRECTS A CITATION ERROR: v1.1 attributed the nickel maximum levels to 'EU 2024/1252', an unrelated instrument. Every nickel row in the register is Commission Regulation (EU) 2024/1987 (regulation_page regulations/eu-2024-1987-nickel-maximum-levels). The substantive conclusion is unchanged and was independently re-verified: every credible nickel food row is plant-matrix, infant formula, baby food or chocolate, so none reaches an animal-derived stock and no near-neighbour read-across is supportable. Nickel is therefore a mandatory reported cell with no invented ceiling; Tier-2 analyte. INGREDIENT-WATER RULING, and a correction to what the basis_guard can actually do. The Cap. 132V packaged-drinking-water and natural-mineral-water rows sit in the SAME basis string as Cap. 132V's food rows ('food as listed in Cap 132V Part 2 Schedule'), so this row's basis_guard does NOT filter them out even though it does filter the EU 2020/2184, US EPA, US 21 CFR 165.110 and Health Canada water instruments, whose basis strings are distinct. v1.2 corrects the earlier claim that the guard stops packaged-water values generally: the Cap. 132V water rows are excluded by DETERMINATION, not by the guard, and they are now named by id on every cell they could otherwise be read as binding. The determination: packaged drinking water and natural mineral water are a distinct beverage commodity, regulated as the sole daily hydration source and consumed by the litre, and formulation water is an INPUT SPECIFICATION rather than a principal component of the finished product. Certified lines are required to use potable water meeting the applicable national drinking-water standard, verified on the ingredient-water specification, rather than by re-deriving the composite ceiling from a water instrument. Applying a water parametric value as a food-content ceiling would hold a soup or a broth to a limit set for a product with a completely different daily intake, which no sovereign has done.

rows.basis: as_consumed
rows.rationale: Inorganic tin is a tinplate migration pathway confined to the canned form; carton (RTD), frozen and refrigerated bone broth have no tin source, so no ceiling is asserted for them. A CANNED bone broth is verified against the canned-foods tin ML, on which three credible regulators converge at 250 mg/kg (250000 ug/kg): Codex CXS 193 (canned foods), FSANZ Schedule 19 (all canned foods) and HK Cap. 132V (canned food other than canned beverages). Instruments checked for a non-canned form: EU 2023/915 (tin appears only as canned-food and canned-beverage MLs), Codex CXS 193, FSANZ Schedule 19, Cap. 132V, US FDA, Health Canada and UK dietary instruments; none sets a tin maximum level for a broth outside a can. The Cap. 132V canned-beverage row (150 mg/kg) is stricter but is not adopted: a ready-to-drink carton broth is not a canned beverage and has no tinplate contact. THE STRICTEST APPLICABLE CANNED-FOOD TIN ML IS THE EU ROW AT 200 mg/kg, NOT THE 250 mg/kg FIGURE v1.1 NAMED. Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 sets tin at 200000 ug/kg (200 mg/kg) for canned foods other than canned beverages, except canned dried and canned powdered products (eu2023_sn_canned_foods_200000, basis product as placed on the market). It is stricter than the three rows v1.1 named as converging at 250 mg/kg (codex_cxs193_sn_canned_250000, aunz_sch19_sn_canned_250000, hk_cap132v_sn_canned-food-other-than-canned-beverages_250000), it is a credible-regulator maximum level in a basis this row accepts, and it was neither named nor dispositioned. This defect was found by hand during the v1.2 remediation and NOT by the compiler safety-net, because the soups row's audit_exclude_scope contained the term `beverage`, which matched the phrase 'canned beverages' inside the EU row's own scope string and suppressed it from every scan; the same class of regex self-defeat the v1.2 audit identified elsewhere. The term is removed. The canned form is verified against the EU value, and the EU instrument's own carve-out for canned dried and canned powdered products is independent confirmation that a tin maximum level does not reach a dry soup mix or a bouillon powder. Stricter still, and disclosed rather than adopted because they reach a different form: canned beverages at 100 mg/kg (eu2023_sn_canned_beverages_100000) and at 150 mg/kg (hk_cap132v_sn_canned-beverages_150000). Where a certified product is a canned drinkable broth presented as a beverage rather than a canned food, the canned-beverage value is the applicable one and the stricter of the two applicable rows governs; no single number is asserted across forms.

rows.basis: as_consumed
rows.rationale: No credible regulator sets an aluminium maximum level for bone broth, for any animal-derived stock, or for any animal-tissue component of one. Instruments checked: EU 2023/915 and EU 2024/1987 (no aluminium entry), Codex CXS 193 (no aluminium entry), FSANZ Schedule 19 (aluminium appears only as infant-formula MLs of 500 and 1000 ug/kg, which are Category 1 scope), Hong Kong Cap. 132V Part 2 Schedule (no aluminium entry), and US FDA, Health Canada and UK dietary instruments (no aluminium ML). Aluminium reaches the credible register only in basis families that cannot anchor a food-content cell: drinking-water parametric values (EU 2020/2184 and US 21 CFR 165.110 at 200 ug/L, Health Canada at 2900 ug/L), food-contact-material specific migration limits (EU 10/2011, a migration figure into a simulant), and toy migration limits. Permitted-additive maxima for aluminium-containing additives exist only in non-credible-tier instruments and are additive-use levels rather than contaminant ceilings. Aluminium is therefore a mandatory reported cell with no invented ceiling; Tier-2 analyte.

rows.basis: read-across from the sovereign total-chromium animal-meat ML (Cap. 132V, food as sold, applied at face value to the as-consumed broth)
rows.rationale: v1.1 recorded this cell as a bare control on the statement that no credible regulator sets a total-chromium maximum level for bone broth. THAT STATEMENT IS FALSE, and it is the same statement that v1.1 itself identified as false and corrected on the other two rows of this category: both composite rows carry the sentence 'v1.0 recorded this cell as a bare control on the statement that no credible regulator sets a total-chromium maximum level ... That statement is false following Hong Kong's admission to the credible-regulator set on 2026-08-17.' Cap. 132V Part 2 Schedule item 7 sets total chromium at 1.0 mg/kg (1000 ug/kg) for Meat of animal and for Meat of poultry. A published standard that retains, on a live row, a factual claim it documents as false elsewhere in the same compiled directory is the single easiest thing for opposing counsel to put in front of a jury, so the falsehood is corrected rather than preserved and the v1.1 note that overclaimed the correction is itself corrected (see _doc_v1_1 and _doc_v1_2). Cap. 132V Note 1 excludes bone from these commodities, so this is a disclosed READ-ACROSS from the nearest applicable sovereign animal-tissue value, ruled once for this row and applied identically to total arsenic and total mercury. The looser and stricter Cap. 132V total-chromium rows are disclosed and not adopted for opposite reasons: meat of poultry at 1000 is equal, and vegetables other than pulses at 500 and pulses, cereals and fish at 1000 are not components of an animal-bone stock (they bind the two composite rows instead). Nothing stricter is applicable: the by-hand scan of every credible live non-infant total-chromium row below 1000 ug/kg returns the EU 10/2011 plastics specific migration limit (10), drinking-water, bottled-water and natural-mineral-water parametric values (25 to 100), and the Cap. 132V vegetable row (500), none of which is an animal-tissue component and all of which the basis_guard would refuse. IT PUBLISHES AS A SCREEN: dietary chromium is overwhelmingly trivalent (an essential nutrient) and the health-relevant hexavalent species is separately determined not material in a cooked, wet, protein-rich broth (Cr-VI cell, speciation-bounded), so the value is not protective as a standalone total-element ceiling. Total chromium remains mandatory on every lot. ESCALATION: a result approaching the screen value is treated as a stainless-steel equipment-leaching signal, investigated against kettle and transfer-line contact time and temperature (a bone broth simmers for many hours, which is the longest hot-metal contact of any row in this category), with a confirmatory second lot before release, and not as a toxicological finding. rows.rationale: Lead at 5 µg/L is the strictest applicable sovereign maximum and it is corroborated four ways: the EU Drinking Water Directive Annex I Part B parametric value, the FDA bottled-water allowable level at 21 CFR 165.110 (0.005 mg/L), the Health Canada maximum acceptable concentration and the NHMRC health-based guideline value. The Directive's 5 µg/L is its end-state value, which member states must meet by 12 January 2036 and below which the transitional value of 10 µg/L applies until then; HMTc adopts the end-state value now, so this cell is stricter than currently-enforced EU practice, but the FDA value of 5 µg/L is in force today and is independently sufficient to compel the number. The looser 10 µg/L values (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, the WHO provisional guideline value, and the Codex/mineral-water family) are named in the candidate set and are not selected because the method takes the strictest applicable value.

rows.basis: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
rows.rationale: Cadmium at 2 µg/L is the NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines health-based guideline value (0.002 mg/L, nhmrc2025_cd_drinking_water_2), the strictest cadmium value any government sets for water. It is published as a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS and not as a direct maximum for this product form, and the reason is stated rather than left to inference. The register records that instrument's product scope as 'drinking water' and its note describes it as a health-based guideline value; the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines are a non-statutory guideline for drinking-water supplies, and Australia regulates packaged water not under the ADWG but under the FSANZ Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code. No FSANZ packaged-water metals row exists in the register: of the AU, NZ and AU-NZ rows, the only water-scoped entries are the eight NHMRC drinking-water guideline values, and Schedule 19 is represented only by commodity rows (formula, cereals, fish, salt and the like). The Australian packaged-water cadmium cell is therefore absent from the register and is logged as a register gap, in the same way Commission Directive 2003/40/EC is logged on the mineral-water row. The category's two textual packaged-water bridges do not carry this instrument either: FDA 21 CFR 165.110(b)(4)(iii) incorporates the EPA maximum contaminant levels (cadmium 5 µg/L) and EU Directive 2020/2184's scope reaches water put into bottles or containers (cadmium 5 µg/L), and neither reaches an Australian guideline. Absence of a packaged-product carve-out is not affirmative scope, so the earlier regulatory-alignment tag overstated what this instrument does. WHAT THE INSTRUMENTS SET FOR THE EXACT CELL IS STATED OPENLY, because the read-across runs in the protective direction and nothing is served by concealing it: the strictest maximum level any government sets for cadmium in this exact packaged-water form is 3 µg/L, then 5 µg/L (EU Drinking Water Directive eu20202184_cd_drinking_water_5, FDA 21 CFR 165.110 fda21cfr165110_cd_bottled_water_5, EPA MCL epa2018_cd_drinking_water_5, California us_ca_swrcb_2024_cd_cadmium_mcl_5ugl), then 7 µg/L (Health Canada healthcanada2025_cd_drinking_water_7). HMTc publishes the stricter 2 µg/L: the substance and the basis are identical, HMTc does not relax a published limit toward a looser instrument, and the value is unchanged from the earlier compilation. Only the provenance tag is corrected, from regulatory-alignment to read-across, so that the record never claims a sovereign packaged-water maximum that no sovereign has written. The 3 µg/L tier for this exact form is Hong Kong Cap 132V (hk_cap132v_cd_bottled-or-packaged-drinking-waters-other-than-natural_3), Israel FCS 2016 (il_fcs2016_cd_17_bottled_drinking_water_and_mineral_water_3) and Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011 (vn_qcvn8_2_2011_cd_bottled-water_3), with the WHO guideline value (who2022_cd_drinking_water_3) at the same figure.

rows.basis: as_consumed
rows.rationale: Mercury in sealed packaged drinking water is present essentially as inorganic Hg(II). Methylation is a microbial process requiring anaerobic sulfate- or iron-reducing activity in sediment or biota; it does not occur in a treated, filtered, disinfected and sealed packaged-water matrix, and there is no aquatic food chain in the product to bioaccumulate methylmercury. Methylmercury is in any event a component of total mercury, so it is bounded by identity at the published total-mercury ceiling of 1 µg/L. No separate methylmercury ceiling is published.

rows.basis: as_consumed
rows.rationale: No sovereign sets a tin maximum for drinking water, bottled water or natural mineral water. The drinking-water instrument family carries no tin parameter at all (EU Directive 2020/2184 Annex I Parts B and C; US EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations; US FDA 21 CFR 165.110 standards of quality; Health Canada; NHMRC; WHO), and none of the national food-schedule packaged-water lines (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, India FSSAI 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Chile Decreto 977/1996, Fiji FSR 2009) carries a tin entry for water. A read-across is not supportable: the nearest sovereign tin maxima are the canned-food and canned-beverage maximum levels, which exist to bound dissolution of tin from a tinplate container wall into an acidic canned matrix, and the canned-beverage value (100 mg/kg inorganic tin) sits roughly four orders of magnitude above anything a packaged water can plausibly contain, so importing it would publish a ceiling that functions as no limit at all. The dominant packaging for this category (PET, HDPE, glass, aluminium) contains no tin. Still bottled water is occasionally presented in aluminium or tin-free steel cans, neither of which is a tin source. Tin therefore remains a mandatory control cell; no number is invented.

rows.rationale: Aluminium at 200 µg/L is the strictest applicable sovereign value and is disclosed here as a non-health-based parameter rather than a toxicological line: it is an Annex I Part C INDICATOR parameter in the EU Drinking Water Directive, a SECONDARY (aesthetically based) allowable level at FDA 21 CFR 165.110, and an AESTHETIC guideline for acid-soluble aluminium in the NHMRC guidelines. The health-based alternatives are far looser (Health Canada's maximum acceptable concentration of 2900 µg/L; California's MCL of 1000 µg/L), so adopting 200 µg/L is the strictest applicable treatment and is materially protective. Its aesthetic derivation is stated rather than concealed because the label of the parameter, not only its number, is part of the provenance.

rows.basis: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
rows.rationale: Total chromium at 25 µg/L is the EU Drinking Water Directive Annex I Part B parametric value, the strictest applicable sovereign maximum; it is the Directive's end-state value, to be met by 12 January 2036, with a transitional value of 50 µg/L in force until then. The 50 µg/L tier (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Health Canada, WHO, California) and the 100 µg/L tier (EPA MCL, FDA 21 CFR 165.110) are named and not selected. This cell is published as a FIRM limit rather than as a screen, which is a deliberate departure from the HMTc default for total chromium and is compelled by the instruments themselves: in a food matrix total chromium is dominated by nutritionally benign Cr(III) and is a poor proxy for the health-relevant species, but the drinking-water instruments regulate total chromium precisely because the two species interconvert in aqueous media, and the Health Canada entry states in terms that the maximum acceptable concentration protects against chromium(VI) effects and is established for total chromium. The hexavalent species is not displaced: it is published separately at 10 µg/L.

rows.basis: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
rows.rationale: The exact cell is unregulated, and the record says so on its face rather than asserting a maximum no government has written for this product form. No jurisdiction in the register sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum for bottled water, packaged water or natural mineral water, and neither of the two textual packaged-water bridges this category relies on reaches the species: FDA 21 CFR 165.110(b)(4)(iii) incorporates the EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulation maximum contaminant levels and EPA sets no hexavalent-chromium MCL, and EU Directive 2020/2184 Annex I carries no hexavalent-chromium parameter. The nearest applicable sovereign value is therefore the California State Water Resources Control Board Title 22 section 64431 Table 64431-A maximum contaminant level of 10 µg/L (0.01 mg/L, us_ca_swrcb_2024_cr-vi_chromium-hexavalent_mcl_10ugl), re-adopted in 2024 after health-risk and feasibility analysis, and it is carried across as a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS. Two hops are disclosed rather than argued around. First, SCOPE: the register records that instrument's product scope as 'public water systems in California', which is utility-delivered tap water and not a packaged good; HMTc has not identified, and does not cite, any California provision applying Title 22 section 64431 maximum contaminant levels to bottled water sold in the state, so this cell must not be read as an assertion that California enforces 10 µg/L against a packaged product. Second, SOVEREIGNTY: California is a sub-national government. The only alternative anywhere in the register is the NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines statement that hexavalent chromium should not exceed 50 µg/L (nhmrc2025_crvi_drinking_water_50), which is five times looser and carries the same drinking-water scope hop; it is named here and not selected because the method takes the strictest applicable value. The value is unchanged from the earlier compilation at 10 µg/L; only the provenance tag is corrected, from regulatory-alignment to read-across. HMTc publishes Cr-VI as its own cell in addition to total chromium: a hexavalent result never satisfies the total-chromium cell and a total-chromium result never satisfies this one, and the total-chromium cell on this row is a direct sovereign maximum for the product form that bounds this species from above.

rows.rationale: This is the Category 15 precedent applied to its home matrix: the BVL toothpaste tier was read across to mucosal-contact products in the live Feminine Care standard on the reasoning that oral mucosa is the closest regulated analogue to other mucosa. Here the analogy is tighter still, because the target form is itself an oral-cavity product. The read-across moves the value DOWN from the directly applicable general-cosmetic tier (2000 to 500 ug/kg), so it cannot be characterised as a convenience selection.

rows.basis: finished oral-care product as placed on market (total nickel content, ug/kg as sold) — read across from the Korean residual finished-cosmetic nickel tier
rows.rationale: Nickel is a mucosal and contact sensitiser and reaches oral-care formulations through hydrated-silica and calcium-carbonate abrasives, mineral pigments, and stainless-steel process contact, so the cell must not be left without a ceiling where a sovereign anchor exists. The exact cell (nickel in a dentifrice, rinse, whitening system or denture-care product) is unregulated in every jurisdiction surveyed, which is why the value is published as a disclosed read-across tagged 'read-across' rather than as regulatory alignment; in Korea a dentifrice is a quasi-drug rather than a cosmetic, so the Korean cosmetic tier does not reach this form by its own terms. Two Korean notices state the same three-tier allowance at identical values: Notice 2024-9 Article 6(2) (kr_mfds2024_9_ni_other_cosmetics_10ugg) and the current Notice No. 2025-63 (the named anchor). The later notice is cited so that this standard and the Category 2 children's-dentifrice standard, which anchors the same cell, cite the same current instrument rather than splitting across two Korean notices for one number. The value is 10000 ug/kg under either notice, neither register row is flagged superseded, and the 2024-9 row remains inside this row's audit scan.

rows.basis: as sold, finished product (wet weight)
rows.rationale: A canned meat product is not a separately named commodity in any credible sovereign contaminant instrument, so the exact cell is unregulated and the ceiling is a disclosed read-across from the maximum levels governing its principal components — the muscle meat of the species it is formulated from. All three credible candidate rows (Hong Kong Cap. 132V meat of cattle/pig/goat/sheep, Hong Kong meat of poultry, FSANZ Schedule 19 multi-species muscle meat excluding offal) sit at 0.1 mg/kg, so the binding value is 100 ug/kg regardless of species mix. BASIS TREATMENT, DISCLOSED IN THE DIRECTION IT ACTUALLY CUTS: the ceiling is applied to the FINISHED product as sold, in the same wet-weight basis the component maximum levels are written in, with no invented conversion factor. Applying a ceiling to the finished product rather than to its meat fraction is the LOOSER of the two available treatments, because a formulation that is part water, starch, rusk and brine can carry a higher concentration in its meat fraction than the muscle-meat maximum level itself allows. The programme does not paper over that with a claim of conservatism it has not earned; it closes the gap with a second, independent test. The meat raw material entering the formulation IS "meat of cattle, pig, goat and sheep" or "meat of poultry" within the meaning of the sovereign instruments, so those maximum levels apply to it as a commodity in their own right: every certified lot must document raw-material compliance against the named component maximum levels IN ADDITION to finished-product compliance against this ceiling, and neither test substitutes for the other. Mechanically separated meat and any lot containing edible offal (liver sausage, blood sausage, pate) is additionally screened against the sovereign offal maximum levels, which govern that ingredient but never loosen this row. BASIS OF THE BINDING INSTRUMENT, DISCLOSED: the two concurring instruments are written on DIFFERENT bases. FSANZ Schedule 19 states its maximum level for the portion ordinarily consumed (an as-consumed basis); Hong Kong Cap. 132V states the identical 0.1 mg/kg as-sold, for the edible portion after removal of bones and fat (Cap. 132V Part 2 Note 1). Because this row publishes an as-sold ceiling, the Hong Kong as-sold row is named as the binding instrument and the FSANZ row is disclosed as an independent sovereign value concurring at the same number. The published ceiling therefore rests on an instrument written in this row's own basis, and no as-consumed value is relabelled as-sold. The number is unaffected: both instruments sit at 100 ug/kg, so the strictest-applicable selection is identical either way. AUDIT DISPOSITION — hk_cap132v_pb_canned-chestnuts-and-canned-chestnuts-puree_50 (0.05 mg/kg, Hong Kong): this row surfaces in the audit scan only because this subcategory's scope regex matches the word 'canned', and it is REVIEWED AND DECLINED. It is a commodity maximum level for canned chestnuts and chestnut puree, a tree-nut food. 'Canned' names a packaging format shared with this row, not a shared product scope; a lead ceiling for a canned nut does not govern canned meat any more than the canned-fruit or canned-vegetable rows in the same instrument do. Hong Kong Cap. 132V sets no canned-meat lead maximum level, which is precisely why this row is a component read-across from the muscle-meat rows rather than a direct government lookup.

rows.basis: as_sold
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets an inorganic-arsenic maximum level for canned meat. Every credible inorganic-arsenic instrument on the register is scoped elsewhere: EU 2023/915 and EU 2025/1891 to rice, rice products, fruit juices, infant food and seafood; UK, Health Canada and US FDA to rice-based and juice matrices; Hong Kong Cap. 132V to rice and aquatic animals. A NOT-MATERIAL determination is deliberately REJECTED for this cell rather than adopted for convenience: organoarsenical feed additives (roxarsone, nitarsone, arsanilic acid, carbarsone) were lawfully administered to poultry and swine in major producing markets within living memory and are documented to leave arsenic residues in edible tissue, so the programme will not make the affirmative claim that no inorganic-arsenic pathway exists in terrestrial animal food. For the ruminant rows, where no equivalent additive history applies, the absence of that pathway does not by itself substantiate a not-material determination either, because neither a sovereign number nor a supportable near-neighbour analogue exists for the cell in any case. rows.basis: as_sold
rows.rationale: Hexavalent chromium is not stable in this matrix. A canned meat product is a wet, reducing, protein- and thiol-rich medium; Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by tissue reductants (cysteine, glutathione, ascorbate) and by the acid and heat of digestion and cooking, so a Cr(VI) figure reported on such a matrix is an artifact of the extraction chemistry of the total-chromium screen rather than a measurement of a species that persists in the food. The determination follows the same reference-method adjudication recorded for the hexavalent-chromium cell in the infant-formula category (data/workbench standards Cr-VI adjudication), applied here to an animal-tissue matrix. Hexavalent chromium is in any event a species of, and bounded by, the published total-chromium screen (Cr-VI <= total Cr). SCOPE OF THIS DETERMINATION — POULTRY CARVE-OUT: this not-material determination rests on the red-meat matrix evidence (saraiva2021, bovine meat) and is NOT extended to a poultry-containing formulation. See the poultry-product Cr-VI cell for the withdrawal record and the mahmud2011-crvi-chicken-pakistan pathway evidence behind it.

rows.basis: as sold, ug of element per kg of the emitting material (product as tested)
rows.rationale: No government anywhere sets a lead content maximum for an air freshener, plug-in evaporator, puff releaser, candle body, wax melt, oil or nebula diffuser, gel or reed diffuser, incense stick, potpourri, vacuum-cleaner fragrance additive or fragrance refill. The only sovereign heavy-metal instrument in any jurisdiction that names a product in this category is the United States CPSC prohibition on lead-cored candlewicks, 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13), mirrored by Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956; it restricts lead in the metal of a wick core and covers no other analyte and no other product form. The cell is therefore a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS, and it is taken on the axis the regulators themselves used: route of administration. Colorado's 2022 heavy-metal table and Maryland's Technical Authority Rev. 6.0 both publish a route LADDER over the same underlying matrices, with the inhalation row strictest, the oral row looser and the topical or cutaneous row looser still. The value is therefore a function of the route, not of the source matrix's chemistry, and Colorado scopes its strictest row in the instrument's own words to "inhaled product or audited product administered by metered-dose nasal spray", which describes a delivery mechanism this category shares. Maryland's own route gap is the sharpest available evidence for that reading: its inhalation-route total-chromium value is 600 ug/kg while its oral and cutaneous values for the same products are 1,100,000 ug/kg. Selected value 500 ug/kg, from Colorado (co2022 inhaled/nasal row). California DCC section 15723 independently sets the identical 0.5 ug/g for inhalable products (us_ca_dcc_2026_pb_inhalable_cannabis_0_5ugg), so two sub-national regulators converge on this value. The looser or route-unspecific values on the register are recorded and NOT selected: Maryland inhalation route 1000 ug/kg, Massachusetts all-uses protocol 500 ug/kg (equal but route-unspecific), Nevada 1200 ug/kg, Israel IMC-GMP Procedure 152 5000 ug/kg. The basis is identical to this row's native basis, micrograms of element per kilogram of product as tested, so no basis conversion, no reconstitution and no dry-to-wet adjustment is performed. The read-across is published as `read-across` and never as `regulatory-alignment`, because no instrument regulates this exact cell. Adopting it tightens rather than relaxes the applicable regulatory position: it is three to four orders of magnitude stricter than every article-content instrument that actually binds these products (RoHS lead at 1,000,000 ug/kg of homogeneous material, the candlewick-core prohibition threshold at 600,000 ug/kg of wick-core metal, REACH cadmium in polymers at 100,000 ug/kg). No occurrence, percentile, feasibility or precautionary input touched the number in either direction. Determined on the fragrance oil charge as supplied, plus the reeds or wood plug analysed as a separate component by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS with collision/reaction-cell control of the interfered masses, with the article's non-emitting components digested and screened separately per this row's component plan. DISPOSITION OF THE ADDITIONAL ANALYSES THIS CELL MANDATES. This cell requires one analysis beyond the published test, and it carries a criterion and a lot consequence, so that no mandatory analysis on this row is an obligation without an outcome. COMPONENT RESULTS, THE FIRST ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS THIS CELL MANDATES. The published ceiling of 500 ug/kg governs the emitting material and is NOT transferred to a component's bulk content: a metal collar, cap or trim, or a ceramic glaze, frit, enamel, lustre, paint or decal on the vessel is or may be substantially metal, metal-plated, metal-glazed or metal-pigmented by construction, and reading an emitting-material value against a structural component's bulk content would be exactly the basis conflation this row's basis guard exists to prevent, failing every compliant article for a metal that never enters the air. Every component result is instead dispositioned in three ordered branches, and no component result is left outside them. (a) WHERE A SOVEREIGN INSTRUMENT REACHES THE COMPONENT AND THIS ANALYTE, that instrument is the criterion. For lead and this row's components, branch (a) is EMPTY, and the instruments checked before saying so are named rather than waved at: EU RoHS 2011/65/EU is scoped to the homogeneous materials of electrical and electronic equipment and this row carries no powered sub-assembly; Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 on batteries is scoped to batteries and this row contains none; REACH Annex XVII entry 63 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2015/628 (eu_2015_628_pb_mouthable_general_public_articles_0_05pct) reaches only articles supplied to the general public that may be placed in the mouth by children; Regulation (EU) 2018/1513 reaches consumer clothing and skin-contact textiles and does not reach a packaging, sachet or decorative textile that is not worn; the EU Toy Safety Directive 2009/48/EC with EN 71-3, the CPSIA surface-coating limit and the Canadian and Australian toy-coating limits reach accessible toy material and toy surface coatings, and none of these articles is a toy; 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13) reaches only the metal of a candlewick core and this row has no wick core; the food-contact ceramic, glassware and enamelware instruments reach only articles intended to come into contact with food. Every component result on this row therefore falls to branch (b) or branch (c), and neither leaves a result without a criterion or without a lot consequence. (b) WHERE THE COMPONENT IS IN THE EMISSION PATH (the rattan reeds, fibre sticks or wood plug, the inner surface of the vessel with any glaze, frit, enamel or lustre the oil wets, the collar and the closure liner), the criterion is the published ceiling itself, applied where its basis makes it meaningful: the test is performed on emitting material sampled from the finished, filled and assembled article rather than from a pre-fill bulk batch, at the end of the declared shelf life at the declared storage conditions, or after the declared maximum in-use period with the reeds in place, whichever is the more demanding, so that any lead transferred out of an emission-path component into the emitting material is carried into the published result rather than escaping it. An emitting-material result at or above 500 ug/kg fails the lot. A rising component result while the emitting material stays below the ceiling does not by itself fail the lot and falls to branch (c). (c) OTHERWISE, for a component outside the emission path that no sovereign instrument reaches for lead, the component result is dispositioned under the HMTc control-and-escalation rule, in the same terms this row's control cells already use: the result is held to ALARA against the manufacturer's demonstrated process capability for that formulation and component set; a result outside that capability band, or an unexplained step change between lots, triggers CAPA and raw-material traceback to the fragrance and carrier-solvent supplier, the reed or wood supplier, the vessel and glaze maker, the closure and liner supplier and the dye supplier; a confirmed uncontrolled source blocks certification until it is removed or substituted; and the analyte goes onto priority surveillance for this row. No component ceiling is invented in branch (c), because no credible sovereign government publishes a total-mercury content maximum for these components in this product form, and an occupational exposure limit, an indoor-air guideline and an ambient-air standard are none of them converted into one.

rows.basis: as sold, ug of element per kg of the emitting material (product as tested)
rows.rationale: No government anywhere sets a total chromium content maximum for an air freshener, plug-in evaporator, puff releaser, candle body, wax melt, oil or nebula diffuser, gel or reed diffuser, incense stick, potpourri, vacuum-cleaner fragrance additive or fragrance refill. The only sovereign heavy-metal instrument in any jurisdiction that names a product in this category is the United States CPSC prohibition on lead-cored candlewicks, 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13), mirrored by Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956; it restricts lead in the metal of a wick core and covers no other analyte and no other product form. The cell is therefore a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS, and it is taken on the axis the regulators themselves used: route of administration. Colorado's 2022 heavy-metal table and Maryland's Technical Authority Rev. 6.0 both publish a route LADDER over the same underlying matrices, with the inhalation row strictest, the oral row looser and the topical or cutaneous row looser still. The value is therefore a function of the route, not of the source matrix's chemistry, and Colorado scopes its strictest row in the instrument's own words to "inhaled product or audited product administered by metered-dose nasal spray", which describes a delivery mechanism this category shares. Maryland's own route gap is the sharpest available evidence for that reading: its inhalation-route total-chromium value is 600 ug/kg while its oral and cutaneous values for the same products are 1,100,000 ug/kg. Selected value 600 ug/kg, from Maryland (inhalation route). Maryland is the only regulator on the register that publishes a chromium value scoped to the inhalation route. The looser or route-unspecific values on the register are recorded and NOT selected: no other jurisdiction on the register publishes a chromium value for any inhaled product: California DCC section 15723, the Colorado route table, the Massachusetts protocol, the Nevada action levels and Israel IMC-GMP Procedure 152 all omit chromium entirely. Maryland's own oral-route and cutaneous-route chromium values for the same products, 1,100,000 ug/kg, are a different route scope and are deliberately not used. The basis is identical to this row's native basis, micrograms of element per kilogram of product as tested, so no basis conversion, no reconstitution and no dry-to-wet adjustment is performed. The read-across is published as `read-across` and never as `regulatory-alignment`, because no instrument regulates this exact cell. Adopting it tightens rather than relaxes the applicable regulatory position: it is three to four orders of magnitude stricter than every article-content instrument that actually binds these products (RoHS lead at 1,000,000 ug/kg of homogeneous material, the candlewick-core prohibition threshold at 600,000 ug/kg of wick-core metal, REACH cadmium in polymers at 100,000 ug/kg). No occurrence, percentile, feasibility or precautionary input touched the number in either direction. Determined on the fragrance oil charge as supplied, plus the reeds or wood plug analysed as a separate component by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS with collision/reaction-cell control of the interfered masses, with the article's non-emitting components digested and screened separately per this row's component plan. DISPOSITION OF THE ADDITIONAL ANALYSES THIS CELL MANDATES. This cell requires one analysis beyond the published test, and it carries a criterion and a lot consequence, so that no mandatory analysis on this row is an obligation without an outcome. COMPONENT RESULTS, THE FIRST ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS THIS CELL MANDATES. The published total-chromium screen of 600 ug/kg governs the emitting material and is NOT transferred to a component's bulk content: a metal collar, cap or trim, or a ceramic glaze, frit, enamel, lustre, paint or decal on the vessel is or may be substantially metal, metal-plated, metal-glazed or metal-pigmented by construction, and reading an emitting-material value against a structural component's bulk content would be exactly the basis conflation this row's basis guard exists to prevent, failing every compliant article for a metal that never enters the air. Every component result is instead dispositioned in three ordered branches, and no component result is left outside them. (a) WHERE A SOVEREIGN INSTRUMENT REACHES THE COMPONENT AND THIS ANALYTE, that instrument is the criterion. For total chromium and this row's components, branch (a) is EMPTY, and the instruments checked before saying so are named rather than waved at: EU RoHS 2011/65/EU restricts HEXAVALENT chromium in the homogeneous materials of electrical and electronic equipment (eu_rohs_2011_crvi_homogeneous_materials_1000000) and publishes no total-chromium value, so it reaches this row's hexavalent-chromium cell if a powered sub-assembly is ever present and never this total-chromium cell, because a species and its total-element parent are not interchangeable in either direction; Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 on batteries restricts mercury, cadmium and lead only and publishes no chromium value, and this row contains no battery in any event; REACH Annex XVII entry 63 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2015/628 (eu_2015_628_pb_mouthable_general_public_articles_0_05pct) reaches only articles supplied to the general public that may be placed in the mouth by children; Regulation (EU) 2018/1513 reaches consumer clothing and skin-contact textiles and does not reach a packaging, sachet or decorative textile that is not worn; the EU Toy Safety Directive 2009/48/EC with EN 71-3, the CPSIA surface-coating limit and the Canadian and Australian toy-coating limits reach accessible toy material and toy surface coatings, and none of these articles is a toy; 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13) reaches only the metal of a candlewick core and this row has no wick core; the food-contact ceramic, glassware and enamelware instruments reach only articles intended to come into contact with food. Every component result on this row therefore falls to branch (b) or branch (c), and neither leaves a result without a criterion or without a lot consequence. (b) WHERE THE COMPONENT IS IN THE EMISSION PATH (the rattan reeds, fibre sticks or wood plug, the inner surface of the vessel with any glaze, frit, enamel or lustre the oil wets, the collar and the closure liner), the criterion is the published total-chromium SCREEN of 600 ug/kg, applied where its basis makes it meaningful: the test is performed on emitting material sampled from the finished, filled and assembled article rather than from a pre-fill bulk batch, at the end of the declared shelf life at the declared storage conditions, or after the declared maximum in-use period with the reeds in place, whichever is the more demanding, so that any chromium transferred out of an emission-path component into the emitting material is carried into the published result rather than escaping it. The screen is a tripwire and never a pass/fail in its own right. An emitting-material total-chromium result reaching half the screen (300 ug/kg) orders reflex hexavalent-chromium speciation on that lot under the reference method published on this row's Cr-VI cell, and that cell's disposition then governs the lot: any hexavalent chromium quantifiable above the method limit of quantitation fails the lot. (c) OTHERWISE, for a component outside the emission path that no sovereign instrument reaches for total chromium, the component result is dispositioned under the HMTc control-and-escalation rule, in the same terms this row's control cells already use: the result is held to ALARA against the manufacturer's demonstrated process capability for that formulation and component set; a result outside that capability band, or an unexplained step change between lots, triggers CAPA and raw-material traceback to the fragrance and carrier-solvent supplier, the reed or wood supplier, the vessel and glaze maker, the closure and liner supplier and the dye supplier; a confirmed uncontrolled source blocks certification until it is removed or substituted; and the analyte goes onto priority surveillance for this row. rows.basis: total lead content of the accessible component, of the dried coating film and of any applied sticker or film (mg/kg)
rows.rationale: The exact cell is unregulated for lead. A child restraint system is motor-vehicle equipment, excluded from the US Consumer Product Safety Act definition of a consumer product by the motor-vehicle-equipment exclusion in 15 U.S.C. 2052(a)(5), so neither CPSIA s.101 (100 mg/kg substrate) nor 16 CFR 1303 (90 mg/kg surface coating) reaches it directly; FMVSS 213, the instrument that does govern it, sets no heavy-metal limit. Rather than assert a direct government limit that does not apply, HMTc reads across the 90 mg/kg accessible-part lead limit from the nearest applicable sovereign article class — consumer products for the carrying and transport of children under four — and applies it to every accessible component of the restraint. The read-across is disclosed on the record and the value is the same 90 mg/kg published on every other row in this category, so a restraint system is held to the children's-product ceiling even though the children's-product statute does not reach it. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value.

rows.basis: total cadmium content of the component material (mg/kg of the homogenised component or of the dried coating film)
rows.rationale: All three candidates are TOTAL-CONTENT limits, so the strictest-of-components selection compares like with like. The EU REACH Annex XVII entry 23 plastic-material value (100 mg/kg) binds the article's moulded polymer components DIRECTLY; the EU painted-article value (1 000 mg/kg) binds its paint layer directly; the Australian coating value (75 mg/kg) is scoped to toys coated with a material and is therefore READ ACROSS to the coatings of a child restraint system or booster car seat, which is not a toy but is a coated article for the same child, in the same mouthing and handling contact. Because the read-across value is the strictest of the three it becomes the published ceiling and is applied to every accessible component, including the polymer components whose own direct limit is 100 mg/kg — deliberate over-compliance, disclosed rather than silent. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value. COMPLIANCE OBLIGATION, stated so this record cannot be read as certifying a value the licensee cannot lawfully sell. The cadmium ceiling published on this row is 75 mg/kg, which sits ABOVE the Washington Children's Safe Product Act prohibition on cadmium exceeding 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component (register row wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b); the Act is codified in Washington's RCW chapter 70A.430). That Act's own definition of a children's product enumerates car seats, products designed to help a child sleep, relax or feed, and products worn as clothing by children, which reaches most of the forms certified on this row. A lot returning cadmium above 40 mg/kg would therefore conform to the HMTc ceiling and still be unlawful to sell in Washington. Any such result is escalated as a jurisdiction-specific regulatory hard stop under the HMTc legal-violation rule and is never certified without that qualification, pending scope-resolved re-ingest of the Washington row through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. The Minnesota cadmium value (75 mg/kg, register row mn_325e3892_2025_cd_covered_consumer_products_75ppm) equals the published ceiling rather than undercutting it, so a lot conforming here conforms there. Where the article incorporates a battery or a battery-powered module — a vibration unit, a sound or music module, a night light, a powered mobile or a powered rocker — the battery is a distinct regulated article with its own instrument, and its limits are not this row's. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 restricts cadmium in a portable battery whether or not incorporated into an appliance (register row eu_batteries_2023_cd_portable_batteries_20000, 20 mg/kg) and mercury in a battery (register row eu_batteries_2023_thg_batteries_5000, 5 mg/kg), both expressed on the weight of the battery. Both are stricter than the values published here and both are recorded as companion obligations on the battery in a battery-by-weight basis; the battery is never homogenised into an accessible-component sample and its instrument is never merged into this row's component-content ceiling. Where the article carries no battery and no powered module the obligation does not arise.

rows.basis: total mercury content of the accessible component material and of the dried non-volatile coating film (mg/kg) — the sovereign value is written for surface coating material and is extended by disclosed read-across, not asserted as direct alignment
rows.rationale: The published value is 10 mg/kg, but it is reached by DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS and not by direct regulatory alignment, because the instrument's scope is narrower than the cell this row publishes. Canada SOR/2016-193 s.5 sets 10 mg/kg total mercury in a dried sample of SURFACE COATING MATERIAL; the register's product_scope for that row is 'surface coating material', which is the coating substance itself. The same instrument distinguishes that scope from the applied-coating scope — its s.6 reaches a sticker, film or surface coating material applied to accessible parts of furniture and products for children (register row ca_sor2016_193_pb_applied_stickers_films_coatings_90000) — and s.6 is lead-only, with no mercury analogue anywhere in the register. Publishing s.5 as a DIRECT sovereign ceiling for the homogenised wood, steel tube, moulded polymer, foam and textile of a child restraint system or booster car seat would therefore over-read the instrument, which is the defect this cell was rebuilt to remove. HMTc reaches the value in two disclosed steps instead. Step one reads s.5 across from the coating material as such to the dried applied film on the finished article; the nearest sovereign instrument written in exactly that applied-coating scope is Canada Toys Regulations SOR/2011-17 s.23(1)(c) (register row ca_sor2011_17_thg_accessible_toy_coating_10), which sets the same 10 mg/kg for total mercury in surface coating materials applied to accessible parts of a child's article, so step one lands on a number a sovereign has already written for an applied coating on a children's product. Step two extends that same 10 mg/kg to every accessible component of a child restraint system or booster car seat, which no sovereign requires and which HMTc adopts as deliberate over-compliance, disclosed here rather than applied silently. At 10 mg/kg the value is six times stricter than the Australian toy-coating mercury value (60 mg/kg, register row au_customs_1956_thg_toys_coating_60mgkg). The EN 71-3 Category III scraped-off-material total-mercury migration value (94 mg/kg, register row eu_2009_48_cat3_thg_toy_migration) measures transfer rather than content, is looser, and is excluded by this row's basis guard. A second and independent ground, recorded here so this record takes ONE consistent position across all of its cells: a child restraint system is motor-vehicle equipment, excluded from the US Consumer Product Safety Act definition of a consumer product by the motor-vehicle-equipment exclusion in 15 U.S.C. 2052(a)(5), and the Canadian position is analogous, restraint systems and booster seats being regulated under motor-vehicle restraint-system law rather than under consumer-product law. Consumer-product-family instruments are therefore applied to this article by disclosed read-across and never as direct alignment — SOR/2018-83 on the lead cell and SOR/2016-193 here. The earlier version of this record asserted direct regulatory alignment for mercury while simultaneously grounding the lead read-across on the proposition that consumer-product law does not reach a restraint system; those two statements could not both be true, and the read-across position is the one adopted.

rows.basis: total chromium content of the coating material and of the accessible component (mg/kg)
rows.rationale: The instrument records chromium as an unspecified species and the register maps it to total chromium. Total chromium in these materials is dominated by benign trivalent chromium — chrome-tanned leather trim, chromium(III) oxide pigments, stainless-steel alloy — so the value is recorded as a screen and is not treated as a standalone protective ceiling. The health-relevant species is Cr(VI), which is dispositioned on this row's Cr-VI control with the REACH Annex XVII entry 47 leather limit as a binding companion. The ASTM F963 total-chromium value (60 mg/kg) is numerically identical but sits in a soluble-element leachate basis and is excluded by this row's basis guard.

rows.basis: hexavalent chromium content on the total dry weight of the component (mg/kg) — leather, coating film, or plated and conversion-coated metal part
rows.rationale: This is the only hexavalent-chromium CONTENT limit in the register that reaches a skin-contact article, and it binds DIRECTLY wherever a child restraint system or booster car seat carries a leather part in skin contact — a leather handlebar or bumper-bar wrap, a harness pad, a leather trim panel or a leather pull tab. For the article's non-leather Cr(VI) pathways — chromate-pigmented coatings, chromate conversion coatings and hexavalent chrome plating on metal parts — no sovereign sets a content maximum, so the 3 mg/kg value is READ ACROSS to them and applied article-wide. The read-across is disclosed and is argued from the material and the contact, not from convenience: it keeps the SAME analyte (Cr(VI) specifically, not total chromium) and the SAME basis (mg/kg of the component's dry mass), and crosses only a material boundary, from chrome-tanned leather to a chromate-pigmented or chromate-passivated surface. The hazard is identical (Cr(VI) skin sensitisation) and the route is identical (dermal transfer under sweat from a surface held against the child), which is exactly why entry 47 was written for skin-contact leather in the first place. Applying it article-wide is deliberate over-compliance and is the same rule this row applies to lead (90 mg/kg applied to a substrate whose own US limit is 100 mg/kg) and to cadmium (75 mg/kg applied to polymer components whose own EU limit is 100 mg/kg); declining to extend it to Cr(VI), the analyte where compliance costs a supplier a change of passivation chemistry, would be selective over-compliance and is not done. The EU RoHS 0.1 % homogeneous-material Cr(VI) value is scoped to electrical and electronic equipment and is over three hundred times more permissive, so it is not used as the read-across source. The EN 71-3 Category I and II Cr(VI) migration values are numerically lower but are leachate limits measuring transfer rather than content, and are excluded by this row's basis guard.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market (total content, ug/kg of product as sold)
rows.rationale: INGESTION-PATHWAY READ-ACROSS. BVL 2017 is the only instrument in the register that separates a swallowed cosmetic from a skin-applied one, and it sets the swallowed tier at 0.5 mg/kg against 2.0 mg/kg general. The stated reason for the toothpaste tier is oral-mucosal contact plus partial swallowing. A lip balm on a 0-5 child is applied directly to the vermilion border, transfers onto the oral mucosa and is swallowed at a fraction at least comparable to toothpaste, and unlike toothpaste it is not rinsed. The swallowed-product tier is therefore the nearest applicable sovereign cell for this pathway, and it is stricter than the general tier that would otherwise apply, so adopting it moves in the protective direction. Category 15 (Feminine Care, live 2026-08-17) established this exact read-across by taking the BVL toothpaste tier onto mucosal-contact products; this row applies the same logic to a more direct ingestion route. The refused alternative is named for the record: BVL's general-cosmetic tier at 2.0 mg/kg would also be a defensible floor, and it is what the corresponding Category 13 adult lip row binds, so the child row here is four times stricter and satisfies the Category 2 floor rule.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market (total content, ug/kg of product as sold)
rows.rationale: DISCLOSED REFUSAL OF A LOOSENING CARVE-OUT. Korea MFDS tiers cosmetic nickel at 10 ug/g for cosmetics other than eye or colour make-up, 30 ug/g for colour make-up and 35 ug/g for eye make-up. This form is a colour cosmetic, so the letter of the instrument gives 30 ug/g. HMTc does not adopt the colour-cosmetic loosening for ages 0-5: nickel is a leading paediatric contact sensitiser, sensitisation is lifelong once established, and the tier exists to accommodate adult pigment loads rather than to describe a tolerable childhood exposure. The cell reads across the same instrument's 10 ug/g tier. The corresponding Category 13 adult row binds 30 ug/g, so the child row is three times stricter and satisfies the Category 2 floor rule. STRICTER-UNSELECTED DISPOSITION: the audit scan surfaces EU REACH 2020/2081 nickel at 5000 ug/kg for tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures; it is not adopted, for the intradermal-route reason recorded in the lead cell of this row.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market (total content, ug/kg of product as sold)
rows.rationale: INGESTION-PATHWAY READ-ACROSS. BVL 2017 is the only instrument in the register that separates a swallowed cosmetic from a skin-applied one, and it sets the swallowed tier at 0.5 mg/kg against 2.0 mg/kg general. The stated reason for the toothpaste tier is oral-mucosal contact plus partial swallowing. A lip balm on a 0-5 child is applied directly to the vermilion border, transfers onto the oral mucosa and is swallowed at a fraction at least comparable to toothpaste, and unlike toothpaste it is not rinsed. The swallowed-product tier is therefore the nearest applicable sovereign cell for this pathway, and it is stricter than the general tier that would otherwise apply, so adopting it moves in the protective direction. Category 15 (Feminine Care, live 2026-08-17) established this exact read-across by taking the BVL toothpaste tier onto mucosal-contact products; this row applies the same logic to a more direct ingestion route. The refused alternative is named for the record: BVL's general-cosmetic tier at 2.0 mg/kg would also be a defensible floor, and it is what the corresponding Category 13 adult lip row binds, so the child row here is four times stricter and satisfies the Category 2 floor rule.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market (total content, ug/kg of product as sold)
rows.rationale: DISCLOSED REFUSAL OF A LOOSENING CARVE-OUT. Korea MFDS tiers cosmetic nickel at 10 ug/g for cosmetics other than eye or colour make-up, 30 ug/g for colour make-up and 35 ug/g for eye make-up. This form is a colour cosmetic, so the letter of the instrument gives 30 ug/g. HMTc does not adopt the colour-cosmetic loosening for ages 0-5: nickel is a leading paediatric contact sensitiser, sensitisation is lifelong once established, and the tier exists to accommodate adult pigment loads rather than to describe a tolerable childhood exposure. The cell reads across the same instrument's 10 ug/g tier. The corresponding Category 13 adult row binds 30 ug/g, so the child row is three times stricter and satisfies the Category 2 floor rule. STRICTER-UNSELECTED DISPOSITION: the audit scan surfaces EU REACH 2020/2081 nickel at 5000 ug/kg for tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures; it is not adopted, for the intradermal-route reason recorded in the lead cell of this row.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market (total content, ug/kg of product as sold)
rows.rationale: Germany's BVL 2017 Table 1 is the strictest sovereign finished-cosmetic lead limit in the register at 2.0 mg/kg, roughly five times stricter than Health Canada (10 mg/kg), China NMPA 2015 (10 mg/kg) and Taiwan MOHW 2024 (10 mg/kg), which are named alongside it so the derivation shows the full sovereign spread rather than one convenient number. BVL is issued by a German federal authority and defines what counts as technically avoidable under Article 17 of EU Regulation 1223/2009, which is binding EU law; it is not a trade-association guideline. The US FDA draft cosmetic lead guidance (10 mg/kg) is gated as draft and is looser in any case. STRICTER-UNSELECTED DISPOSITION: the compiler audit scan surfaces EU REACH Regulation 2020/2081 lead at 700 ug/kg (and nickel at 5000 ug/kg) for tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures, both stricter than this row's bindings. Neither is adopted. That instrument governs a mixture deposited INTRADERMALLY, bypassing the skin barrier entirely; it is a different exposure route, a different product class and a different risk basis from a surface-applied children's cosmetic, and no instrument scope compels borrowing it. It is recorded here rather than suppressed so the reader can see that the candidate was examined and rejected on stated grounds.

rows.rationale: DISCLOSED REFUSAL OF A LOOSENING CARVE-OUT. Korea MFDS tiers cosmetic nickel at 10 ug/g for cosmetics other than eye or colour make-up, 30 ug/g for colour make-up and 35 ug/g for eye make-up. This form is a colour cosmetic, so the letter of the instrument gives 30 ug/g. HMTc does not adopt the colour-cosmetic loosening for ages 0-5: nickel is a leading paediatric contact sensitiser, sensitisation is lifelong once established, and the tier exists to accommodate adult pigment loads rather than to describe a tolerable childhood exposure. The cell reads across the same instrument's 10 ug/g tier. The corresponding Category 13 adult row binds 30 ug/g, so the child row is three times stricter and satisfies the Category 2 floor rule. STRICTER-UNSELECTED DISPOSITION: the audit scan surfaces EU REACH 2020/2081 nickel at 5000 ug/kg for tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures; it is not adopted, for the intradermal-route reason recorded in the lead cell of this row.

rows.basis: total lead content of the fastener component and of its dried plating, lacquer or coating film (mg/kg)
rows.rationale: A fastener on an infant product is an accessible part of a children's product and its plating or lacquer is a surface coating material, so all five named instruments reach it directly and the strictest, 90 mg/kg, is published. This matters more here than on any other row in the category: leaded brass and leaded zinc die-cast are the historic failure mode for small metal children's-product components, and the CPSIA 100 mg/kg substrate value is the looser of the two US numbers, so HMTc publishes 90 mg/kg and applies it to the alloy body as well as to the plating. The Canadian children's-jewellery lead limit (SOR/2018-82 s.2, 90 mg/kg) and the Chinese GB 28480 children's-jewellery total-lead value (300 mg/kg) are recorded as near-neighbour instruments; the Canadian value is identical to the published one and the Chinese value is looser, so neither changes the result. The EU REACH Annex XVII entry 63 mouthable-article value (500 mg/kg) and its brass-alloy exception (5 000 mg/kg) are far looser and are not selected — HMTc does not take the brass exception. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value.
