rows.rationale: All three candidates are TOTAL-CONTENT limits, so the strictest-of-components selection compares like with like. EU REACH Annex XVII entry 23 paragraph 1 (100 mg/kg cadmium in articles produced from the listed synthetic organic polymers) binds a moulded acetal or nylon fastener body DIRECTLY. Entry 23 paragraph 10 (100 mg/kg cadmium in metal beads and other metal components for jewellery making, metal parts of jewellery and imitation jewellery, and hair accessories) is READ ACROSS to a metal snap, zip or button: a fastener is not jewellery, but it is the same class of small plated metal component worn against a child's skin all day, and it is the nearest sovereign cadmium content limit for that component. The Australian coating value (75 mg/kg) is read across from coated toys to the enamel and lacquer on a fastener cap, and being the strictest of the three it becomes the published ceiling for the whole fastener. Near-neighbour instruments recorded and not selected: Canada SOR/2018-82 s.3 (130 mg/kg cadmium in small children's jewellery) is looser; Connecticut PA 10-113 and Minnesota Ch. 347 (75 mg/kg in children's jewellery) are sub-national and jewellery-scoped, the Minnesota value additionally sitting in a soluble basis; California SB 929 (300 mg/kg) is looser. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value. COMPLIANCE OBLIGATION, stated so this record cannot be read as certifying a value the licensee cannot lawfully sell. The cadmium ceiling published on this row is 75 mg/kg, which sits ABOVE the Washington Children's Safe Product Act prohibition on cadmium exceeding 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component (register row wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b); the Act is codified in Washington's RCW chapter 70A.430). That Act's own definition of a children's product enumerates car seats, products designed to help a child sleep, relax or feed, and products worn as clothing by children, which reaches most of the forms certified on this row. A lot returning cadmium above 40 mg/kg would therefore conform to the HMTc ceiling and still be unlawful to sell in Washington. Any such result is escalated as a jurisdiction-specific regulatory hard stop under the HMTc legal-violation rule and is never certified without that qualification, pending scope-resolved re-ingest of the Washington row through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. The Minnesota cadmium value (75 mg/kg, register row mn_325e3892_2025_cd_covered_consumer_products_75ppm) equals the published ceiling rather than undercutting it, so a lot conforming here conforms there. Where the article incorporates a battery or a battery-powered module — a vibration unit, a sound or music module, a night light, a powered mobile or a powered rocker — the battery is a distinct regulated article with its own instrument, and its limits are not this row's. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 restricts cadmium in a portable battery whether or not incorporated into an appliance (register row eu_batteries_2023_cd_portable_batteries_20000, 20 mg/kg) and mercury in a battery (register row eu_batteries_2023_thg_batteries_5000, 5 mg/kg), both expressed on the weight of the battery. Both are stricter than the values published here and both are recorded as companion obligations on the battery in a battery-by-weight basis; the battery is never homogenised into an accessible-component sample and its instrument is never merged into this row's component-content ceiling. Where the article carries no battery and no powered module the obligation does not arise.

rows.basis: hexavalent chromium content on the total dry weight of the component (mg/kg) — leather, coating film, or plated and conversion-coated metal part
rows.rationale: This is the only hexavalent-chromium CONTENT limit in the register that reaches a skin-contact article, and it binds DIRECTLY wherever a snap, zip, button, buckle, rivet, eyelet or other clasp or fastener on an infant product carries a leather part in skin contact — a leather handlebar or bumper-bar wrap, a harness pad, a leather trim panel or a leather pull tab. For the article's non-leather Cr(VI) pathways — chromate-pigmented coatings, chromate conversion coatings and hexavalent chrome plating on metal parts — no sovereign sets a content maximum, so the 3 mg/kg value is READ ACROSS to them and applied article-wide. The read-across is disclosed and is argued from the material and the contact, not from convenience: it keeps the SAME analyte (Cr(VI) specifically, not total chromium) and the SAME basis (mg/kg of the component's dry mass), and crosses only a material boundary, from chrome-tanned leather to a chromate-pigmented or chromate-passivated surface. The hazard is identical (Cr(VI) skin sensitisation) and the route is identical (dermal transfer under sweat from a surface held against the child), which is exactly why entry 47 was written for skin-contact leather in the first place. Applying it article-wide is deliberate over-compliance and is the same rule this row applies to lead (90 mg/kg applied to a substrate whose own US limit is 100 mg/kg) and to cadmium (75 mg/kg applied to polymer components whose own EU limit is 100 mg/kg); declining to extend it to Cr(VI), the analyte where compliance costs a supplier a change of passivation chemistry, would be selective over-compliance and is not done. The EU RoHS 0.1 % homogeneous-material Cr(VI) value is scoped to electrical and electronic equipment and is over three hundred times more permissive, so it is not used as the read-across source. The EN 71-3 Category I and II Cr(VI) migration values are numerically lower but are leachate limits measuring transfer rather than content, and are excluded by this row's basis guard.

rows.basis: as_sold
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign sets a lead maximum level for cocoa powder, drinking chocolate or a malted drink powder. This is a real and consequential gap, and it is disclosed rather than filled. EU 2023/915 writes cadmium cells for cocoa powder and for every chocolate cocoa-solids band but no lead cell for any of them; Codex CXS 193, FSANZ Schedule 19, Health Canada and Hong Kong Cap 132V likewise set no lead maximum level for cocoa powder, drinking chocolate or malted drink powder. The read-across candidates were examined and all rejected: the Hong Kong Milk cell (20 ug/kg) is an as-consumed liquid value and applying it to a dry powder that is reconstituted at roughly one part in ten would be a basis conflation in the strict direction; the sugar cells cover a different, refined commodity that supplies little of a mix's lead; the tea and coffee commodity cells are unrelated botanicals. Lead is the analyte of greatest concern in cocoa supply chains, so this control is written with a hard escalation rule rather than a soft one. Lead is a Tier-1 analyte, so a control here means mandatory lot testing with an escalation rule, not an absence of scrutiny; no ceiling is invented from occurrence data.

rows.basis: dry cocoa or drinking-chocolate powder as sold (edible portion, no reconstitution applied)
rows.rationale: Direct regulatory lookup across three named sovereign cells, taking the strictest applicable rather than the most convenient. The FSANZ cell binds at 500 ug/kg: its scope phrase reaches cocoa products generally rather than confectionery only, so it applies to a drinking-cocoa or hot-chocolate powder without any extension of scope, and it is stricter than the EU cell that names this form most precisely. Its basis, the portion ordinarily consumed, is the edible portion of the food as listed, which for a powder that is consumed in its entirety is the powder as sold; no reconstitution factor is applied, and if the phrase were instead read as the prepared drink the FSANZ ceiling would be an order of magnitude stricter still, so adopting it on the as-sold powder is the conservative reading in the applicant's favour and is disclosed as such. The stricter cells the audit scan flags are all CHOCOLATE CONFECTIONERY bands and are rejected on scope, not on convenience: EU 2023/915 writes a cocoa-solids band structure for chocolate (milk chocolate under 30 percent dry cocoa solids at 100 ug/kg, chocolate under 50 percent at 300 ug/kg, chocolate at or above 50 percent at 800 ug/kg) and Hong Kong writes the same structure (300 to 900 ug/kg), and both drafted those bands alongside a separate, dedicated cell for the drinking powder. Eating chocolate is a different product form, excluded from this row by its own scope note and routed to the confectionery category. Method v2.0 step 4 requires HMTc to preserve the product-form split the government itself wrote rather than to import a confectionery band into a beverage powder because it produces a lower number. Cadmium in cocoa is origin-driven and well characterised, so this cell is a declared Standards Ratchet priority under Governance Policy section 12; occurrence data may inform surveillance but may not select the number.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market — total element content per unit mass of undiluted product as sold (µg/kg). Not a dietary basis, not a migration or leachate basis, and no use-pattern dilution credit.
rows.rationale: BVL 2017 Table 1 (German Federal Office of Consumer Protection and Food Safety, with the Länder cosmetics working group) publishes the technically avoidable heavy-metal content of cosmetic products in general; lead is 2.0 mg/kg, and a content above the table is treated as technically avoidable under good manufacturing practice. Its status is a federal-authority guidance value rather than a statute, and it is disclosed as such, but it is the strictest published sovereign finished-cosmetic lead maximum and Method v2.0 takes the strictest applicable value. The named comparator set shows how far the binding sits below the field: Health Canada, China NMPA 2015 and Taiwan MOHW 2024 are five times looser at 10 mg/kg; Korea, ASEAN and its Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia transpositions, and Kenya KS 2937:2021 are ten times looser at 20 mg/kg; Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations threshold is 125 times looser at 250 mg/kg. Two sovereign cosmetic lead values in the register are stricter than the binding — the BVL 2017 toothpaste tier at 500 µg/kg and Washington State's Toxics-Free Cosmetics Act toothpaste limit at 1000 µg/kg — and the compiler's stricter-unselected audit flags both on every row of this category. Neither is applicable. Both are scoped by their own instruments to toothpaste, a dentifrice that sits on the oral mucosa and is partly swallowed; that ingestion pathway is the stated reason the toothpaste tier is tighter. Categories 20 and 2 carry the dentifrice forms and use those instruments. A shampoo, body wash, scrub or depilatory has no ingestion pathway inside either instrument's scope, so reading a toothpaste tier onto a hair or body rinse-off product would have HMTc inventing a stricter number that no government set for this form. Method v2.0 forbids that as squarely as it forbids inventing a looser one: applicability is a real constraint, and the strictest APPLICABLE value governs. The compiler's audit also flags EU REACH Annex XVII entry 75, which sets 700 µg/kg for lead in mixtures placed on the market for tattooing and permanent make-up. That value is stricter than the binding and is deliberately not adopted: the instrument governs a mixture INJECTED INTO THE DERMIS, on a 'mixture for tattooing or permanent make-up by weight' basis, and a rinse-off shampoo or body wash is not such a mixture on any reading of the entry. The row is held out by this row's basis_guard as well as on scope. It is surfaced rather than filtered out of the scan so that the record shows it was found and disposed of, not missed. Colour-additive and colourant purity specifications (21 CFR 73 and 74, the New Zealand and Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles, the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 permitted-colours entries, the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant entries) are raw-material ingredient specifications, not finished-product maxima. They are held out of every cell by this row's basis_guard, and none of them is in any case stricter than the binding for this analyte.

rows.rationale: BVL 2017 Table 1 sets mercury in cosmetic products in general at 0.1 mg/kg, and BVL's toothpaste tier is the same value, so mercury carries no dentifrice split. The comparator set is deliberately wide here because mercury in cosmetics is the one contaminant with a hard, enforceable US rule and an active illegal-adulteration problem: 21 CFR 700.13(d)(2)(i) deems a cosmetic adulterated unless its mercury content is unavoidable under good manufacturing practice and below 1 ppm, and Hong Kong Cap. 640 sets the same 1 ppm expressly for unintentional trace mercury in cosmetics including skin-lightening products. Health Canada, China NMPA 2015, Korea MFDS, Taiwan MOHW 2024, ASEAN 2019 with its Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia transpositions, and the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 all land at the same 1 mg/kg; Kenya KS 2937:2021 is 2 mg/kg. The HMTc binding is therefore ten to twenty times stricter than every one of them. Mercury used as an intentional skin-lightening active, and the eye-area thiomersal and phenylmercuric preservative allowances in the India, Hong Kong and South Africa instruments, are ingredient permissions rather than contaminant ceilings; HMTc does not adopt them, and a rinse-off product formulated with an intentional mercury ingredient is not certifiable at all. Colour-additive and colourant purity specifications (21 CFR 73 and 74, the New Zealand and Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles, the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 permitted-colours entries, the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant entries) are raw-material ingredient specifications, not finished-product maxima. They are held out of every cell by this row's basis_guard, and none of them is in any case stricter than the binding for this analyte.

rows.rationale: Korea is the only jurisdiction in the register that sets a nickel content limit for finished cosmetics, and it tiers it by form: 10 µg/g for cosmetic products other than eye makeup and colour cosmetics, 30 µg/g for colour makeup, 35 µg/g for eye makeup. Every Category 14 form is a cleansing, conditioning, shaving, depilatory or hair-colouring preparation and none is an eye-makeup or colour-makeup product in the MFDS product taxonomy, so the strictest of the three tiers — 10 µg/g — is the directly applicable one, not a read-across. Korea MFDS Notice 2025-63 carries the same 10 µg/g value for the same scope and corroborates it; it is not named as a candidate because its register note contradicts its own value (the note reads '1 microgram/g = 1000 ug/kg' against a stored value of 10000 µg/kg), and a litigation-facing citation should not carry that discrepancy forward. The EU REACH restriction on nickel in tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures (5000 µg/kg) is stricter but governs a mixture injected into the dermis, a different form on a different basis, and is held out by this row's basis_guard. Nickel is a leading contact sensitiser, so the programme additionally holds it under ALARA post-publication and treats the published ceiling as an outer bound rather than a target.

rows.basis: drinking water
rows.rationale: No government sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum level for any food in any jurisdiction. This reads across the strictest drinking-water (oral-intake) Cr(VI) limit as a conservative species ceiling: the California State Water Resources Control Board Cr(VI) MCL, 10 ug/L (about 11 ug/kg at an oil density of 0.91, applied at 10 as slightly conservative). That MCL is a feasibility-set enforceable limit, not a health-based no-effect level; it is adopted only as the strictest real sovereign oral-intake Cr(VI) number. The value sits far below the total-chromium screen (300 ug/kg), so the species constraint holds. In a lipid food matrix hexavalent chromium reduces to trivalent chromium, so any total-chromium exceedance is reflex-speciated by IC-ICP-MS (EPA 3060A alkaline digestion + EPA 6800 / EN 15192) and any quantifiable Cr(VI) above 10 ug/kg fails.

rows.basis: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
rows.rationale: The exact cell is unregulated: the food-contact surface is a cured liquid-applied coating, and coatings and varnishes are a Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, while Reg (EU) 10/2011 reaches plastic layers in multi-material multi-layer articles but was not written for a sprayed and stoved coating system. The nearest applicable sovereign value in the identical basis is the EU 10/2011 Annex II element requirement for a polymeric food-contact layer, read across with disclosure. The read-across holds the basis constant: source and destination are the same measured quantity, specific element migration into food or a food simulant in µg/kg food, determined by the same test conventions. The analogy is on basis and exposure endpoint, not on material identity, and it is disclosed as a read-across rather than presented as a limit written for this article. Lead is on the Annex II point 2 not-detectable list, so the published ceiling is the 0.01 mg/kg food detection limit and not a positive migration allowance. The read-across is held to the coated article as placed on market and after the declared abrasion and thermal conditioning; the exposed-rivet and breached-coating configurations are handled by the component plan under the alloy-release control regime rather than by relaxing this value. This is a migration ceiling on the food or simulant and is never reported as a limit on the material's lead content; the material-content instruments (US CPSIA total lead in children's-product substrate, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS 2024-29 percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals and solder) are separate obligations in a different basis and are not this cell.

The nearest applicable sovereign value in the identical basis is the EU 10/2011 Annex II element requirement for a polymeric food-contact layer, read across with disclosure. The read-across holds the basis constant: source and destination are the same measured quantity, specific element migration into food or a food simulant in µg/kg food, determined by the same test conventions. The analogy is on basis and exposure endpoint, not on material identity, and it is disclosed as a read-across rather than presented as a limit written for this article. Aluminium carries a positive specific migration limit of 1 mg/kg food, added by Reg (EU) 2016/1416. The read-across is held to the coated article as placed on market and after the declared abrasion and thermal conditioning; the exposed-rivet and breached-coating configurations are handled by the component plan under the alloy-release control regime rather than by relaxing this value. This value governs the polymeric food-contact surface; it is not applied to an aluminium metal article, because an instrument written for plastics did not contemplate an article whose food-contact surface is the element itself.

rows.basis: total lead content of the accessible component, of the dried coating film and of any applied sticker or film (mg/kg)
rows.rationale: Five directly applicable total-content instruments are named and the strictest is taken. The US CPSIA s.101 children's-product substrate limit (100 mg/kg for any part of the product) and the 16 CFR 1303 surface-coating limit (90 mg/kg on the weight of the total non-volatile content of the dried paint film) both reach a crib or bassinet as a children's product; Canada SOR/2018-83 s.2(1) sets 90 mg/kg in each accessible part of consumer products for the sleep, relaxation, hygiene, carrying or transport of children under four; Canada SOR/2016-193 s.2(1) sets 90 mg/kg in a dried sample of surface coating material and s.6 sets 90 mg/kg in stickers, films and applied surface coatings on accessible parts of furniture and products for children. HMTc publishes 90 mg/kg and applies it to every accessible component, including the substrate whose own federal US limit is 100 mg/kg. The EU REACH Annex XVII entry 63 mouthable-article value (500 mg/kg) and the brass-alloy exception (5 000 mg/kg) are far looser and are not selected. A crib is furniture and a product for the sleep of a child under four, so it sits inside both Canadian scopes on their face. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value.

rows.basis: total cadmium content of the component material (mg/kg of the homogenised component or of the dried coating film)
rows.rationale: All three candidates are TOTAL-CONTENT limits, so the strictest-of-components selection compares like with like. The EU REACH Annex XVII entry 23 plastic-material value (100 mg/kg) binds the article's moulded polymer components DIRECTLY; the EU painted-article value (1 000 mg/kg) binds its paint layer directly; the Australian coating value (75 mg/kg) is scoped to toys coated with a material and is therefore READ ACROSS to the coatings of a crib or bassinet, which is not a toy but is a coated article for the same child, in the same mouthing and handling contact. Because the read-across value is the strictest of the three it becomes the published ceiling and is applied to every accessible component, including the polymer components whose own direct limit is 100 mg/kg — deliberate over-compliance, disclosed rather than silent. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value. COMPLIANCE OBLIGATION, stated so this record cannot be read as certifying a value the licensee cannot lawfully sell. The cadmium ceiling published on this row is 75 mg/kg, which sits ABOVE the Washington Children's Safe Product Act prohibition on cadmium exceeding 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component (register row wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b); the Act is codified in Washington's RCW chapter 70A.430). That Act's own definition of a children's product enumerates car seats, products designed to help a child sleep, relax or feed, and products worn as clothing by children, which reaches most of the forms certified on this row. A lot returning cadmium above 40 mg/kg would therefore conform to the HMTc ceiling and still be unlawful to sell in Washington. Any such result is escalated as a jurisdiction-specific regulatory hard stop under the HMTc legal-violation rule and is never certified without that qualification, pending scope-resolved re-ingest of the Washington row through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. The Minnesota cadmium value (75 mg/kg, register row mn_325e3892_2025_cd_covered_consumer_products_75ppm) equals the published ceiling rather than undercutting it, so a lot conforming here conforms there. Where the article incorporates a battery or a battery-powered module — a vibration unit, a sound or music module, a night light, a powered mobile or a powered rocker — the battery is a distinct regulated article with its own instrument, and its limits are not this row's. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 restricts cadmium in a portable battery whether or not incorporated into an appliance (register row eu_batteries_2023_cd_portable_batteries_20000, 20 mg/kg) and mercury in a battery (register row eu_batteries_2023_thg_batteries_5000, 5 mg/kg), both expressed on the weight of the battery. Both are stricter than the values published here and both are recorded as companion obligations on the battery in a battery-by-weight basis; the battery is never homogenised into an accessible-component sample and its instrument is never merged into this row's component-content ceiling.

rows.basis: total mercury content of the accessible component material and of the dried non-volatile coating film (mg/kg) — the sovereign value is written for surface coating material and is extended by disclosed read-across, not asserted as direct alignment
rows.rationale: The published value is 10 mg/kg, but it is reached by DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS and not by direct regulatory alignment, because the instrument's scope is narrower than the cell this row publishes. Canada SOR/2016-193 s.5 sets 10 mg/kg total mercury in a dried sample of SURFACE COATING MATERIAL; the register's product_scope for that row is 'surface coating material', which is the coating substance itself. The same instrument distinguishes that scope from the applied-coating scope — its s.6 reaches a sticker, film or surface coating material applied to accessible parts of furniture and products for children (register row ca_sor2016_193_pb_applied_stickers_films_coatings_90000) — and s.6 is lead-only, with no mercury analogue anywhere in the register. Publishing s.5 as a DIRECT sovereign ceiling for the homogenised wood, steel tube, moulded polymer, foam and textile of a crib or bassinet would therefore over-read the instrument, which is the defect this cell was rebuilt to remove. HMTc reaches the value in two disclosed steps instead. Step one reads s.5 across from the coating material as such to the dried applied film on the finished article; the nearest sovereign instrument written in exactly that applied-coating scope is Canada Toys Regulations SOR/2011-17 s.23(1)(c) (register row ca_sor2011_17_thg_accessible_toy_coating_10), which sets the same 10 mg/kg for total mercury in surface coating materials applied to accessible parts of a child's article, so step one lands on a number a sovereign has already written for an applied coating on a children's product. Step two extends that same 10 mg/kg to every accessible component of a crib or bassinet, which no sovereign requires and which HMTc adopts as deliberate over-compliance, disclosed here rather than applied silently. At 10 mg/kg the value is six times stricter than the Australian toy-coating mercury value (60 mg/kg, register row au_customs_1956_thg_toys_coating_60mgkg). The EN 71-3 Category III scraped-off-material total-mercury migration value (94 mg/kg, register row eu_2009_48_cat3_thg_toy_migration) measures transfer rather than content, is looser, and is excluded by this row's basis guard.

rows.basis: total chromium content of the coating material and of the accessible component (mg/kg)
rows.rationale: The instrument records chromium as an unspecified species and the register maps it to total chromium. Total chromium in these materials is dominated by benign trivalent chromium — chrome-tanned leather trim, chromium(III) oxide pigments, stainless-steel alloy — so the value is recorded as a screen and is not treated as a standalone protective ceiling. The health-relevant species is Cr(VI), which is dispositioned on this row's Cr-VI control with the REACH Annex XVII entry 47 leather limit as a binding companion. The ASTM F963 total-chromium value (60 mg/kg) is numerically identical but sits in a soluble-element leachate basis and is excluded by this row's basis guard.

rows.basis: hexavalent chromium content on the total dry weight of the component (mg/kg) — leather, coating film, or plated and conversion-coated metal part
rows.rationale: This is the only hexavalent-chromium CONTENT limit in the register that reaches a skin-contact article, and it binds DIRECTLY wherever a crib or bassinet carries a leather part in skin contact — a leather handlebar or bumper-bar wrap, a harness pad, a leather trim panel or a leather pull tab. For the article's non-leather Cr(VI) pathways — chromate-pigmented coatings, chromate conversion coatings and hexavalent chrome plating on metal parts — no sovereign sets a content maximum, so the 3 mg/kg value is READ ACROSS to them and applied article-wide. The read-across is disclosed and is argued from the material and the contact, not from convenience: it keeps the SAME analyte (Cr(VI) specifically, not total chromium) and the SAME basis (mg/kg of the component's dry mass), and crosses only a material boundary, from chrome-tanned leather to a chromate-pigmented or chromate-passivated surface. The hazard is identical (Cr(VI) skin sensitisation) and the route is identical (dermal transfer under sweat from a surface held against the child), which is exactly why entry 47 was written for skin-contact leather in the first place. Applying it article-wide is deliberate over-compliance and is the same rule this row applies to lead (90 mg/kg applied to a substrate whose own US limit is 100 mg/kg) and to cadmium (75 mg/kg applied to polymer components whose own EU limit is 100 mg/kg); declining to extend it to Cr(VI), the analyte where compliance costs a supplier a change of passivation chemistry, would be selective over-compliance and is not done. The EU RoHS 0.1 % homogeneous-material Cr(VI) value is scoped to electrical and electronic equipment and is over three hundred times more permissive, so it is not used as the read-across source. The EN 71-3 Category I and II Cr(VI) migration values are numerically lower but are leachate limits measuring transfer rather than content, and are excluded by this row's basis guard.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market — total element content per unit mass of undiluted product as sold (µg/kg). Not a dietary basis, not a migration or leachate basis, and no use-pattern dilution credit.
rows.rationale: BVL 2017 Table 1 (German Federal Office of Consumer Protection and Food Safety, with the Länder cosmetics working group) publishes the technically avoidable heavy-metal content of cosmetic products in general; lead is 2.0 mg/kg, and a content above the table is treated as technically avoidable under good manufacturing practice. Its status is a federal-authority guidance value rather than a statute, and it is disclosed as such, but it is the strictest published sovereign finished-cosmetic lead maximum and Method v2.0 takes the strictest applicable value. The named comparator set shows how far the binding sits below the field: Health Canada, China NMPA 2015 and Taiwan MOHW 2024 are five times looser at 10 mg/kg; Korea, ASEAN and its Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia transpositions, and Kenya KS 2937:2021 are ten times looser at 20 mg/kg; Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations threshold is 125 times looser at 250 mg/kg. rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market — total element content per unit mass of undiluted product as sold (µg/kg). Not a dietary basis, not a migration or leachate basis, and no use-pattern dilution credit.
rows.rationale: Korea is the only jurisdiction in the register that sets a nickel content limit for finished cosmetics, and it tiers it by form: 10 µg/g for cosmetic products other than eye makeup and colour cosmetics, 30 µg/g for colour makeup, 35 µg/g for eye makeup. Every Category 14 form is a cleansing, conditioning, shaving, depilatory or hair-colouring preparation and none is an eye-makeup or colour-makeup product in the MFDS product taxonomy, so the strictest of the three tiers — 10 µg/g — is the directly applicable one, not a read-across. Korea MFDS Notice 2025-63 carries the same 10 µg/g value for the same scope and corroborates it; it is not named as a candidate because its register note contradicts its own value (the note reads '1 microgram/g = 1000 ug/kg' against a stored value of 10000 µg/kg), and a litigation-facing citation should not carry that discrepancy forward. The EU REACH restriction on nickel in tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures (5000 µg/kg) is stricter but governs a mixture injected into the dermis, a different form on a different basis, and is held out by this row's basis_guard. Nickel is a leading contact sensitiser, so the programme additionally holds it under ALARA post-publication and treats the published ceiling as an outer bound rather than a target.

rows.basis: finished dentifrice as placed on market (total lead content, ug/kg as sold)
rows.rationale: Germany BVL 2017 is the only instrument in the register that publishes a SEPARATE, STRICTER toothpaste tier alongside its general-cosmetic tier. That tier exists because a dentifrice is applied to the oral mucosa and is partly swallowed, which is the exposure pattern every formulated row in this category shares. The binding German value carries register status 'guidance impurity limit' (the BVL technically-avoidable-content table, the basis on which German competent authorities object to a cosmetic under Regulation (EC) 1223/2009 Article 17); the selection is not a status judgement and does not depend on one. WASHINGTON STATE IS DISCLOSED AND NOT NAMED. Its Toxics-Free Cosmetics Act toothpaste lead value (register id wa_tfca_pb_toothpaste_1000) is a statutory limit at 1000 ug/kg, twice as loose as the German value, so it could never bind this cell. It is not carried in the candidate set because its register basis reads only 'product as sold' — a string that identifies neither the cosmetic nor the oral form, and that consequently cannot pass this row's corrected basis guard, which admits only a basis naming a cosmetic or finished oral product. Correcting that register basis is logged as a register gap for the verified regulatory-fetch pathway rather than done here, because the same register row is named by the children's-toothpaste row of the Category 2 standard under a looser guard, and amending the basis in isolation would resolve that sibling cell to a GAP. Washington remains inside this row's audit scan: jurisdiction US-WA is in the credible set and its product scope 'toothpaste' matches the audit scope, so were the value ever revised below the German tier the compiler would flag it as a stricter unselected anchor rather than let it pass unnoticed.

rows.basis: finished oral-care product as placed on market (total nickel content, ug/kg as sold) — read across from the Korean residual finished-cosmetic nickel tier
rows.rationale: Nickel is a mucosal and contact sensitiser and reaches oral-care formulations through hydrated-silica and calcium-carbonate abrasives, mineral pigments, and stainless-steel process contact, so the cell must not be left without a ceiling where a sovereign anchor exists. The exact cell (nickel in a dentifrice, rinse, whitening system or denture-care product) is unregulated in every jurisdiction surveyed, which is why the value is published as a disclosed read-across tagged 'read-across' rather than as regulatory alignment; in Korea a dentifrice is a quasi-drug rather than a cosmetic, so the Korean cosmetic tier does not reach this form by its own terms. Two Korean notices state the same three-tier allowance at identical values: Notice 2024-9 Article 6(2) (kr_mfds2024_9_ni_other_cosmetics_10ugg) and the current Notice No. 2025-63 (the named anchor). The later notice is cited so that this standard and the Category 2 children's-dentifrice standard, which anchors the same cell, cite the same current instrument rather than splitting across two Korean notices for one number. The value is 10000 ug/kg under either notice, neither register row is flagged superseded, and the 2024-9 row remains inside this row's audit scan.

rows.basis: finished dentifrice as placed on market (total content, ug/kg as sold)
rows.rationale: No jurisdiction sets a tin content limit for any oral-care or cosmetic product; the sovereign tin maximum levels in the register are canned-food and food-contact values written for tinplate migration into food and are a different basis entirely. Tin is additionally not a pure impurity in this category: stannous fluoride and stannous chloride are authorised anticaries and antigingivitis actives in dentifrices and mouthrinses, so a finished-product tin ceiling would be exceeded by design in a compliant stannous formulation and would be meaningless as a contaminant control. The cell is held under mandatory analytical control with a declaration reconciliation rather than declared not-material, because tin is unambiguously present at material levels in this category and an absence claim would be contradicted on its face.

rows.basis: Finished cosmetic total content as placed on market (ug/kg of product as sold); technically-unavoidable-impurity basis. Not migration, not leachate, not dietary, not an ingredient purity specification.
rows.rationale: Applicable sovereign maxima surveyed for this exact form: Germany BVL 2017 general cosmetic orientation value, 2000 ug/kg; China NMPA 2015, 10000; Health Canada, 10000; Taiwan MOHW 2024, 10000; Korea MFDS Notice 2025-63, 20000; Singapore HSA 2024 and the ASEAN directive with its Indonesian and Malaysian transpositions, 20000; Kenya KS 2937:2021, 20000. Looser and therefore non-binding: the EAEU natural-raw-material tier (5000), the Korean clay-powder tier (50000), the India IS 3959:2004 skin-powder rows (20000 and 10000) and the Australian customs value (250000). The German value binds. Its own scope excludes the make-up categories the same table lists at 5000 ug/kg (make-up powder, rouge, eye shadow, eyeliner, kajal and theatrical make-up); none of those forms falls in this row, so the general branch is the applicable cell. The US FDA draft lead guidance for lip and externally applied cosmetics (10000) carries draft status in the register, is gated out by the compiler, and is looser in any case. No colour-additive or ingredient purity specification is used as an anchor: the US 21 CFR 73/74 cosmetic-use specifications (10000-20000 ug/kg), the India permitted-colour specification (20000), the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant specification (20000) and the New Zealand / Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles (10000) bound one raw material's purity rather than the finished product, they are refused by this row's basis guard, and every one of them is looser than the binding value in any event.

rows.basis: Finished cosmetic total content as placed on market (ug/kg of product as sold); technically-unavoidable-impurity basis. Not migration, not leachate, not dietary, not an ingredient purity specification.
rows.rationale: Korea MFDS is the ONLY authority in the register that publishes a nickel maximum for a finished cosmetic, and the instrument tiers it by product class: eye makeup 35000 ug/kg, colour makeup 30000, all other cosmetics 10000. Method step 4 requires the government's own product-form split to be preserved, so the applicable branch is selected rather than the strictest branch overall. Both register transpositions of the instrument (MFDS Notice 2024-9 and Notice 2025-63) are named and carry identical values, which is the cross-edition check. No other credible authority publishes a cosmetic nickel ceiling: the EU prohibits nickel compounds as intentional cosmetic ingredients under Regulation 1223/2009 Annex II without setting a numeric trace maximum, and Germany's BVL 2017 table covers only lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury and antimony. This row is neither an eye-makeup nor a colour-makeup product, so the 10000 ug/kg branch is the applicable cell and it binds. Where the mapping of an HMTc row onto the Korean product classes is not unambiguous, or where a row's forms straddle two branches, HMTc takes the stricter branch rather than claiming the looser one.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market (total content, ug/kg of product as sold)
rows.rationale: Germany's BVL 2017 Table 1 is the strictest sovereign finished-cosmetic lead limit in the register at 2.0 mg/kg, roughly five times stricter than Health Canada (10 mg/kg), China NMPA 2015 (10 mg/kg) and Taiwan MOHW 2024 (10 mg/kg), which are named alongside it so the derivation shows the full sovereign spread rather than one convenient number. BVL is issued by a German federal authority and defines what counts as technically avoidable under Article 17 of EU Regulation 1223/2009, which is binding EU law; it is not a trade-association guideline. The US FDA draft cosmetic lead guidance (10 mg/kg) is gated as draft and is looser in any case. Health Canada's cosmetic impurity guidance is NOT named on this row: the guidance states on its face that products regulated in Canada as drugs or natural health products - it names sunscreens, zinc-oxide skin protectants and therapeutic toothpaste - fall outside its cosmetic scope. Naming it here would be a scope conflation.

rows.basis: nickel release, direct and prolonged skin contact (EN 1811)
rows.rationale: Nickel release limit for direct and prolonged skin-contact articles, 0.5 µg/cm²/week (former EU Nickel Directive 94/27/EC, now REACH entry 27). rows.basis: as_sold_dry
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets a methylmercury maximum level for this product form, and no not-material determination is supportable for it: the routed corpus quantifies methylmercury in edible plant and fungal tissue (wang2021-houttuynia-mercury-china measured methylmercury in the leaf and root tissue of an edible leafy vegetable at an LOD of 0.002 ug/kg; stasinos2014-heavy-metals-tubers-review in root and tuber tissue; asensio2023-madrid-mushrooms-mercury), so the species is not absent from produce and the biological premise of a not-material determination is rebutted inside this very category. This row is the concentrated form of the fresh commodity, whose own methylmercury cell is held under the same control; a concentrated derivative is never granted a weaker determination than the fresh row it derives from. Methylmercury is therefore held under mandatory analytical control rather than recorded not-material, and it remains bounded by identity below the published total-mercury ceiling for this row (Israel MOH FCS-2016 category 3.1, 150 ug/kg); methylmercury cannot exceed total mercury. No methylmercury ceiling is invented.

rows.basis: as_sold_dry
rows.rationale: Every tin maximum level in the register is scoped to canned product: EU Reg. 2023/915 sets 200000 ug/kg for canned foods and 100000 ug/kg for canned beverages, Codex CXS 193-1995 and AU-NZ Schedule 19 set 250000 ug/kg for canned foods, and Hong Kong Cap. 132V sets 250000 ug/kg for canned food other than canned beverages. Those limits regulate one contamination pathway, dissolution of tin from tinplate into the packed food. This row is not packed in tinplate, so the pathway that every sovereign tin limit addresses is physically absent and any tin present is dietary background rather than packaging migration. The EU tin maximum levels expressly exclude canned dried and canned powdered products from their own scope, which is the regulator's own recognition that tin dissolution from tinplate is a wet-pack phenomenon; even a canned dried fruit therefore falls outside every sovereign tin maximum level. Hermetically sealed tinplate presentations of this commodity route to the canned-foods row in Category 7 and carry the canned-foods tin maximum level there.

rows.basis: as_sold_dry
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets an aluminium contaminant maximum level for any fruit, vegetable or produce form in any jurisdiction. The register's aluminium limits are drinking-water and bottled-water parameters, infant-formula maximum levels, a food-contact plastics specific migration limit, toy migration limits, and permitted-additive levels for baked and starch foods; none of them regulates aluminium as a contaminant of produce. Aluminium is also the third most abundant element in the earth's crust and appears in produce largely as soil-derived and root-associated mineral content rather than as process contamination, so no near-neighbour read-across is supportable either. Under the government-limit-only method HMTc publishes no standalone aluminium number for this row.

rows.basis: Finished cosmetic total content as placed on market (ug/kg of product as sold); technically-unavoidable-impurity basis. Not migration, not leachate, not dietary, not an ingredient purity specification.
rows.rationale: The form-specific instruments are named so the derivation shows they were considered: India IS 3959:2004 skin powders at 20000 ug/kg with its ECO Mark tier at 10000, both finished-product rows for a skin powder, and the EAEU TR CU 009/2011 natural-plant-or-mineral-raw-material tier at 5000, which a starch base can reach through its natural-plant limb. All are looser than the German general cosmetic value of 2000 ug/kg, which binds. A dusting powder is not one of the make-up categories the German table lists at 5000, so the general branch is the applicable cell. The Korean clay-powder branch (50000) is looser and is scoped to clay, which a starch base is not. No colour-additive or ingredient purity specification is used as an anchor: the US 21 CFR 73/74 cosmetic-use specifications (10000-20000 ug/kg), the India permitted-colour specification (20000), the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant specification (20000) and the New Zealand / Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles (10000) bound one raw material's purity rather than the finished product, they are refused by this row's basis guard, and every one of them is looser than the binding value in any event.

rows.basis: Finished cosmetic total content as placed on market (ug/kg of product as sold); technically-unavoidable-impurity basis. Not migration, not leachate, not dietary, not an ingredient purity specification.
rows.rationale: Korea MFDS is the ONLY authority in the register that publishes a nickel maximum for a finished cosmetic, and the instrument tiers it by product class: eye makeup 35000 ug/kg, colour makeup 30000, all other cosmetics 10000. Method step 4 requires the government's own product-form split to be preserved, so the applicable branch is selected rather than the strictest branch overall. Both register transpositions of the instrument (MFDS Notice 2024-9 and Notice 2025-63) are named and carry identical values, which is the cross-edition check. No other credible authority publishes a cosmetic nickel ceiling: the EU prohibits nickel compounds as intentional cosmetic ingredients under Regulation 1223/2009 Annex II without setting a numeric trace maximum, and Germany's BVL 2017 table covers only lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury and antimony. This row is neither an eye-makeup nor a colour-makeup product, so the 10000 ug/kg branch is the applicable cell and it binds. Where the mapping of an HMTc row onto the Korean product classes is not unambiguous, or where a row's forms straddle two branches, HMTc takes the stricter branch rather than claiming the looser one.

rows.basis: Finished cosmetic total content as placed on market (ug/kg of product as sold); technically-unavoidable-impurity basis. Not migration, not leachate, not dietary, not an ingredient purity specification.
rows.rationale: Every form-specific sovereign instrument for this product form was surveyed and named so the derivation shows they were considered rather than missed: India IS 3959:2004 skin powders, 20000 ug/kg, and its ECO Mark tier, 10000; the EAEU TR CU 009/2011 natural-plant-or-mineral-raw-material tier, 5000, which does reach a talc base. All are looser than the German general cosmetic value of 2000 ug/kg, which therefore binds. The Korean clay-powder branch (50000) is both looser and scoped to clay rather than talc. A mineral-base dusting powder is not one of the make-up categories the German table lists at 5000, so the general branch is the applicable cell. No colour-additive or ingredient purity specification is used as an anchor: the US 21 CFR 73/74 cosmetic-use specifications (10000-20000 ug/kg), the India permitted-colour specification (20000), the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant specification (20000) and the New Zealand / Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles (10000) bound one raw material's purity rather than the finished product, they are refused by this row's basis guard, and every one of them is looser than the binding value in any event.

rows.basis: Finished cosmetic total content as placed on market (ug/kg of product as sold); technically-unavoidable-impurity basis. Not migration, not leachate, not dietary, not an ingredient purity specification.
rows.rationale: The EAEU natural-plant-or-mineral-raw-material tier (5000 ug/kg) is the only arsenic instrument written specifically for a mineral-bearing cosmetic and it is named here, but it is ten-fold looser than the German general value of 500 ug/kg, which binds. This is the strictest cell in the category relative to the raw material: a talc, kaolin or bentonite base carries geogenic arsenic, so 500 ug/kg total arsenic on a mineral powder is a demanding value, and it is nonetheless the government value rather than a feasibility-adjusted one. rows.basis: Finished cosmetic total content as placed on market (ug/kg of product as sold); technically-unavoidable-impurity basis. Not migration, not leachate, not dietary, not an ingredient purity specification.
rows.rationale: Korea MFDS is the ONLY authority in the register that publishes a nickel maximum for a finished cosmetic, and the instrument tiers it by product class: eye makeup 35000 ug/kg, colour makeup 30000, all other cosmetics 10000. Method step 4 requires the government's own product-form split to be preserved, so the applicable branch is selected rather than the strictest branch overall. Both register transpositions of the instrument (MFDS Notice 2024-9 and Notice 2025-63) are named and carry identical values, which is the cross-edition check. No other credible authority publishes a cosmetic nickel ceiling: the EU prohibits nickel compounds as intentional cosmetic ingredients under Regulation 1223/2009 Annex II without setting a numeric trace maximum, and Germany's BVL 2017 table covers only lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury and antimony. This row is neither an eye-makeup nor a colour-makeup product, so the 10000 ug/kg branch is the applicable cell and it binds. Where the mapping of an HMTc row onto the Korean product classes is not unambiguous, or where a row's forms straddle two branches, HMTc takes the stricter branch rather than claiming the looser one.

rows.basis: as_sold
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets an inorganic-arsenic maximum level for eggs or egg products. Every credible inorganic-arsenic instrument on the register is scoped elsewhere: EU 2023/915 and EU 2025/1891 to rice, rice products, fruit juices, infant food and seafood; UK, Health Canada and US FDA to rice-based and juice matrices; Hong Kong Cap. 132V to rice and aquatic animals. A NOT-MATERIAL determination is deliberately REJECTED for this cell rather than adopted for convenience: organoarsenical feed additives (roxarsone, nitarsone, arsanilic acid, carbarsone) were lawfully administered to poultry and swine in major producing markets within living memory and are documented to leave arsenic residues in edible tissue, so the programme will not make the affirmative claim that no inorganic-arsenic pathway exists in terrestrial animal food. For the ruminant rows, where no equivalent additive history applies, the absence of that pathway does not by itself substantiate a not-material determination either, because neither a sovereign number nor a supportable near-neighbour analogue exists for the cell in any case. rows.basis: as sold, ug of element per kg of the emitting material (product as tested)
rows.rationale: No government anywhere sets a lead content maximum for an air freshener, plug-in evaporator, puff releaser, candle body, wax melt, oil or nebula diffuser, gel or reed diffuser, incense stick, potpourri, vacuum-cleaner fragrance additive or fragrance refill. The only sovereign heavy-metal instrument in any jurisdiction that names a product in this category is the United States CPSC prohibition on lead-cored candlewicks, 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13), mirrored by Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956; it restricts lead in the metal of a wick core and covers no other analyte and no other product form. The cell is therefore a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS, and it is taken on the axis the regulators themselves used: route of administration. Colorado's 2022 heavy-metal table and Maryland's Technical Authority Rev. 6.0 both publish a route LADDER over the same underlying matrices, with the inhalation row strictest, the oral row looser and the topical or cutaneous row looser still. The value is therefore a function of the route, not of the source matrix's chemistry, and Colorado scopes its strictest row in the instrument's own words to "inhaled product or audited product administered by metered-dose nasal spray", which describes a delivery mechanism this category shares. Maryland's own route gap is the sharpest available evidence for that reading: its inhalation-route total-chromium value is 600 ug/kg while its oral and cutaneous values for the same products are 1,100,000 ug/kg. Selected value 500 ug/kg, from Colorado (co2022 inhaled/nasal row). California DCC section 15723 independently sets the identical 0.5 ug/g for inhalable products (us_ca_dcc_2026_pb_inhalable_cannabis_0_5ugg), so two sub-national regulators converge on this value. The looser or route-unspecific values on the register are recorded and NOT selected: Maryland inhalation route 1000 ug/kg, Massachusetts all-uses protocol 500 ug/kg (equal but route-unspecific), Nevada 1200 ug/kg, Israel IMC-GMP Procedure 152 5000 ug/kg. The basis is identical to this row's native basis, micrograms of element per kilogram of product as tested, so no basis conversion, no reconstitution and no dry-to-wet adjustment is performed. The read-across is published as `read-across` and never as `regulatory-alignment`, because no instrument regulates this exact cell. Adopting it tightens rather than relaxes the applicable regulatory position: it is three to four orders of magnitude stricter than every article-content instrument that actually binds these products (RoHS lead at 1,000,000 ug/kg of homogeneous material, the candlewick-core prohibition threshold at 600,000 ug/kg of wick-core metal, REACH cadmium in polymers at 100,000 ug/kg). No occurrence, percentile, feasibility or precautionary input touched the number in either direction. Determined on the refill fragrance oil charge by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS with collision/reaction-cell control of the interfered masses, with the article's non-emitting components digested and screened separately per this row's component plan. DISPOSITION OF THE ADDITIONAL ANALYSES THIS CELL MANDATES. This cell requires one analysis beyond the published test, and it carries a criterion and a lot consequence, so that no mandatory analysis on this row is an obligation without an outcome. COMPONENT RESULTS, THE FIRST ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS THIS CELL MANDATES. The published ceiling of 500 ug/kg governs the emitting material and is NOT transferred to a component's bulk content: a mains plug pin, a nickel-plated or tin-plated contact, a solder joint, a resistive or PTC heater element or a pigmented moulded housing is or may be substantially metal, metal-plated, metal-glazed or metal-pigmented by construction, and reading an emitting-material value against a structural component's bulk content would be exactly the basis conflation this row's basis guard exists to prevent, failing every compliant article for a metal that never enters the air. Every component result is instead dispositioned in three ordered branches, and no component result is left outside them. (a) WHERE A SOVEREIGN INSTRUMENT REACHES THE COMPONENT AND THIS ANALYTE, that instrument is the criterion. The instrument that reaches this row's components for lead is: EU Directive 2011/65/EU (RoHS) restricts lead to 1,000,000 ug/kg of any homogeneous material of electrical and electronic equipment (register row eu_rohs_2011_pb_homogeneous_materials_1000000), and this row's powered sub-assembly is such equipment, so its printed circuit assembly, solder joints, heater or drive element, plated contacts, pins and connectors, and moulded housing are each tested as separate homogeneous materials against that value. It is applied in its own basis at its own threshold, on the component it actually governs, and an exceedance blocks certification of the lot outright irrespective of the emitting-material result. That article-and-component value is never republished as this row's emitting-material limit, because it is three to four orders of magnitude looser and republishing it would misrepresent a component prohibition as a product permission. (b) WHERE THE COMPONENT IS IN THE EMISSION PATH (the wick, the refill vial with its cap and gasket, and the heated surface the wick contacts), the criterion is the published ceiling itself, applied where its basis makes it meaningful: the test is performed on emitting material sampled from the finished, filled and assembled article rather than from a pre-fill bulk batch, at the end of the declared shelf life or after the declared maximum continuous run of the heater, whichever is the more demanding, so that any lead transferred out of an emission-path component into the emitting material is carried into the published result rather than escaping it. An emitting-material result at or above 500 ug/kg fails the lot. A rising component result while the emitting material stays below the ceiling does not by itself fail the lot and falls to branch (c). (c) OTHERWISE, for a component outside the emission path that no sovereign instrument reaches for lead, the component result is dispositioned under the HMTc control-and-escalation rule, in the same terms this row's control cells already use: the result is held to ALARA against the manufacturer's demonstrated process capability for that formulation and component set; a result outside that capability band, or an unexplained step change between lots, triggers CAPA and raw-material traceback to the fragrance house, the wick supplier, the vial and closure moulder, the heater-element maker, the electronics contract manufacturer and the housing moulder with its pigment-masterbatch supplier; a confirmed uncontrolled source blocks certification until it is removed or substituted; and the analyte goes onto priority surveillance for this row. No component ceiling is invented in branch (c), because no credible sovereign government publishes a lead content maximum for these components in this product form, and an occupational exposure limit, an indoor-air guideline and an ambient-air standard are none of them converted into one.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market — total element content per unit mass of undiluted product as sold (µg/kg). Not a dietary basis, not a migration or leachate basis, and no use-pattern dilution credit.
rows.rationale: BVL 2017 Table 1 (German Federal Office of Consumer Protection and Food Safety, with the Länder cosmetics working group) publishes the technically avoidable heavy-metal content of cosmetic products in general; lead is 2.0 mg/kg, and a content above the table is treated as technically avoidable under good manufacturing practice. Its status is a federal-authority guidance value rather than a statute, and it is disclosed as such, but it is the strictest published sovereign finished-cosmetic lead maximum and Method v2.0 takes the strictest applicable value. The named comparator set shows how far the binding sits below the field: Health Canada, China NMPA 2015 and Taiwan MOHW 2024 are five times looser at 10 mg/kg; Korea, ASEAN and its Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia transpositions, and Kenya KS 2937:2021 are ten times looser at 20 mg/kg; Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations threshold is 125 times looser at 250 mg/kg. Two sovereign cosmetic lead values in the register are stricter than the binding — the BVL 2017 toothpaste tier at 500 µg/kg and Washington State's Toxics-Free Cosmetics Act toothpaste limit at 1000 µg/kg — and the compiler's stricter-unselected audit flags both on every row of this category. Neither is applicable. Both are scoped by their own instruments to toothpaste, a dentifrice that sits on the oral mucosa and is partly swallowed; that ingestion pathway is the stated reason the toothpaste tier is tighter. Categories 20 and 2 carry the dentifrice forms and use those instruments. A shampoo, body wash, scrub or depilatory has no ingestion pathway inside either instrument's scope, so reading a toothpaste tier onto a hair or body rinse-off product would have HMTc inventing a stricter number that no government set for this form. Method v2.0 forbids that as squarely as it forbids inventing a looser one: applicability is a real constraint, and the strictest APPLICABLE value governs. The compiler's audit also flags EU REACH Annex XVII entry 75, which sets 700 µg/kg for lead in mixtures placed on the market for tattooing and permanent make-up. That value is stricter than the binding and is deliberately not adopted: the instrument governs a mixture INJECTED INTO THE DERMIS, on a 'mixture for tattooing or permanent make-up by weight' basis, and a rinse-off shampoo or body wash is not such a mixture on any reading of the entry. The row is held out by this row's basis_guard as well as on scope. It is surfaced rather than filtered out of the scan so that the record shows it was found and disposed of, not missed. Colour-additive and colourant purity specifications (21 CFR 73 and 74, the New Zealand and Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles, the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 permitted-colours entries, the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant entries) are raw-material ingredient specifications, not finished-product maxima. They are held out of every cell by this row's basis_guard, and none of them is in any case stricter than the binding for this analyte. This row additionally names the two sovereign tiers written for mineral-bearing cosmetics, so that the record shows they were evaluated rather than passed over: EAEU TR CU 009/2011 sets 5 mg/kg for perfumery-cosmetic products containing more than 1 percent natural plant or natural mineral raw material, and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-9 carves powder products using clay as a raw material out of its 20 µg/g tier and gives them 50 µg/g. Both are LOOSER accommodations for the geogenic metal load of mineral raw materials, at 2.5 and 25 times the binding. Method v2.0 takes the strictest applicable value, so neither relaxes this row: a clay, pumice or salt scrub is certified at 2000 µg/kg like every other rinse-off form. Adopting the mineral accommodation would be selecting a number for convenience, which is the precise failure this method forbids.

rows.rationale: BVL 2017 Table 1 sets mercury in cosmetic products in general at 0.1 mg/kg, and BVL's toothpaste tier is the same value, so mercury carries no dentifrice split. The comparator set is deliberately wide here because mercury in cosmetics is the one contaminant with a hard, enforceable US rule and an active illegal-adulteration problem: 21 CFR 700.13(d)(2)(i) deems a cosmetic adulterated unless its mercury content is unavoidable under good manufacturing practice and below 1 ppm, and Hong Kong Cap. 640 sets the same 1 ppm expressly for unintentional trace mercury in cosmetics including skin-lightening products. Health Canada, China NMPA 2015, Korea MFDS, Taiwan MOHW 2024, ASEAN 2019 with its Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia transpositions, and the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 all land at the same 1 mg/kg; Kenya KS 2937:2021 is 2 mg/kg. The HMTc binding is therefore ten to twenty times stricter than every one of them. Mercury used as an intentional skin-lightening active, and the eye-area thiomersal and phenylmercuric preservative allowances in the India, Hong Kong and South Africa instruments, are ingredient permissions rather than contaminant ceilings; HMTc does not adopt them, and a rinse-off product formulated with an intentional mercury ingredient is not certifiable at all. Colour-additive and colourant purity specifications (21 CFR 73 and 74, the New Zealand and Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles, the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 permitted-colours entries, the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant entries) are raw-material ingredient specifications, not finished-product maxima. They are held out of every cell by this row's basis_guard, and none of them is in any case stricter than the binding for this analyte. The EAEU natural-plant-or-mineral raw-material tier (1 mg/kg) is named on this row and evaluated; at ten times the binding it does not relax it.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market — total element content per unit mass of undiluted product as sold (µg/kg). Not a dietary basis, not a migration or leachate basis, and no use-pattern dilution credit.
rows.rationale: Korea is the only jurisdiction in the register that sets a nickel content limit for finished cosmetics, and it tiers it by form: 10 µg/g for cosmetic products other than eye makeup and colour cosmetics, 30 µg/g for colour makeup, 35 µg/g for eye makeup. Every Category 14 form is a cleansing, conditioning, shaving, depilatory or hair-colouring preparation and none is an eye-makeup or colour-makeup product in the MFDS product taxonomy, so the strictest of the three tiers — 10 µg/g — is the directly applicable one, not a read-across. Korea MFDS Notice 2025-63 carries the same 10 µg/g value for the same scope and corroborates it; it is not named as a candidate because its register note contradicts its own value (the note reads '1 microgram/g = 1000 ug/kg' against a stored value of 10000 µg/kg), and a litigation-facing citation should not carry that discrepancy forward. The EU REACH restriction on nickel in tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures (5000 µg/kg) is stricter but governs a mixture injected into the dermis, a different form on a different basis, and is held out by this row's basis_guard. Nickel is a leading contact sensitiser, so the programme additionally holds it under ALARA post-publication and treats the published ceiling as an outer bound rather than a target.

rows.basis: Finished cosmetic total content as placed on market (ug/kg of product as sold); technically-unavoidable-impurity basis. Not migration, not leachate, not dietary, not an ingredient purity specification.
rows.rationale: The German table lists eye shadow, eyeliner and kajal in its higher-lead group at 5000 ug/kg; mascara, brow products, lash adhesives and lash serums are not listed and take the general branch at 2000. Both branches are named. The row binds at 2000 because that is the government value for the unlisted forms and is protective of the listed ones; the next instruments are China NMPA 2015, Health Canada and Taiwan MOHW 2024 at 10000, then Korea, Singapore, the ASEAN transpositions and Kenya at 20000. For eye shadow and eyeliner considered alone the government value is 5000, so this row's ceiling is disclosed over-compliance for those forms. No colour-additive or ingredient purity specification is used as an anchor: the US 21 CFR 73/74 cosmetic-use specifications (10000-20000 ug/kg), the India permitted-colour specification (20000), the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant specification (20000) and the New Zealand / Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles (10000) bound one raw material's purity rather than the finished product, they are refused by this row's basis guard, and every one of them is looser than the binding value in any event.

rows.basis: Finished cosmetic total content as placed on market (ug/kg of product as sold); technically-unavoidable-impurity basis. Not migration, not leachate, not dietary, not an ingredient purity specification.
rows.rationale: Korea MFDS is the ONLY authority in the register that publishes a nickel maximum for a finished cosmetic, and the instrument tiers it by product class: eye makeup 35000 ug/kg, colour makeup 30000, all other cosmetics 10000. Method step 4 requires the government's own product-form split to be preserved, so the applicable branch is selected rather than the strictest branch overall. Both register transpositions of the instrument (MFDS Notice 2024-9 and Notice 2025-63) are named and carry identical values, which is the cross-edition check. No other credible authority publishes a cosmetic nickel ceiling: the EU prohibits nickel compounds as intentional cosmetic ingredients under Regulation 1223/2009 Annex II without setting a numeric trace maximum, and Germany's BVL 2017 table covers only lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury and antimony. This row is MIXED against the Korean product classes: eye shadows, eyeliners, mascara and brow colour products sit inside the eye-makeup class at 35000 ug/kg, while false-lash adhesives and lash and brow conditioning serums are treatment products rather than eye makeup and take the 'other cosmetics' branch at 10000. Because one published ceiling has to be protective for every form certified against the row, the row binds at 10000 ug/kg. That is three and a half times stricter than the Korean value for the row's colour forms and is disclosed over-compliance for them. Nickel on the lid margin is the most consequential sensitisation site in this category, so the aggregation happens to run in the protective direction here; the REASON for the value is nonetheless the mixed membership of the row, not a precautionary override, which Method v2.0 retires. The Korean eye-makeup branch of 35000 ug/kg is preserved on the traditional-eye-cosmetics row, where every form does sit inside it.

rows.basis: total lead content of the product as placed on the market (consumer-chemical product-content basis; disclosed read-across)
rows.rationale: Program-wide consistency ruling (2026-08-17): the German BVL 2017 orientation values are treated as SELECTABLE anchors across HMTc. The live Category 15 standard tags three of these same register rows regulatory-alignment, and Categories 2, 13, 14 and 20 bind them directly, so the earlier Category 19 position that a register status of 'guidance impurity limit' makes them unselectable contradicted five sibling categories on the identical rows, and did so in the looser direction (5x on lead, 50x on cadmium, 4x on total arsenic, 10x on total mercury). BVL is a single coherent sovereign consumer-chemical regime covering all four toxics, so reading it across preserves this category's own rule of adopting one coherent regime per analyte rather than picking the lowest number across regimes. The China NMPA 2015 value previously published is retained as a named looser comparator. Whether a national enforcement orientation value ranks as a sovereign maximum level is a genuine governance question, recorded for ratification as OI-20260817-bvl-selectability-ruling; until it is ruled on, every category states the same rule. Previously bound: cn_nmpa2015_pb_cosmetics_10.
