rows.basis: drained product as sold, wet weight
rows.rationale: R1 direct maximum levels; the row binds the strictest applicable to any member. WHY THE COMMODITY CLASSES REACH THE PICKLED FORM UNDER THIS INSTRUMENT. MERCOSUR writes separate rows where it intends a processed form to have its own value: table olives and tomato concentrates each get one. It writes NO pickled-cucumber, sauerkraut, kimchi or pickled-onion row, and its vegetable classes are written without a 'fresh' qualifier ('fruiting vegetables of the Cucurbitaceae family', 'bulb vegetables and sheathing leaves'), in contrast to its fruit classes, which are expressly 'fresh fruits excluding berries and small fruits'. A pickled cucumber is a fruiting vegetable of the Cucurbitaceae family, so under MERCOSUR it sits in that class at 100 ug/kg, and a pickled onion sits in the bulb class at 100 ug/kg. This is the same canon of construction this category applies to Israel for dried fruit: where an instrument demonstrably knows how to write a carve-out for a processed form and declines to, the commodity class governs. CORRECTION OF RECORD: an earlier draft of this cell published 300 ug/kg on the table-olive rows alone, with Hong Kong vegetables at 500 ug/kg as the only other named candidate. Table olives are one member of this row; the dominant members had no named candidate at all, and the fresh commodity classes three times stricter were named nowhere and dispositioned nowhere. The row's scan could not surface them because its audit_scope carried only pickle, ferment and olive tokens and its exclusion list carried a bare 'fruit' token that also matched 'fruiting vegetables'; both have been widened and narrowed respectively so the scan can now see these rows. CONSISTENCY WITH THIS ROW'S OTHER ARSENIC CELL: the inorganic-arsenic cell already applies exactly this reasoning, reading 60 ug/kg across from the fresh fruits-and-vegetables class on the ground that acidification, fermentation and brining do not create or concentrate arsenic in the drained product. That argument is analyte-level, not species-level, so it applies with identical force to total arsenic; publishing 300 ug/kg for total arsenic while reading 60 ug/kg across for the species was internally contradictory. THE LEAD CELL IS DIFFERENT ON PURPOSE AND THAT IS NOT A CONTRADICTION: there, Hong Kong writes an express pickled-cucumber lead row at 100 ug/kg against its fresh cucurbit value of 50 ug/kg, so a sovereign has expressly ruled that brine contact adds a lead pathway the fresh value does not cover, and the express pickled row is the applicable cell. No sovereign writes any pickled-form arsenic row, so no such ruling exists for arsenic and the commodity class governs. CONSEQUENCE, DISCLOSED: the table-olive members are held at 100 ug/kg against the 300 ug/kg their own MERCOSUR class allows, which is the same strictest-member over-compliance this row already applies to lead (table olives held at the pickled-cucumber value) and cadmium (fermented brassicas held at the table-olive value). Splitting table olives out of this row is the recommended taxonomy fix. Total arsenic is never satisfied by the inorganic-arsenic cell; both are reported, and the 60 ug/kg species value remains the operative arsenic constraint.

rows.basis: drained_as_sold
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum level for any solid food in any jurisdiction. The register's only INGESTED Cr(VI) parameters are drinking-water maxima (Australia NHMRC 2025, 50 ug/L, nhmrc2025_crvi_drinking_water_50; California SWRCB, 10 ug/L, us_ca_swrcb_2024_cr-vi_chromium-hexavalent_mcl_10ugl and ca_swrcb_crvi_drinking_water_10), which are water-basis parameters expressed per litre of a consumed liquid and supply no applicable ceiling for a solid produce row in this row's native basis; every remaining Cr(VI) row in the register is an article or material limit (toys, textiles, leather, fertilisers, electrical equipment). rows.basis: as sold, finished product (wet weight)
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets a lead maximum level for a meat analogue, so the exact cell is unregulated and the ceiling reads across from the maximum levels governing the principal protein components. Hong Kong Cap. 132V sets 0.1 mg/kg for pulses and 0.1 mg/kg for legume vegetables, the commodity classes from which pea and soy protein are drawn; FSANZ Schedule 19 sets 0.2 mg/kg for cereals, the class from which wheat gluten is drawn. The strictest applicable component value binds at 100 ug/kg, so a wheat-gluten-based analogue is held to the pulse ceiling rather than the looser cereal one. BASIS TREATMENT, DISCLOSED IN THE DIRECTION IT ACTUALLY CUTS: the component maximum levels are written on dry commodities as placed on the market and are applied to the hydrated finished product as sold, with no dry-to-wet conversion, because Method v2.0 forbids inventing a basis conversion. That is the LOOSER of the two available treatments, not a conservative one: a hydrated extrudate is mostly water, so a protein ingredient can exceed its own commodity maximum level and still leave the finished product inside this ceiling. The programme states that openly and closes the gap with a second, independent requirement rather than with a conversion factor: every certified lot must carry supplier documentation of the source commodity for each protein ingredient, tested against the named component maximum levels in the commodity own basis, in addition to finished-product compliance against this ceiling. The ingredient-basis treatment is the natural candidate for the first Standards Ratchet review on this row once eligible certified-lot data exist. ADDED-FAT FRACTION, ADOPTED (adversarial audit, 2026-08-17): the superseded component set named only protein-source commodities and published 100 ug/kg, which was not the strictest applicable value for a declared component. Added fat is a principal component of this product form, typically 10-20% by mass and frequently exceeding the protein fraction, and two credible sovereigns regulate it: Hong Kong Cap. 132V sets 0.08 mg/kg for edible fats and oils and EU Regulation (EU) 2023/915 sets 0.1 mg/kg for fats and oils including milk fat. Both are named and the stricter binds, lowering this cell from 100 to 80 ug/kg. Declining the fat rows would have been indefensible on this row's own logic: it already applies the cereal maximum level to a formulation that may contain no wheat gluten at all, so excluding a commodity class present in essentially every formulation, solely because its maximum level is stricter, would be a selection made for convenience rather than compelled by the instruments. The Hong Kong fat-spreads-and-blended-spreads row (hk_cap132v_pb_fat-spreads-and-blended-spreads_80) sits at the same 80 ug/kg and is not separately named: a table spread is a finished food, not a formulation fat, and naming it would not change the binding value. PRINCIPAL-COMPONENT BOUNDARY, APPLIED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: the principal components of this row are the plant-protein fraction (pulses, legume vegetables, soy, and cereal/wheat gluten) and the added-fat fraction (edible fats and oils). Widening this row's audit scope to include vegetable, fat and oil tokens surfaces discrete vegetable-commodity rows that are NOT principal components, and they are reviewed and declined on that single stated ground. The boundary is the same one that COMPELLED adoption of the added-fat rows in the lead and total-arsenic cells: added fat is 10-20% of formulation mass and is present in essentially every formulation, so its stricter maximum levels bind. A fruiting-vegetable, brassica or leafy-vegetable maximum level governs a discrete vegetable commodity that enters a meat analogue, if at all, as a minor flavour, colour or binding ingredient at low single-digit percentages of formulation weight. Declining those rows is therefore not a strictness judgement made for convenience; it is the same mass-fraction and commodity-identity test that produced two tightenings in this same row. A lot whose formulation is principally vegetable rather than pulse, soy, cereal protein or added fat is not certified on this row at all: it routes to the vegetable rows in Categories 27 and 28. AUDIT DISPOSITION — hk_cap132v_pb_fruiting-vegetables-cucurbits_50 and hk_cap132v_pb_fruiting-vegetables-other-than-cucurbits_50 (0.05 mg/kg each, Hong Kong): REVIEWED AND DECLINED on that ground. Cucurbits (cucumber, squash, melon) and non-cucurbit fruiting vegetables (tomato, pepper, aubergine) are not protein or fat sources and are not principal components of a meat analogue; Cap. 132V regulates them as fresh vegetable commodities in their own right. BASIS DIRECTION FOR THE FAT COMPONENT, DISCLOSED: the treatment cuts the OPPOSITE way for the fat fraction than it does for the protein commodities, and the programme states both rather than only the flattering one. A dry protein commodity is CONCENTRATED relative to the hydrated finished product, so applying its maximum level to the finished product is the LOOSER treatment (disclosed above). Added fat is DILUTED in the finished product, typically 10-20% of mass, so applying the edible-fats-and-oils maximum level to the whole finished product is the STRICTER treatment: the finished patty must meet a ceiling written for neat oil. The programme does not choose between these directions to suit a preferred number. Method v2.0 takes the strictest applicable component value in the row's native basis and invents no basis conversion in either direction, and the consequence here is simply that this row's lead ceiling is set by its fat fraction while its cadmium and nickel ceilings are set by its protein fraction. Certification accordingly requires source-commodity documentation for the added-fat ingredient tested in its own basis, exactly as it does for each protein ingredient.

rows.basis: as sold, finished product (wet weight)
rows.rationale: Two Hong Kong Cap. 132V rows govern the principal components of this row and both are named. PULSE AND LEGUME-VEGETABLE COMPONENT (pea and soy protein): Cap. 132V sets 0.01 mg/kg total mercury for 'Vegetables, other than edible fungi'. That row covers pulses and legume vegetables, and the instrument's own drafting convention establishes it three times over. In the cadmium item the residual row is written 'Vegetables (other than those vegetables specified in this item)' and sits alongside separately named 'Pulses' and 'Legume vegetables' rows, which is only coherent if pulses and legume vegetables are vegetables within the item. In the total-chromium item the row is written 'Vegetables, other than pulses', a carve-out that would be unnecessary if 'Vegetables' did not otherwise include them. In the total-arsenic item the row is written 'Vegetables' with no carve-out at all and no separate pulses row, so pulses take the vegetables value. The mercury item carves out ONLY edible fungi (which take their own 0.1 mg/kg row) and writes no separate pulses or legume-vegetable row, so pulses and legume vegetables fall inside the 0.01 mg/kg vegetables row. This is the same commodity class this config already names for lead (hk_cap132v_pb_pulses_100, hk_cap132v_pb_legume-vegetables_100) and for nickel (eu2024_ni_pulses_4000, eu2024_ni_legume_vegetables_1000), so Hong Kong does set a mercury value covering components this row is built from. CEREAL COMPONENT (wheat gluten): Cap. 132V sets 0.02 mg/kg total mercury for rice, husked rice, polished rice, maize, maize flour, wheat and wheat flour. The strictest applicable component value binds at 10 ug/kg. CORRECTION OF RECORD (adversarial audit, 2026-08-17): the superseded substantiation for this cell asserted that 'no credible instrument sets a mercury value for pulses or soy beans' and published 20 ug/kg on the cereal row alone. That assertion was FALSE against the register it was compiled from, and it published a ceiling twice the strictest applicable value. The compiler's stricter-unselected safety net could not catch it because this row's audit-scope regex matched no token in the scope string 'Vegetables, other than edible fungi'; 'vegetable' has been added to the scope regex so that commodity-group rows covering a component without naming it surface in future scans. The resulting 10 ug/kg ceiling is five times stricter than the 50 ug/kg terrestrial-meat mercury ceiling elsewhere in this category. That asymmetry is a fact about the sovereign instruments and is disclosed, not harmonised: the method selects the strictest applicable component value and does not adjust a plant-matrix ceiling upward to match an animal-matrix one. rows.basis: as sold, finished product (wet weight)
rows.rationale: This is the one row in Category 11 where nickel is NOT a control, because the EU nickel maximum levels are drawn over exactly the plant commodities this row is formulated from. All four applicable component rows are named and disclosed: cereals 0.8 mg/kg, legume vegetables 1.0 mg/kg, pulses 4.0 mg/kg, soy beans and edamame 6.0 mg/kg. The strictest applicable component value binds at 800 ug/kg. Nickel matters here in a way it does not for muscle meat: pulses and soy are genuine nickel accumulators, and catalytic hydrogenation of plant fats is a nickel pathway, so a plant-protein analogue is the form in which a nickel ceiling is both available and warranted. The looser soy-bean oilseed row (15 mg/kg) and dry-bean row (12 mg/kg) were reviewed and not adopted: they describe whole oilseed and dry pulse commodities rather than the protein fraction used here, and adopting them would loosen the ceiling by an order of magnitude for no instrument-compelled reason. ADDED-FAT FRACTION: no credible sovereign government sets a nickel maximum level for edible fats and oils, so the added-fat fraction contributes no candidate to this cell. PRINCIPAL-COMPONENT BOUNDARY, APPLIED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: the principal components of this row are the plant-protein fraction (pulses, legume vegetables, soy, and cereal/wheat gluten) and the added-fat fraction (edible fats and oils). Widening this row's audit scope to include vegetable, fat and oil tokens surfaces discrete vegetable-commodity rows that are NOT principal components, and they are reviewed and declined on that single stated ground. The boundary is the same one that COMPELLED adoption of the added-fat rows in the lead and total-arsenic cells: added fat is 10-20% of formulation mass and is present in essentially every formulation, so its stricter maximum levels bind. A fruiting-vegetable, brassica or leafy-vegetable maximum level governs a discrete vegetable commodity that enters a meat analogue, if at all, as a minor flavour, colour or binding ingredient at low single-digit percentages of formulation weight. Declining those rows is therefore not a strictness judgement made for convenience; it is the same mass-fraction and commodity-identity test that produced two tightenings in this same row. A lot whose formulation is principally vegetable rather than pulse, soy, cereal protein or added fat is not certified on this row at all: it routes to the vegetable rows in Categories 27 and 28. AUDIT DISPOSITION — eu2024_ni_fruiting_veg_400 (fruiting vegetables, 0.4 mg/kg), eu2024_ni_brassica_500 (brassica vegetables, 0.5 mg/kg) and eu2024_ni_leafy_veg_500 (leafy vegetables except fresh herbs, 0.5 mg/kg): REVIEWED AND DECLINED on that ground. Each governs a discrete fresh vegetable commodity, none of which is a protein or fat source for this product form. The four named nickel components remain the protein commodities this row is actually formulated from, and no credible sovereign sets a nickel maximum level for edible fats and oils. AUDIT DISPOSITION — eu2024_ni_juice_250 (fruit/vegetable juices and nectars, 0.25 mg/kg): REVIEWED AND DECLINED on a second and independent ground as well. A juice or nectar is a finished beverage commodity in a liquid basis, not an ingredient of a formulated solid analogue; adopting a beverage maximum level as the ceiling for a burger patty would be both a scope and a basis conflation.

rows.basis: as consumed, ready-to-drink liquid (read across from the sovereign dairy-milk cell)
rows.rationale: A almond, oat, cashew, coconut, hemp or pea drink is not milk, and this is stated rather than glossed: the read-across rests on form and use, not on composition. The candidate set was the sovereign cells reachable in the same as-consumed liquid basis: the Hong Kong milk cell (20 ug/kg), the EU and Codex fruit-juice cells (30 ug/kg, a juice this product is not), and the Hong Kong carbonated-beverage cell (200 ug/kg, a carbonation form this product does not take). The milk cell is both the nearest by form and use and the strictest of those three, so no convenience selection is available among them. The packaged-drinking-water quality standards are stricter still (US 21 CFR 165.110 lead at 5 ug/kg, Hong Kong packaged drinking water at 10 ug/kg) and were considered and rejected on applicability: they govern water sold as water, they are Category 8 instruments under the taxonomy boundary rule, and a plant-based drink is an opaque formulated beverage carrying several percent suspended and dissolved plant solids plus mineral fortificants, which is not the matrix those standards were written for. The row's nut, oat and seed bases are grown in soils whose lead burden varies by origin, which is why lead is a mandatory lot test and a Standards Ratchet surveillance analyte here rather than a formality. The dry-commodity lead cells for the source seed, grain or nut are written in an as-sold dry basis and are deliberately NOT applied to the liquid drink; converting between them would require an invented dilution factor, which Method v2.0 confines to the infant-formula 8:1 reconstitution and forbids elsewhere.

rows.basis: as_consumed
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign sets an aluminium maximum level for a soy-based plant drink. The only sovereign aluminium values in a dietary basis are the packaged-drinking-water quality standards (US 21 CFR 165.110 secondary allowable level 200 ug/kg, EU 2020/2184, Health Canada 2900 ug/kg), which govern water sold as water and are Category 8 instruments, and the FSANZ infant-formula aluminium limits, which are Category 1 and are excluded from this category's anchor set by the taxonomy boundary rule. In this form aluminium is a packaging and processing signal (aluminium cans and can linings, closures, filter aids, additive carry-over) rather than a raw-material contaminant. Plant-based drinks additionally carry mineral-fortification premixes and stabiliser systems, so an aluminium result is investigated against the fortificant and stabiliser specifications as well as the packaging.

rows.basis: total lead content of the accessible component, of the dried coating film and of any applied sticker or film (mg/kg)
rows.rationale: Five directly applicable total-content instruments are named and the strictest is taken. The US CPSIA s.101 children's-product substrate limit (100 mg/kg for any part of the product) and the 16 CFR 1303 surface-coating limit (90 mg/kg on the weight of the total non-volatile content of the dried paint film) both reach a play yard, gate or play enclosure as a children's product; Canada SOR/2018-83 s.2(1) sets 90 mg/kg in each accessible part of consumer products for the sleep, relaxation, hygiene, carrying or transport of children under four; Canada SOR/2016-193 s.2(1) sets 90 mg/kg in a dried sample of surface coating material and s.6 sets 90 mg/kg in stickers, films and applied surface coatings on accessible parts of furniture and products for children. HMTc publishes 90 mg/kg and applies it to every accessible component, including the substrate whose own federal US limit is 100 mg/kg. The EU REACH Annex XVII entry 63 mouthable-article value (500 mg/kg) and the brass-alloy exception (5 000 mg/kg) are far looser and are not selected. A play yard and a safety gate are children's products under CPSIA and are products for the relaxation and play of a child under four under SOR/2018-83. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value.

rows.basis: total cadmium content of the component material (mg/kg of the homogenised component or of the dried coating film)
rows.rationale: All three candidates are TOTAL-CONTENT limits, so the strictest-of-components selection compares like with like. The EU REACH Annex XVII entry 23 plastic-material value (100 mg/kg) binds the article's moulded polymer components DIRECTLY; the EU painted-article value (1 000 mg/kg) binds its paint layer directly; the Australian coating value (75 mg/kg) is scoped to toys coated with a material and is therefore READ ACROSS to the coatings of a play yard, playpen, safety gate or play enclosure, which is not a toy but is a coated article for the same child, in the same mouthing and handling contact. Because the read-across value is the strictest of the three it becomes the published ceiling and is applied to every accessible component, including the polymer components whose own direct limit is 100 mg/kg — deliberate over-compliance, disclosed rather than silent. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value. COMPLIANCE OBLIGATION, stated so this record cannot be read as certifying a value the licensee cannot lawfully sell. The cadmium ceiling published on this row is 75 mg/kg, which sits ABOVE the Washington Children's Safe Product Act prohibition on cadmium exceeding 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component (register row wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b); the Act is codified in Washington's RCW chapter 70A.430). That Act's own definition of a children's product enumerates car seats, products designed to help a child sleep, relax or feed, and products worn as clothing by children, which reaches most of the forms certified on this row. A lot returning cadmium above 40 mg/kg would therefore conform to the HMTc ceiling and still be unlawful to sell in Washington. Any such result is escalated as a jurisdiction-specific regulatory hard stop under the HMTc legal-violation rule and is never certified without that qualification, pending scope-resolved re-ingest of the Washington row through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. The Minnesota cadmium value (75 mg/kg, register row mn_325e3892_2025_cd_covered_consumer_products_75ppm) equals the published ceiling rather than undercutting it, so a lot conforming here conforms there. Where the article incorporates a battery or a battery-powered module — a vibration unit, a sound or music module, a night light, a powered mobile or a powered rocker — the battery is a distinct regulated article with its own instrument, and its limits are not this row's. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 restricts cadmium in a portable battery whether or not incorporated into an appliance (register row eu_batteries_2023_cd_portable_batteries_20000, 20 mg/kg) and mercury in a battery (register row eu_batteries_2023_thg_batteries_5000, 5 mg/kg), both expressed on the weight of the battery. Both are stricter than the values published here and both are recorded as companion obligations on the battery in a battery-by-weight basis; the battery is never homogenised into an accessible-component sample and its instrument is never merged into this row's component-content ceiling.

rows.basis: total mercury content of the accessible component material and of the dried non-volatile coating film (mg/kg) — the sovereign value is written for surface coating material and is extended by disclosed read-across, not asserted as direct alignment
rows.rationale: The published value is 10 mg/kg, but it is reached by DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS and not by direct regulatory alignment, because the instrument's scope is narrower than the cell this row publishes. Canada SOR/2016-193 s.5 sets 10 mg/kg total mercury in a dried sample of SURFACE COATING MATERIAL; the register's product_scope for that row is 'surface coating material', which is the coating substance itself. The same instrument distinguishes that scope from the applied-coating scope — its s.6 reaches a sticker, film or surface coating material applied to accessible parts of furniture and products for children (register row ca_sor2016_193_pb_applied_stickers_films_coatings_90000) — and s.6 is lead-only, with no mercury analogue anywhere in the register. Publishing s.5 as a DIRECT sovereign ceiling for the homogenised wood, steel tube, moulded polymer, foam and textile of a play yard, playpen, safety gate or play enclosure would therefore over-read the instrument, which is the defect this cell was rebuilt to remove. HMTc reaches the value in two disclosed steps instead. Step one reads s.5 across from the coating material as such to the dried applied film on the finished article; the nearest sovereign instrument written in exactly that applied-coating scope is Canada Toys Regulations SOR/2011-17 s.23(1)(c) (register row ca_sor2011_17_thg_accessible_toy_coating_10), which sets the same 10 mg/kg for total mercury in surface coating materials applied to accessible parts of a child's article, so step one lands on a number a sovereign has already written for an applied coating on a children's product. Step two extends that same 10 mg/kg to every accessible component of a play yard, playpen, safety gate or play enclosure, which no sovereign requires and which HMTc adopts as deliberate over-compliance, disclosed here rather than applied silently. At 10 mg/kg the value is six times stricter than the Australian toy-coating mercury value (60 mg/kg, register row au_customs_1956_thg_toys_coating_60mgkg). The EN 71-3 Category III scraped-off-material total-mercury migration value (94 mg/kg, register row eu_2009_48_cat3_thg_toy_migration) measures transfer rather than content, is looser, and is excluded by this row's basis guard.

rows.basis: hexavalent chromium content on the total dry weight of the component (mg/kg) — leather, coating film, or plated and conversion-coated metal part
rows.rationale: This is the only hexavalent-chromium CONTENT limit in the register that reaches a skin-contact article, and it binds DIRECTLY wherever a play yard, playpen, safety gate or play enclosure carries a leather part in skin contact — a leather handlebar or bumper-bar wrap, a harness pad, a leather trim panel or a leather pull tab. For the article's non-leather Cr(VI) pathways — chromate-pigmented coatings, chromate conversion coatings and hexavalent chrome plating on metal parts — no sovereign sets a content maximum, so the 3 mg/kg value is READ ACROSS to them and applied article-wide. The read-across is disclosed and is argued from the material and the contact, not from convenience: it keeps the SAME analyte (Cr(VI) specifically, not total chromium) and the SAME basis (mg/kg of the component's dry mass), and crosses only a material boundary, from chrome-tanned leather to a chromate-pigmented or chromate-passivated surface. The hazard is identical (Cr(VI) skin sensitisation) and the route is identical (dermal transfer under sweat from a surface held against the child), which is exactly why entry 47 was written for skin-contact leather in the first place. Applying it article-wide is deliberate over-compliance and is the same rule this row applies to lead (90 mg/kg applied to a substrate whose own US limit is 100 mg/kg) and to cadmium (75 mg/kg applied to polymer components whose own EU limit is 100 mg/kg); declining to extend it to Cr(VI), the analyte where compliance costs a supplier a change of passivation chemistry, would be selective over-compliance and is not done. The EU RoHS 0.1 % homogeneous-material Cr(VI) value is scoped to electrical and electronic equipment and is over three hundred times more permissive, so it is not used as the read-across source. The EN 71-3 Category I and II Cr(VI) migration values are numerically lower but are leachate limits measuring transfer rather than content, and are excluded by this row's basis guard.

rows.basis: as sold, edible portion (wet weight)
rows.rationale: Two credible sovereign instruments regulate this exact cell and agree: FSANZ Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code Schedule 19 sets 0.1 mg/kg for meat of cattle, sheep, pig and poultry excluding offal, and Hong Kong Cap. 132V Part 2 sets 0.1 mg/kg for meat of cattle, pig, goat and sheep. The corresponding EU Regulation (EU) 2023/915 and Codex CXS 193-1995 muscle-meat lead rows are ABSENT from this register and are therefore not named and not assigned a value from memory; they are recorded as register gaps for ingestion through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. Because Method v2.0 selects the strictest applicable value, ingesting them can only lower this cell or leave it unchanged, never raise it, and this cell must be re-derived when they land. The looser edible-offal lead maximum levels (Hong Kong 0.15-0.20 mg/kg, FSANZ 0.5 mg/kg) are a DIFFERENT product scope and are deliberately not used to anchor this muscle-meat row: Porcine offal is a separately-tested sub-lot governed by the offal maximum levels of its own species. BASIS OF THE BINDING INSTRUMENT, DISCLOSED: the two concurring instruments are written on DIFFERENT bases. FSANZ Schedule 19 states its maximum level for the portion ordinarily consumed (an as-consumed basis); Hong Kong Cap. 132V states the identical 0.1 mg/kg as-sold, for the edible portion after removal of bones and fat (Cap. 132V Part 2 Note 1). Because this row publishes an as-sold ceiling, the Hong Kong as-sold row is named as the binding instrument and the FSANZ row is disclosed as an independent sovereign value concurring at the same number. The published ceiling therefore rests on an instrument written in this row's own basis, and no as-consumed value is relabelled as-sold. The number is unaffected: both instruments sit at 100 ug/kg, so the strictest-applicable selection is identical either way.

rows.basis: as_sold
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets an inorganic-arsenic maximum level for terrestrial red-meat muscle tissue. rows.basis: as_sold
rows.rationale: Inorganic tin in food is a tinplate-packaging pathway: tin migrates into the food from the internal surface of an unlacquered or damaged tinplate can, which is why every credible sovereign tin maximum level on the register is written against canned food rather than against the food itself. Fresh, chilled, frozen and vacuum- or modified-atmosphere-packed red meat is not packed in tinplate, so the pathway that the canned-food maximum levels exist to control is absent and no sovereign number governs the cell. A lot of this product form that is retorted or packed in a metal can is not certified against this row at all: it is certified against the canned-meats row, whose tin cell carries the binding canned-foods maximum level. No tin ceiling is invented for the non-canned form.

rows.basis: as_sold
rows.rationale: Hexavalent chromium is not stable in this matrix. Raw and cooked red-meat muscle tissue is a wet, reducing, protein- and thiol-rich medium; Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by tissue reductants (cysteine, glutathione, ascorbate) and by the acid and heat of digestion and cooking, so a Cr(VI) figure reported on such a matrix is an artifact of the extraction chemistry of the total-chromium screen rather than a measurement of a species that persists in the food. The determination follows the same reference-method adjudication recorded for the hexavalent-chromium cell in the infant-formula category (data/workbench standards Cr-VI adjudication), applied here to an animal-tissue matrix. Hexavalent chromium is in any event a species of, and bounded by, the published total-chromium screen (Cr-VI <= total Cr).

rows.basis: as sold, ug of element per kg of the emitting material (product as tested)
rows.rationale: No government anywhere sets a lead content maximum for an air freshener, plug-in evaporator, puff releaser, candle body, wax melt, oil or nebula diffuser, gel or reed diffuser, incense stick, potpourri, vacuum-cleaner fragrance additive or fragrance refill. The only sovereign heavy-metal instrument in any jurisdiction that names a product in this category is the United States CPSC prohibition on lead-cored candlewicks, 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13), mirrored by Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956; it restricts lead in the metal of a wick core and covers no other analyte and no other product form. The cell is therefore a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS, and it is taken on the axis the regulators themselves used: route of administration. Colorado's 2022 heavy-metal table and Maryland's Technical Authority Rev. 6.0 both publish a route LADDER over the same underlying matrices, with the inhalation row strictest, the oral row looser and the topical or cutaneous row looser still. The value is therefore a function of the route, not of the source matrix's chemistry, and Colorado scopes its strictest row in the instrument's own words to "inhaled product or audited product administered by metered-dose nasal spray", which describes a delivery mechanism this category shares. Maryland's own route gap is the sharpest available evidence for that reading: its inhalation-route total-chromium value is 600 ug/kg while its oral and cutaneous values for the same products are 1,100,000 ug/kg. Selected value 500 ug/kg, from Colorado (co2022 inhaled/nasal row). California DCC section 15723 independently sets the identical 0.5 ug/g for inhalable products (us_ca_dcc_2026_pb_inhalable_cannabis_0_5ugg), so two sub-national regulators converge on this value. The looser or route-unspecific values on the register are recorded and NOT selected: Maryland inhalation route 1000 ug/kg, Massachusetts all-uses protocol 500 ug/kg (equal but route-unspecific), Nevada 1200 ug/kg, Israel IMC-GMP Procedure 152 5000 ug/kg. The basis is identical to this row's native basis, micrograms of element per kilogram of product as tested, so no basis conversion, no reconstitution and no dry-to-wet adjustment is performed. The read-across is published as `read-across` and never as `regulatory-alignment`, because no instrument regulates this exact cell. Adopting it tightens rather than relaxes the applicable regulatory position: it is three to four orders of magnitude stricter than every article-content instrument that actually binds these products (RoHS lead at 1,000,000 ug/kg of homogeneous material, the candlewick-core prohibition threshold at 600,000 ug/kg of wick-core metal, REACH cadmium in polymers at 100,000 ug/kg). No occurrence, percentile, feasibility or precautionary input touched the number in either direction. Determined on the dried botanical mass with its applied oil and dye, homogenised across the retail unit, with the sachet material analysed as a separate component by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS with collision/reaction-cell control of the interfered masses, with the article's non-emitting components digested and screened separately per this row's component plan. DISPOSITION OF THE ADDITIONAL ANALYSES THIS CELL MANDATES. This cell requires one analysis beyond the published test, and it carries a criterion and a lot consequence, so that no mandatory analysis on this row is an obligation without an outcome. COMPONENT RESULTS, THE FIRST ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS THIS CELL MANDATES. The published ceiling of 500 ug/kg governs the emitting material and is NOT transferred to a component's bulk content: a metal or plastic closure or hanging hardware, a decorative mineral, shell or coral element, or a mordanted or chrome-pigmented sachet fabric is or may be substantially metal, metal-plated, metal-glazed or metal-pigmented by construction, and reading an emitting-material value against a structural component's bulk content would be exactly the basis conflation this row's basis guard exists to prevent, failing every compliant article for a metal that never enters the air. Every component result is instead dispositioned in three ordered branches, and no component result is left outside them. (a) WHERE A SOVEREIGN INSTRUMENT REACHES THE COMPONENT AND THIS ANALYTE, that instrument is the criterion. For lead and this row's components, branch (a) is EMPTY, and the instruments checked before saying so are named rather than waved at: EU RoHS 2011/65/EU is scoped to the homogeneous materials of electrical and electronic equipment and this row carries no powered sub-assembly; Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 on batteries is scoped to batteries and this row contains none; REACH Annex XVII entry 63 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2015/628 (eu_2015_628_pb_mouthable_general_public_articles_0_05pct) reaches only articles supplied to the general public that may be placed in the mouth by children; Regulation (EU) 2018/1513 reaches consumer clothing and skin-contact textiles and does not reach a packaging, sachet or decorative textile that is not worn; the EU Toy Safety Directive 2009/48/EC with EN 71-3, the CPSIA surface-coating limit and the Canadian and Australian toy-coating limits reach accessible toy material and toy surface coatings, and none of these articles is a toy; 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13) reaches only the metal of a candlewick core and this row has no wick core; the food-contact ceramic, glassware and enamelware instruments reach only articles intended to come into contact with food. Every component result on this row therefore falls to branch (b) or branch (c), and neither leaves a result without a criterion or without a lot consequence. (b) WHERE THE COMPONENT IS IN THE EMISSION PATH (the dried botanical mass with its applied oil and dye, any decorative mineral, shell, coral or other marine element in contact with it, and the fabric, paper or mesh through which the fragrance passes), the criterion is the published ceiling itself, applied where its basis makes it meaningful: the test is performed on emitting material sampled from the finished, filled and assembled article rather than from a pre-fill bulk batch, at the end of the declared shelf life at the declared storage conditions, with the sample homogenised across the retail unit, so that any lead transferred out of an emission-path component into the emitting material is carried into the published result rather than escaping it. An emitting-material result at or above 500 ug/kg fails the lot. A rising component result while the emitting material stays below the ceiling does not by itself fail the lot and falls to branch (c). (c) OTHERWISE, for a component outside the emission path that no sovereign instrument reaches for lead, the component result is dispositioned under the HMTc control-and-escalation rule, in the same terms this row's control cells already use: the result is held to ALARA against the manufacturer's demonstrated process capability for that formulation and component set; a result outside that capability band, or an unexplained step change between lots, triggers CAPA and raw-material traceback to the botanical grower and consolidator by country and region of origin, the fragrance house, the dye supplier, the sachet-fabric supplier and the closure and hardware supplier; a confirmed uncontrolled source blocks certification until it is removed or substituted; and the analyte goes onto priority surveillance for this row. No component ceiling is invented in branch (c), because no credible sovereign government publishes a lead content maximum for these components in this product form, and an occupational exposure limit, an indoor-air guideline and an ambient-air standard are none of them converted into one.

rows.basis: as_sold
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets an inorganic-arsenic maximum level for poultry muscle meat, skin or edible fat. Every credible inorganic-arsenic instrument on the register is scoped elsewhere: EU 2023/915 and EU 2025/1891 to rice, rice products, fruit juices, infant food and seafood; UK, Health Canada and US FDA to rice-based and juice matrices; Hong Kong Cap. 132V to rice and aquatic animals. A NOT-MATERIAL determination is deliberately REJECTED for this cell rather than adopted for convenience: organoarsenical feed additives (roxarsone, nitarsone, arsanilic acid, carbarsone) were lawfully administered to poultry and swine in major producing markets within living memory and are documented to leave arsenic residues in edible tissue, so the programme will not make the affirmative claim that no inorganic-arsenic pathway exists in terrestrial animal food. rows.basis: as_sold
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets a hexavalent-chromium content limit for any food, and no near-neighbour read-across is supportable: every credible Cr(VI) instrument on the register is an article, textile, leather, toy-migration, tattoo-ink, fertiliser or electrical-equipment limit written in a non-food basis, and applying one to a poultry-meat matrix would be the basis conflation this row's basis guard exists to reject. No ceiling is invented. THIS CELL WAS PREVIOUSLY CARRIED AS A NOT-MATERIAL DETERMINATION AND THAT DETERMINATION IS WITHDRAWN FOR POULTRY, for two independent reasons. First, the reference-method evidence behind the reduction argument does not reach this matrix. That argument (Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by tissue reductants and does not persist, so a reported Cr(VI) figure is an artifact of the extraction chemistry) rests on saraiva2021, species-specific isotope-dilution HPLC-ICP-MS, in which Cr(VI) was unquantified in every sample and spiked Cr(VI) was reduced essentially completely during workup. That study covers bovine meat, infant formula milk and semi-skimmed milk. It does not cover poultry. A not-material claim is an affirmative claim and may not be extended by analogy to a matrix the underlying method study never examined; it continues to support the beef, pork and lamb rows, where the matrix was directly measured. Second, the routed corpus contradicts the claim for this exact row. mahmud2011-crvi-chicken-pakistan (peer-reviewed, B-tier) reports author-declared Cr(VI) means of 0.233 to 1.266 mg/kg across chicken meat parts (leg muscle highest at 1.266 mg/kg) and 0.323 to 1.433 mg/kg across bones (head bone highest). The muscle-meat figures alone reach 1.27 times this row's own total-chromium screen of 1 mg/kg, and the row is scoped to muscle meat, so the exceedance does not depend on the bone values.  The paper and attributes them to a documented mechanical supply-chain pathway: chrome-tanned leather offcuts fed to poultry as cheap protein, carrying residual hexavalent chromium from K2CrO4 and K2Cr2O7 tanning liquors. The routed occurrence pool for poultry-product|Cr-VI is not quarantined and carries a stable sensitivity band. The programme records openly that mahmud2011 is weak evidence of SPECIATION: muffle-furnace ashing and nitric-acid digestion followed by atomic absorption calibrated against potassium dichromate, with no chromatographic separation and no speciation-preservation validation, measures total chromium irrespective of oxidation state, and the reported values sit in the same range as the total-chromium screen, which is what a total-chromium measurement mislabelled as Cr(VI) would look like. That caveat is why this cell does not publish a number derived from those values, and it could not in any case: occurrence never selects an HMTc limit. But the FEED-INPUT PATHWAY the paper documents is not an analytical artifact, and the correct response to a real pathway measured by an inadequate method is to require an adequate method, not to declare the analyte not material. Under the programme's fail-safe rule a cell in this position is a control.

rows.basis: total lead content of the product as placed on the market (consumer-chemical product-content basis; disclosed read-across)
rows.rationale: Program-wide consistency ruling (2026-08-17): the German BVL 2017 orientation values are treated as SELECTABLE anchors across HMTc. The live Category 15 standard tags three of these same register rows regulatory-alignment, and Categories 2, 13, 14 and 20 bind them directly, so the earlier Category 19 position that a register status of 'guidance impurity limit' makes them unselectable contradicted five sibling categories on the identical rows, and did so in the looser direction (5x on lead, 50x on cadmium, 4x on total arsenic, 10x on total mercury). BVL is a single coherent sovereign consumer-chemical regime covering all four toxics, so reading it across preserves this category's own rule of adopting one coherent regime per analyte rather than picking the lowest number across regimes. The China NMPA 2015 value previously published is retained as a named looser comparator. Whether a national enforcement orientation value ranks as a sovereign maximum level is a genuine governance question, recorded for ratification as OI-20260817-bvl-selectability-ruling; until it is ruled on, every category states the same rule. Previously bound: cn_nmpa2015_pb_cosmetics_10.

rows.basis: total nickel content of the product as placed on the market (consumer-chemical product-content basis; disclosed read-across)
rows.rationale: Nickel is the analyte this category's exposure pathway is built around: nickel is a confirmed dermal sensitiser, and a residue deposited on fabric that is then worn is prolonged, repeated dermal contact. No sovereign sets a nickel maximum for a laundry or fabric-care product. Instruments checked: China GB 14930.1-2022 (the only sovereign detergent contaminant standard in the register; scope is Type A detergents used directly for food cleaning and Type B detergents for tableware and food-contact tools, equipment, packaging and containers, and it sets a total-arsenic ceiling only); China NMPA 2015 Safety and Technical Standards for Cosmetics Table 2 (lead, arsenic, mercury, cadmium); Korea MFDS Notice 2025-63 and its predecessor Notice 2024-9 (lead, cadmium, nickel, antimony, arsenic, mercury); Germany BVL 2017 technically-avoidable heavy metals in cosmetics (lead, cadmium, mercury, arsenic, antimony); Health Canada cosmetic heavy-metal impurity limits; the ASEAN Cosmetic Directive Annex (2019) and the Malaysia NPRA, Singapore HSA, Indonesia BPOM, Taiwan MoHW and New Zealand cosmetic group-standard equivalents; EAEU TR CU 009/2011; EU REACH Annex XVII entry 20 (organotin), entry 23 (cadmium in listed polymers and paints), entry 47 as amended by Regulation (EU) 301/2014 (Cr(VI) in skin-contact leather), entry 72 with Appendix 12 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2018/1513 (lead, cadmium, arsenic and Cr(VI) in consumer clothing and skin-contact textiles) and entry 75 under Regulation (EU) 2020/2081 (tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures); EU Directive 2009/48/EC toy-safety migration limits; EU RoHS 2011/65/EU; and the dietary contaminant regimes (EU 2023/915, EU 2024/1987, Codex CXS 193, US FDA, FSANZ, Health Canada, UK, Hong Kong Cap. 132V), which are inapplicable both on scope and on basis. China NMPA 2015 Table 2 — the instrument that anchors lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury on this row — sets no nickel limit at all, so for nickel the nearest applicable sovereign consumer-chemical value is the Korean statutory limit, which is the only regime in the register that sets one. The Korean instrument writes a product-form split (eye make-up 35, colour make-up 30, all other cosmetic products 10 mg/kg); the split is preserved and the "all other products" tier is the applicable one, because a fabric-care product is not a decorative make-up. A single coherent sovereign regime is read across per analyte rather than the lowest number picked across regimes, which would build a ceiling no sovereign enforces. China NMPA 2015 Table 2 is the strictest coherent STATUTORY consumer-chemical regime for lead, cadmium, total arsenic and total mercury (Korea MFDS is looser on lead at 20 and on total arsenic at 10 mg/kg; the ASEAN, Health Canada and Germany BVL values are cosmetics-scoped administrative or technical-avoidability findings rather than statutory maximum levels, and are on-scope-only under governance ruling GR-2026-08-17-BVL), and the same instrument is already the published read-across anchor of the live Category 12 (Household Cleaning and Dishwashing) standard for the identical logical move, verified 2026-08-17 against the live page https://heavymetalcertified.com/standards/all-purpose-cleaners (Category 12 standard version 1.0, dated 2026-08-13), which publishes lead 10, cadmium 5, total arsenic 2 and total mercury 1 mg/kg with provenance read-across and binding source China Safety and Technical Standards for Cosmetics (2015, NMPA), the values carried by register rows cn_nmpa2015_pb_cosmetics_10, cn_nmpa2015_cd_cosmetics_5, cn_nmpa2015_tas_cosmetics_2 and cn_nmpa2015_thg_cosmetics_1, and which states the same single-coherent-regime rule; the Category 12 records were rendered by a dedicated certification-repository builder rather than through this repository's compiled-standards manifest, so the live page and not an in-repo artifact is the citation a reader checks. Nickel is not regulated by the Chinese instrument at all, so for nickel the nearest applicable sovereign consumer-chemical value is the Korean statutory limit; that is the only regime in the register that sets one, and no number in this row was chosen by comparing outcomes. EU REACH Annex XVII entry 27 restricts nickel RELEASE from articles in prolonged skin contact rather than nickel content in a mixture and is not carried in the register as a content limit, so it is not read across; EU REACH Annex XVII entry 72 Appendix 12 sets no nickel row for consumer textiles, so no downstream fabric content ceiling is available for this analyte. EU REACH Annex XVII entry 75 (Regulation (EU) 2020/2081) sets the strictest sovereign consumer-mixture metal limits in the register (lead 0.7, cadmium 0.5, total arsenic 0.5, mercury 0.5, Cr(VI) 0.5 and nickel 5 mg/kg), but its scope is mixtures for tattooing and permanent make-up, an intradermal-injection route. Reading an injected-mixture ceiling across to a rinse-off or fabric-deposited topical product would conflate exposure routes, and its register basis is a tattoo/permanent-make-up mixture basis that this row's basis_guard excludes. Nickel is measured in soaps, detergents and household hygienic products in the routed corpus and is named for laundry care by greenseal2020-gs51-laundry-care-products, nydec2020-cleansing-product-disclosure-bmp and ecetoc1992-tr045-ni-co-cr-consumer-products, so a not-material determination is unavailable on the facts. Complete disposition of the stricter rows the compiler's audit safety-net surfaces for this row, none of which is adopted. (1) de_bvl2017_pb_cosmetics_general_2000 (2 mg/kg), de_bvl2017_cd_cosmetics_general_100 (0.1), de_bvl2017_tas_cosmetics_general_500 (0.5) and de_bvl2017_thg_cosmetics_general_100 (0.1): Germany BVL 2017 technical-avoidability findings for cosmetic manufacture, register status 'guidance impurity limit', dispositioned under HMTc governance ruling GR-2026-08-17-BVL as on-scope-only and therefore unavailable as a read-across anchor for a non-cosmetic product class. The ruling is stated in full in this configuration's credible_note and is the single programme-wide rule the live Category 15 (Feminine Care) standard and this category both now state; Category 15 binds these same four BVL rows because its rows ARE cosmetics, and every number Category 15 publishes is unaffected by the ruling. (2) hc_cosmetic_cd_3ppm (3 mg/kg): a Health Canada cosmetic impurity guidance limit, excluded for the same reason, and adopting it for cadmium alone would additionally mix regimes. (3) eu_2018_1513_pb_consumer_textiles_1mgkg, eu_2018_1513_cd_consumer_textiles_1mgkg and eu_2018_1513_tas_consumer_textiles_1mgkg (1 mg/kg each): the EU consumer-textile restriction, which governs the FABRIC and not the product applied to it, on a homogeneous-material-after-extraction basis rather than this row's product-content basis; carried as a downstream constraint and companion limit, and blocked from anchoring by the row's basis_guard. The audit_exclude_scope on this row removes only the oral/mucosal toothpaste tier, tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures, and colour-additive and colourant specifications; against the register as built it suppresses no row that the audit scope would otherwise surface, so nothing was excluded to make this list shorter. (4) Two further stricter rows exist that the compiler's audit safety-net structurally CANNOT surface, because it filters to the credible-regulator set, and they are therefore recorded by hand rather than left invisible. asean2019_th_cd_cosmetic_products_3000 (Thailand, cadmium 3 mg/kg) is a guidance impurity limit and falls to the same reasoning as the Health Canada value. eaeu_trcu009_2011_pb_natural_raw_material_cosmetics_5mgkg (EAEU, lead 5 mg/kg) is the only STATUTORY row anywhere in the consumer-chemical product-content basis family that is stricter than an anchor adopted here, and it is not adopted for three reasons: the EAEU is not in the HMTc credible-regulator set and admitting it is a governance ruling outside this derivation; its scope is formulation-conditioned (perfumery-cosmetic products containing more than 1 per cent natural plant or natural mineral raw material) rather than the general product tier, and that condition would be satisfied by some but not all rows in this category, which would fracture the category on a formulation test no sovereign wrote for laundry products; and the EAEU instrument does not dominate the adopted regime, since it is stricter on lead (5 against 10 mg/kg) but LOOSER on total arsenic (5 against 2 mg/kg), identical on mercury and silent on cadmium, so taking its lead value while keeping the Chinese arsenic value would compose a ceiling no sovereign enforces, which is precisely what the single-coherent-regime discipline exists to prevent. This enumeration is the output of a credible-set-blind sweep of every one of the 80 register rows the basis_guard admits, not of the automated scan alone, and it is complete as of this build. Verification method: total nickel by microwave-assisted closed-vessel acid digestion (HNO3/H2O2, with a hydrofluoric-acid or lithium-metaborate fusion step where an aluminosilicate, silicate or clay mineral phase is present) followed by ICP-MS quantification against matrix-matched calibration standards, with a certified reference material and a reagent blank in every run. The sampling unit is one composite sample per production lot, drawn from the product as placed on the market, with component-level sampling of the concentrate and, for stick and roll-on formats, the applicator wick or pad; trigger-spray and aerosol hardware in the product-contact path is sampled separately. Disposition rule, stated identically in every cell and every row of this category: the published ceiling applies to EACH sampled component independently, and the lot fails if ANY single component result is at or above the ceiling. The whole-article composite is additionally measured and reported on the lot record, but the composite is never the basis of the pass or fail determination, because diluting a contaminated component in the mass of the rest of the article does not reduce the exposure that component delivers to the skin it contacts. A lot in which every component is inside the ceiling, but in which any component sits outside the running per-row control band, is escalated to ALARA review with raw-material trace-back to the specific component that moved.

rows.basis: as sold, finished product (wet weight)
rows.rationale: A formulated processed-meat product is not a separately named commodity in any credible sovereign contaminant instrument, so the exact cell is unregulated and the ceiling is a disclosed read-across from the maximum levels governing its principal components — the muscle meat of the species it is formulated from. All three credible candidate rows (Hong Kong Cap. 132V meat of cattle/pig/goat/sheep, Hong Kong meat of poultry, FSANZ Schedule 19 multi-species muscle meat excluding offal) sit at 0.1 mg/kg, so the binding value is 100 ug/kg regardless of species mix. BASIS TREATMENT, DISCLOSED IN THE DIRECTION IT ACTUALLY CUTS: the ceiling is applied to the FINISHED product as sold, in the same wet-weight basis the component maximum levels are written in, with no invented conversion factor. Applying a ceiling to the finished product rather than to its meat fraction is the LOOSER of the two available treatments, because a formulation that is part water, starch, rusk and brine can carry a higher concentration in its meat fraction than the muscle-meat maximum level itself allows. The programme does not paper over that with a claim of conservatism it has not earned; it closes the gap with a second, independent test. The meat raw material entering the formulation IS "meat of cattle, pig, goat and sheep" or "meat of poultry" within the meaning of the sovereign instruments, so those maximum levels apply to it as a commodity in their own right: every certified lot must document raw-material compliance against the named component maximum levels IN ADDITION to finished-product compliance against this ceiling, and neither test substitutes for the other. Mechanically separated meat and any lot containing edible offal (liver sausage, blood sausage, pate) is additionally screened against the sovereign offal maximum levels, which govern that ingredient but never loosen this row. BASIS OF THE BINDING INSTRUMENT, DISCLOSED: the two concurring instruments are written on DIFFERENT bases. FSANZ Schedule 19 states its maximum level for the portion ordinarily consumed (an as-consumed basis); Hong Kong Cap. 132V states the identical 0.1 mg/kg as-sold, for the edible portion after removal of bones and fat (Cap. 132V Part 2 Note 1). Because this row publishes an as-sold ceiling, the Hong Kong as-sold row is named as the binding instrument and the FSANZ row is disclosed as an independent sovereign value concurring at the same number. The published ceiling therefore rests on an instrument written in this row's own basis, and no as-consumed value is relabelled as-sold. The number is unaffected: both instruments sit at 100 ug/kg, so the strictest-applicable selection is identical either way.

rows.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets an inorganic-arsenic maximum level for formulated processed meat. A formulated processed-meat product is a wet, reducing, protein- and thiol-rich medium; Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by tissue reductants (cysteine, glutathione, ascorbate) and by the acid and heat of digestion and cooking, so a Cr(VI) figure reported on such a matrix is an artifact of the extraction chemistry of the total-chromium screen rather than a measurement of a species that persists in the food. The determination follows the same reference-method adjudication recorded for the hexavalent-chromium cell in the infant-formula category (data/workbench standards Cr-VI adjudication), applied here to an animal-tissue matrix. rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market — total element content per unit mass of undiluted product as sold (µg/kg). Not a dietary basis, not a migration or leachate basis, and no use-pattern dilution credit.
rows.rationale: BVL 2017 Table 1 (German Federal Office of Consumer Protection and Food Safety, with the Länder cosmetics working group) publishes the technically avoidable heavy-metal content of cosmetic products in general; lead is 2.0 mg/kg, and a content above the table is treated as technically avoidable under good manufacturing practice. Its status is a federal-authority guidance value rather than a statute, and it is disclosed as such, but it is the strictest published sovereign finished-cosmetic lead maximum and Method v2.0 takes the strictest applicable value. The named comparator set shows how far the binding sits below the field: Health Canada, China NMPA 2015 and Taiwan MOHW 2024 are five times looser at 10 mg/kg; Korea, ASEAN and its Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia transpositions, and Kenya KS 2937:2021 are ten times looser at 20 mg/kg; Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations threshold is 125 times looser at 250 mg/kg. Two sovereign cosmetic lead values in the register are stricter than the binding — the BVL 2017 toothpaste tier at 500 µg/kg and Washington State's Toxics-Free Cosmetics Act toothpaste limit at 1000 µg/kg — and the compiler's stricter-unselected audit flags both on every row of this category. Neither is applicable. Both are scoped by their own instruments to toothpaste, a dentifrice that sits on the oral mucosa and is partly swallowed; that ingestion pathway is the stated reason the toothpaste tier is tighter. Categories 20 and 2 carry the dentifrice forms and use those instruments. A shampoo, body wash, scrub or depilatory has no ingestion pathway inside either instrument's scope, so reading a toothpaste tier onto a hair or body rinse-off product would have HMTc inventing a stricter number that no government set for this form. Method v2.0 forbids that as squarely as it forbids inventing a looser one: applicability is a real constraint, and the strictest APPLICABLE value governs. The compiler's audit also flags EU REACH Annex XVII entry 75, which sets 700 µg/kg for lead in mixtures placed on the market for tattooing and permanent make-up. That value is stricter than the binding and is deliberately not adopted: the instrument governs a mixture INJECTED INTO THE DERMIS, on a 'mixture for tattooing or permanent make-up by weight' basis, and a rinse-off shampoo or body wash is not such a mixture on any reading of the entry. The row is held out by this row's basis_guard as well as on scope. It is surfaced rather than filtered out of the scan so that the record shows it was found and disposed of, not missed. Colour-additive and colourant purity specifications (21 CFR 73 and 74, the New Zealand and Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles, the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 permitted-colours entries, the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant entries) are raw-material ingredient specifications, not finished-product maxima. They are held out of every cell by this row's basis_guard, and none of them is in any case stricter than the binding for this analyte.

rows.rationale: Korea is the only jurisdiction in the register that sets a nickel content limit for finished cosmetics, and it tiers it by form: 10 µg/g for cosmetic products other than eye makeup and colour cosmetics, 30 µg/g for colour makeup, 35 µg/g for eye makeup. Every Category 14 form is a cleansing, conditioning, shaving, depilatory or hair-colouring preparation and none is an eye-makeup or colour-makeup product in the MFDS product taxonomy, so the strictest of the three tiers — 10 µg/g — is the directly applicable one, not a read-across. Korea MFDS Notice 2025-63 carries the same 10 µg/g value for the same scope and corroborates it; it is not named as a candidate because its register note contradicts its own value (the note reads '1 microgram/g = 1000 ug/kg' against a stored value of 10000 µg/kg), and a litigation-facing citation should not carry that discrepancy forward. The EU REACH restriction on nickel in tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures (5000 µg/kg) is stricter but governs a mixture injected into the dermis, a different form on a different basis, and is held out by this row's basis_guard. Nickel is a leading contact sensitiser, so the programme additionally holds it under ALARA post-publication and treats the published ceiling as an outer bound rather than a target.

rows.basis: as_sold
rows.rationale: Every tin maximum level in the register is scoped to canned product: EU Reg. 2023/915 sets 200000 ug/kg for canned foods and 100000 ug/kg for canned beverages, Codex CXS 193-1995 and AU-NZ Schedule 19 set 250000 ug/kg for canned foods, and Hong Kong Cap. 132V sets 250000 ug/kg for canned food other than canned beverages. Hermetically sealed tinplate presentations of this commodity route to the canned-foods row in Category 7 and carry the canned-foods tin maximum level there.

rows.basis: as_sold
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets an aluminium contaminant maximum level for any fruit, vegetable or produce form in any jurisdiction. The register's aluminium limits are drinking-water and bottled-water parameters, infant-formula maximum levels, a food-contact plastics specific migration limit, toy migration limits, and permitted-additive levels for baked and starch foods; none of them regulates aluminium as a contaminant of produce. Aluminium is also the third most abundant element in the earth's crust and appears in produce largely as soil-derived and root-associated mineral content rather than as process contamination, so no near-neighbour read-across is supportable either. Under the government-limit-only method HMTc publishes no standalone aluminium number for this row.

rows.basis: as_sold
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum level for any solid food in any jurisdiction. The register's only INGESTED Cr(VI) parameters are drinking-water maxima (Australia NHMRC 2025, 50 ug/L, nhmrc2025_crvi_drinking_water_50; California SWRCB, 10 ug/L, us_ca_swrcb_2024_cr-vi_chromium-hexavalent_mcl_10ugl and ca_swrcb_crvi_drinking_water_10), which are water-basis parameters expressed per litre of a consumed liquid and supply no applicable ceiling for a solid produce row in this row's native basis; every remaining Cr(VI) row in the register is an article or material limit (toys, textiles, leather, fertilisers, electrical equipment). Chromium in produce is dominated by nutritionally essential Cr(III), and Cr(VI) is not stable in the plant matrix: fruit and vegetable tissue is an aqueous, organic-acid and ascorbate-rich reducing medium in which Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III), so a reported Cr(VI) value in this matrix reflects extraction conditions rather than the chromium species the consumer ingests. Hexavalent chromium is therefore bounded by the published total-chromium screen for this row (Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 7, 500 ug/kg) and controlled by reflex speciation rather than by a published number.

rows.basis: as sold, ug of element per kg of the emitting material (product as tested)
rows.rationale: No government anywhere sets a lead content maximum for an air freshener, plug-in evaporator, puff releaser, candle body, wax melt, oil or nebula diffuser, gel or reed diffuser, incense stick, potpourri, vacuum-cleaner fragrance additive or fragrance refill. The only sovereign heavy-metal instrument in any jurisdiction that names a product in this category is the United States CPSC prohibition on lead-cored candlewicks, 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13), mirrored by Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956; it restricts lead in the metal of a wick core and covers no other analyte and no other product form. The cell is therefore a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS, and it is taken on the axis the regulators themselves used: route of administration. Colorado's 2022 heavy-metal table and Maryland's Technical Authority Rev. 6.0 both publish a route LADDER over the same underlying matrices, with the inhalation row strictest, the oral row looser and the topical or cutaneous row looser still. The value is therefore a function of the route, not of the source matrix's chemistry, and Colorado scopes its strictest row in the instrument's own words to "inhaled product or audited product administered by metered-dose nasal spray", which describes a delivery mechanism this category shares. Maryland's own route gap is the sharpest available evidence for that reading: its inhalation-route total-chromium value is 600 ug/kg while its oral and cutaneous values for the same products are 1,100,000 ug/kg. Selected value 500 ug/kg, from Colorado (co2022 inhaled/nasal row). California DCC section 15723 independently sets the identical 0.5 ug/g for inhalable products (us_ca_dcc_2026_pb_inhalable_cannabis_0_5ugg), so two sub-national regulators converge on this value. The looser or route-unspecific values on the register are recorded and NOT selected: Maryland inhalation route 1000 ug/kg, Massachusetts all-uses protocol 500 ug/kg (equal but route-unspecific), Nevada 1200 ug/kg, Israel IMC-GMP Procedure 152 5000 ug/kg. The basis is identical to this row's native basis, micrograms of element per kilogram of product as tested, so no basis conversion, no reconstitution and no dry-to-wet adjustment is performed. The read-across is published as `read-across` and never as `regulatory-alignment`, because no instrument regulates this exact cell. Adopting it tightens rather than relaxes the applicable regulatory position: it is three to four orders of magnitude stricter than every article-content instrument that actually binds these products (RoHS lead at 1,000,000 ug/kg of homogeneous material, the candlewick-core prohibition threshold at 600,000 ug/kg of wick-core metal, REACH cadmium in polymers at 100,000 ug/kg). No occurrence, percentile, feasibility or precautionary input touched the number in either direction. Determined on the unburnt wax-and-fragrance body, sampled through its full depth by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS with collision/reaction-cell control of the interfered masses, with the article's non-emitting components digested and screened separately per this row's component plan. Post-burn residue and ash are analysed in addition to the unburnt article, because combustion removes volatile mass and concentrates non-volatile metal in what is left and in what is emitted. DISPOSITION OF THE ADDITIONAL ANALYSES THIS CELL MANDATES. This cell requires two analyses beyond the published test, and each carries a criterion and a lot consequence, so that no mandatory analysis on this row is an obligation without an outcome. COMPONENT RESULTS, THE FIRST ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS THIS CELL MANDATES. The published ceiling of 500 ug/kg governs the emitting material and is NOT transferred to a component's bulk content: a tinplate or aluminium vessel, a metal wick core or sustainer tab, or a ceramic glaze, enamel, lustre or metallic surface coating is or may be substantially metal, metal-plated, metal-glazed or metal-pigmented by construction, and reading an emitting-material value against a structural component's bulk content would be exactly the basis conflation this row's basis guard exists to prevent, failing every compliant article for a metal that never enters the air. Every component result is instead dispositioned in three ordered branches, and no component result is left outside them. (a) WHERE A SOVEREIGN INSTRUMENT REACHES THE COMPONENT AND THIS ANALYTE, that instrument is the criterion. The instrument that reaches this row's components for lead is: the United States CPSC prohibition at 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13), which makes a candle whose wick core exceeds 0.06 percent lead by weight of the core metal a banned hazardous substance (register row us_16cfr1500_17a13_pb_lead_cored_candle_wicks_600ppm, 600,000 ug/kg of wick-core metal), mirrored by Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956; every metal-cored wick is sampled separately, its core metal digested and analysed for lead by ICP-MS, and a core above 0.06 percent lead is a prohibited article irrespective of this row's 500 ug/kg emitting-material ceiling. It is applied in its own basis at its own threshold, on the component it actually governs, and an exceedance blocks certification of the lot outright irrespective of the emitting-material result. That article-and-component value is never republished as this row's emitting-material limit, because it is three to four orders of magnitude looser and republishing it would misrepresent a component prohibition as a product permission. (b) WHERE THE COMPONENT IS IN THE EMISSION PATH (the wick with its core, sustainer tab and adhesive, and the inner surface of the vessel with any glaze, enamel, lustre or coating on it that the molten pool wets), the criterion is the published ceiling itself, applied where its basis makes it meaningful: the test is performed on emitting material sampled from the finished, filled and assembled article rather than from a pre-fill bulk batch, at the end of the declared shelf life or after the declared maximum burn cycle, whichever is the more demanding, with the sample drawn through the full depth of the remaining body, so that any lead transferred out of an emission-path component into the emitting material is carried into the published result rather than escaping it. An emitting-material result at or above 500 ug/kg fails the lot. A rising component result while the emitting material stays below the ceiling does not by itself fail the lot and falls to branch (c). (c) OTHERWISE, for a component outside the emission path that no sovereign instrument reaches for lead, the component result is dispositioned under the HMTc control-and-escalation rule, in the same terms this row's control cells already use: the result is held to ALARA against the manufacturer's demonstrated process capability for that formulation and component set; a result outside that capability band, or an unexplained step change between lots, triggers CAPA and raw-material traceback to the wax refiner, the fragrance house, the dye or pigment supplier, the hardener and additive supplier, the wick maker and the vessel, glaze and decoration supplier; a confirmed uncontrolled source blocks certification until it is removed or substituted; and the analyte goes onto priority surveillance for this row. No component ceiling is invented in branch (c), because no credible sovereign government publishes a lead content maximum for these components in this product form, and an occupational exposure limit, an indoor-air guideline and an ambient-air standard are none of them converted into one. POST-BURN RESIDUE AND ASH, THE SECOND ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS THIS CELL MANDATES. The post-burn residue and ash analysis is a mass-balance check on the published test, not a second ceiling, because the burn removes most of the article's mass, so a concentration expressed per kilogram of ash carries a denominator one to two orders of magnitude smaller than the published basis and is not comparable to it. It is dispositioned in three steps, so that it too carries an outcome. First, the published ceiling of 500 ug/kg governs certification on the emitting material as sampled above: an emitting-material result at or above 500 ug/kg fails the lot, whatever the post-burn residue and ash analysis shows. Second, the residue result is reconciled to the published basis: the measured residue concentration is multiplied by the measured residue yield (residue and ash mass divided by initial article mass) to give the mass of element retained per kilogram of the original article, and the balance against the unburnt-article content is the fraction that left the article in the plume; where that reconciliation cannot be closed within the combined expanded uncertainty of the two determinations, or where the residue concentration implies a retention inconsistent with the declared formulation, the published test is treated as having been run on an unrepresentative sample, the lot is held, re-sampled through the full burn depth and re-tested, and a confirmed unrepresentative published test fails the lot. Third, the result itself is dispositioned under the control-and-escalation rule stated above, with CAPA and raw-material traceback on an unexplained step change and a block on certification where an uncontrolled source is confirmed. No residue ceiling, emission-rate limit, per-actuation dose limit or indoor-air concentration limit is published for this row, because no credible sovereign government sets one for any product in this category, and none is manufactured from an occupational exposure limit or an ambient-air guideline.
