rows.basis: as sold, ug of element per kg of the emitting material (product as tested)
rows.rationale: No government anywhere sets a total chromium content maximum for an air freshener, plug-in evaporator, puff releaser, candle body, wax melt, oil or nebula diffuser, gel or reed diffuser, incense stick, potpourri, vacuum-cleaner fragrance additive or fragrance refill. The only sovereign heavy-metal instrument in any jurisdiction that names a product in this category is the United States CPSC prohibition on lead-cored candlewicks, 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13), mirrored by Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956; it restricts lead in the metal of a wick core and covers no other analyte and no other product form. The cell is therefore a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS, and it is taken on the axis the regulators themselves used: route of administration. Colorado's 2022 heavy-metal table and Maryland's Technical Authority Rev. 6.0 both publish a route LADDER over the same underlying matrices, with the inhalation row strictest, the oral row looser and the topical or cutaneous row looser still. The value is therefore a function of the route, not of the source matrix's chemistry, and Colorado scopes its strictest row in the instrument's own words to "inhaled product or audited product administered by metered-dose nasal spray", which describes a delivery mechanism this category shares. Maryland's own route gap is the sharpest available evidence for that reading: its inhalation-route total-chromium value is 600 ug/kg while its oral and cutaneous values for the same products are 1,100,000 ug/kg. Selected value 600 ug/kg, from Maryland (inhalation route). Maryland is the only regulator on the register that publishes a chromium value scoped to the inhalation route. The looser or route-unspecific values on the register are recorded and NOT selected: no other jurisdiction on the register publishes a chromium value for any inhaled product: California DCC section 15723, the Colorado route table, the Massachusetts protocol, the Nevada action levels and Israel IMC-GMP Procedure 152 all omit chromium entirely. Maryland's own oral-route and cutaneous-route chromium values for the same products, 1,100,000 ug/kg, are a different route scope and are deliberately not used. The basis is identical to this row's native basis, micrograms of element per kilogram of product as tested, so no basis conversion, no reconstitution and no dry-to-wet adjustment is performed. The read-across is published as `read-across` and never as `regulatory-alignment`, because no instrument regulates this exact cell. Adopting it tightens rather than relaxes the applicable regulatory position: it is three to four orders of magnitude stricter than every article-content instrument that actually binds these products (RoHS lead at 1,000,000 ug/kg of homogeneous material, the candlewick-core prohibition threshold at 600,000 ug/kg of wick-core metal, REACH cadmium in polymers at 100,000 ug/kg). No occurrence, percentile, feasibility or precautionary input touched the number in either direction. Determined on the metered cartridge formulation as dispensed, including propellant by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS with collision/reaction-cell control of the interfered masses, with the article's non-emitting components digested and screened separately per this row's component plan. DISPOSITION OF THE ADDITIONAL ANALYSES THIS CELL MANDATES. This cell requires one analysis beyond the published test, and it carries a criterion and a lot consequence, so that no mandatory analysis on this row is an obligation without an outcome. COMPONENT RESULTS, THE FIRST ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS THIS CELL MANDATES. The published total-chromium screen of 600 ug/kg governs the emitting material and is NOT transferred to a component's bulk content: a metering valve, a pyroelectric sensor element, a solenoid or motor, a solder joint, a cell contact or spring, or a pigmented moulded housing is or may be substantially metal, metal-plated, metal-glazed or metal-pigmented by construction, and reading an emitting-material value against a structural component's bulk content would be exactly the basis conflation this row's basis guard exists to prevent, failing every compliant article for a metal that never enters the air. Every component result is instead dispositioned in three ordered branches, and no component result is left outside them. (a) WHERE A SOVEREIGN INSTRUMENT REACHES THE COMPONENT AND THIS ANALYTE, that instrument is the criterion. For total chromium and this row's components, branch (a) is EMPTY, and the instruments checked before saying so are named rather than waved at: EU RoHS 2011/65/EU restricts HEXAVALENT chromium in the homogeneous materials of electrical and electronic equipment (eu_rohs_2011_crvi_homogeneous_materials_1000000) and publishes no total-chromium value, so it reaches this row's hexavalent-chromium cell on the powered sub-assembly this row carries and never this total-chromium cell, because a species and its total-element parent are not interchangeable in either direction; Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 on batteries restricts mercury, cadmium and lead only and publishes no chromium value, so it does not reach this cell even on the primary or rechargeable cells this row carries; REACH Annex XVII entry 63 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2015/628 (eu_2015_628_pb_mouthable_general_public_articles_0_05pct) reaches only articles supplied to the general public that may be placed in the mouth by children; Regulation (EU) 2018/1513 reaches consumer clothing and skin-contact textiles and does not reach a packaging, sachet or decorative textile that is not worn; the EU Toy Safety Directive 2009/48/EC with EN 71-3, the CPSIA surface-coating limit and the Canadian and Australian toy-coating limits reach accessible toy material and toy surface coatings, and none of these articles is a toy; 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13) reaches only the metal of a candlewick core and this row has no wick core; the food-contact ceramic, glassware and enamelware instruments reach only articles intended to come into contact with food. Every component result on this row therefore falls to branch (b) or branch (c), and neither leaves a result without a criterion or without a lot consequence. (b) WHERE THE COMPONENT IS IN THE EMISSION PATH (the cartridge's internal lacquer, the metering valve with its stem and gasket, and the actuator nozzle), the criterion is the published total-chromium SCREEN of 600 ug/kg, applied where its basis makes it meaningful: the test is performed on emitting material sampled from the finished, filled and assembled article rather than from a pre-fill bulk batch, at the end of the declared shelf life or after the declared maximum number of metered actuations, whichever is the more demanding, so that any chromium transferred out of an emission-path component into the emitting material is carried into the published result rather than escaping it. The screen is a tripwire and never a pass/fail in its own right. An emitting-material total-chromium result reaching half the screen (300 ug/kg) orders reflex hexavalent-chromium speciation on that lot under the reference method published on this row's Cr-VI cell, and that cell's disposition then governs the lot: any hexavalent chromium quantifiable above the method limit of quantitation fails the lot. A rising component result while the emitting material stays below the reflex trigger does not by itself fail the lot and falls to branch (c). (c) OTHERWISE, for a component outside the emission path that no sovereign instrument reaches for total chromium, the component result is dispositioned under the HMTc control-and-escalation rule, in the same terms this row's control cells already use: the result is held to ALARA against the manufacturer's demonstrated process capability for that formulation and component set; a result outside that capability band, or an unexplained step change between lots, triggers CAPA and raw-material traceback to the fragrance house, the propellant and cartridge supplier, the metering-valve maker, the sensor and electronics contract manufacturer, the cell supplier and the housing moulder; a confirmed uncontrolled source blocks certification until it is removed or substituted; and the analyte goes onto priority surveillance for this row. No component ceiling is invented in branch (c), because no credible sovereign government publishes a total-chromium content maximum for these components in this product form, and an occupational exposure limit, an indoor-air guideline and an ambient-air standard are none of them converted into one.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market — total element content per unit mass of undiluted product as sold (µg/kg). Not a dietary basis, not a migration or leachate basis, and no use-pattern dilution credit.
rows.rationale: BVL 2017 Table 1 (German Federal Office of Consumer Protection and Food Safety, with the Länder cosmetics working group) publishes the technically avoidable heavy-metal content of cosmetic products in general; lead is 2.0 mg/kg, and a content above the table is treated as technically avoidable under good manufacturing practice. Its status is a federal-authority guidance value rather than a statute, and it is disclosed as such, but it is the strictest published sovereign finished-cosmetic lead maximum and Method v2.0 takes the strictest applicable value. The named comparator set shows how far the binding sits below the field: Health Canada, China NMPA 2015 and Taiwan MOHW 2024 are five times looser at 10 mg/kg; Korea, ASEAN and its Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia transpositions, and Kenya KS 2937:2021 are ten times looser at 20 mg/kg; Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations threshold is 125 times looser at 250 mg/kg. Two sovereign cosmetic lead values in the register are stricter than the binding — the BVL 2017 toothpaste tier at 500 µg/kg and Washington State's Toxics-Free Cosmetics Act toothpaste limit at 1000 µg/kg — and the compiler's stricter-unselected audit flags both on every row of this category. Neither is applicable. Both are scoped by their own instruments to toothpaste, a dentifrice that sits on the oral mucosa and is partly swallowed; that ingestion pathway is the stated reason the toothpaste tier is tighter. Categories 20 and 2 carry the dentifrice forms and use those instruments. A shampoo, body wash, scrub or depilatory has no ingestion pathway inside either instrument's scope, so reading a toothpaste tier onto a hair or body rinse-off product would have HMTc inventing a stricter number that no government set for this form. Method v2.0 forbids that as squarely as it forbids inventing a looser one: applicability is a real constraint, and the strictest APPLICABLE value governs. The compiler's audit also flags EU REACH Annex XVII entry 75, which sets 700 µg/kg for lead in mixtures placed on the market for tattooing and permanent make-up. That value is stricter than the binding and is deliberately not adopted: the instrument governs a mixture INJECTED INTO THE DERMIS, on a 'mixture for tattooing or permanent make-up by weight' basis, and a rinse-off shampoo or body wash is not such a mixture on any reading of the entry. The row is held out by this row's basis_guard as well as on scope. It is surfaced rather than filtered out of the scan so that the record shows it was found and disposed of, not missed. Colour-additive and colourant purity specifications (21 CFR 73 and 74, the New Zealand and Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles, the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 permitted-colours entries, the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant entries) are raw-material ingredient specifications, not finished-product maxima. They are held out of every cell by this row's basis_guard, and none of them is in any case stricter than the binding for this analyte.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market — total element content per unit mass of undiluted product as sold (µg/kg). Not a dietary basis, not a migration or leachate basis, and no use-pattern dilution credit.
rows.rationale: BVL 2017 Table 1 sets mercury in cosmetic products in general at 0.1 mg/kg, and BVL's toothpaste tier is the same value, so mercury carries no dentifrice split. The comparator set is deliberately wide here because mercury in cosmetics is the one contaminant with a hard, enforceable US rule and an active illegal-adulteration problem: 21 CFR 700.13(d)(2)(i) deems a cosmetic adulterated unless its mercury content is unavoidable under good manufacturing practice and below 1 ppm, and Hong Kong Cap. 640 sets the same 1 ppm expressly for unintentional trace mercury in cosmetics including skin-lightening products. Health Canada, China NMPA 2015, Korea MFDS, Taiwan MOHW 2024, ASEAN 2019 with its Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia transpositions, and the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 all land at the same 1 mg/kg; Kenya KS 2937:2021 is 2 mg/kg. The HMTc binding is therefore ten to twenty times stricter than every one of them. Mercury used as an intentional skin-lightening active, and the eye-area thiomersal and phenylmercuric preservative allowances in the India, Hong Kong and South Africa instruments, are ingredient permissions rather than contaminant ceilings; HMTc does not adopt them, and a rinse-off product formulated with an intentional mercury ingredient is not certifiable at all. Colour-additive and colourant purity specifications (21 CFR 73 and 74, the New Zealand and Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles, the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 permitted-colours entries, the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant entries) are raw-material ingredient specifications, not finished-product maxima. They are held out of every cell by this row's basis_guard, and none of them is in any case stricter than the binding for this analyte.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market — total element content per unit mass of undiluted product as sold (µg/kg). Not a dietary basis, not a migration or leachate basis, and no use-pattern dilution credit.
rows.rationale: Korea is the only jurisdiction in the register that sets a nickel content limit for finished cosmetics, and it tiers it by form: 10 µg/g for cosmetic products other than eye makeup and colour cosmetics, 30 µg/g for colour makeup, 35 µg/g for eye makeup. Every Category 14 form is a cleansing, conditioning, shaving, depilatory or hair-colouring preparation and none is an eye-makeup or colour-makeup product in the MFDS product taxonomy, so the strictest of the three tiers — 10 µg/g — is the directly applicable one, not a read-across. Korea MFDS Notice 2025-63 carries the same 10 µg/g value for the same scope and corroborates it; it is not named as a candidate because its register note contradicts its own value (the note reads '1 microgram/g = 1000 ug/kg' against a stored value of 10000 µg/kg), and a litigation-facing citation should not carry that discrepancy forward. The EU REACH restriction on nickel in tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures (5000 µg/kg) is stricter but governs a mixture injected into the dermis, a different form on a different basis, and is held out by this row's basis_guard. Nickel is a leading contact sensitiser, so the programme additionally holds it under ALARA post-publication and treats the published ceiling as an outer bound rather than a target.

rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market — total element content per unit mass of undiluted product as sold (µg/kg). Not a dietary basis, not a migration or leachate basis, and no use-pattern dilution credit.
rows.rationale: BVL 2017 Table 1 (German Federal Office of Consumer Protection and Food Safety, with the Länder cosmetics working group) publishes the technically avoidable heavy-metal content of cosmetic products in general; lead is 2.0 mg/kg, and a content above the table is treated as technically avoidable under good manufacturing practice. Its status is a federal-authority guidance value rather than a statute, and it is disclosed as such, but it is the strictest published sovereign finished-cosmetic lead maximum and Method v2.0 takes the strictest applicable value. The named comparator set shows how far the binding sits below the field: Health Canada, China NMPA 2015 and Taiwan MOHW 2024 are five times looser at 10 mg/kg; Korea, ASEAN and its Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia transpositions, and Kenya KS 2937:2021 are ten times looser at 20 mg/kg; Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations threshold is 125 times looser at 250 mg/kg. Two sovereign cosmetic lead values in the register are stricter than the binding — the BVL 2017 toothpaste tier at 500 µg/kg and Washington State's Toxics-Free Cosmetics Act toothpaste limit at 1000 µg/kg — and the compiler's stricter-unselected audit flags both on every row of this category. Neither is applicable. Both are scoped by their own instruments to toothpaste, a dentifrice that sits on the oral mucosa and is partly swallowed; that ingestion pathway is the stated reason the toothpaste tier is tighter. Categories 20 and 2 carry the dentifrice forms and use those instruments. A shampoo, body wash, scrub or depilatory has no ingestion pathway inside either instrument's scope, so reading a toothpaste tier onto a hair or body rinse-off product would have HMTc inventing a stricter number that no government set for this form. Method v2.0 forbids that as squarely as it forbids inventing a looser one: applicability is a real constraint, and the strictest APPLICABLE value governs. The compiler's audit also flags EU REACH Annex XVII entry 75, which sets 700 µg/kg for lead in mixtures placed on the market for tattooing and permanent make-up. That value is stricter than the binding and is deliberately not adopted: the instrument governs a mixture INJECTED INTO THE DERMIS, on a 'mixture for tattooing or permanent make-up by weight' basis, and a rinse-off shampoo or body wash is not such a mixture on any reading of the entry. The row is held out by this row's basis_guard as well as on scope. It is surfaced rather than filtered out of the scan so that the record shows it was found and disposed of, not missed. Colour-additive and colourant purity specifications (21 CFR 73 and 74, the New Zealand and Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles, the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 permitted-colours entries, the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant entries) are raw-material ingredient specifications, not finished-product maxima. They are held out of every cell by this row's basis_guard, and none of them is in any case stricter than the binding for this analyte.

Health Canada, China NMPA 2015, Korea MFDS, Taiwan MOHW 2024, ASEAN 2019 with its Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia transpositions, and the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 all land at the same 1 mg/kg; Kenya KS 2937:2021 is 2 mg/kg. The HMTc binding is therefore ten to twenty times stricter than every one of them. Mercury used as an intentional skin-lightening active, and the eye-area thiomersal and phenylmercuric preservative allowances in the India, Hong Kong and South Africa instruments, are ingredient permissions rather than contaminant ceilings; HMTc does not adopt them, and a rinse-off product formulated with an intentional mercury ingredient is not certifiable at all. Colour-additive and colourant purity specifications (21 CFR 73 and 74, the New Zealand and Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles, the India Cosmetics Rules 2020 permitted-colours entries, the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant entries) are raw-material ingredient specifications, not finished-product maxima. rows.basis: finished cosmetic as placed on market — total element content per unit mass of undiluted product as sold (µg/kg). Not a dietary basis, not a migration or leachate basis, and no use-pattern dilution credit.
rows.rationale: Korea is the only jurisdiction in the register that sets a nickel content limit for finished cosmetics, and it tiers it by form: 10 µg/g for cosmetic products other than eye makeup and colour cosmetics, 30 µg/g for colour makeup, 35 µg/g for eye makeup. Every Category 14 form is a cleansing, conditioning, shaving, depilatory or hair-colouring preparation and none is an eye-makeup or colour-makeup product in the MFDS product taxonomy, so the strictest of the three tiers — 10 µg/g — is the directly applicable one, not a read-across. Korea MFDS Notice 2025-63 carries the same 10 µg/g value for the same scope and corroborates it; it is not named as a candidate because its register note contradicts its own value (the note reads '1 microgram/g = 1000 ug/kg' against a stored value of 10000 µg/kg), and a litigation-facing citation should not carry that discrepancy forward. The EU REACH restriction on nickel in tattoo and permanent-make-up mixtures (5000 µg/kg) is stricter but governs a mixture injected into the dermis, a different form on a different basis, and is held out by this row's basis_guard. Nickel is a leading contact sensitiser, so the programme additionally holds it under ALARA post-publication and treats the published ceiling as an outer bound rather than a target.

rows.basis: as consumed, ready-to-drink carbonated or still soft drink, or concentrate as dispensed or reconstituted to the label dilution (read across from the Hong Kong carbonated-beverage cell)
rows.rationale: The provenance is recorded as read-across and not as regulatory-alignment because this row's scope is wider than the instrument's. For a cola, a tonic water or a ginger ale the Hong Kong cell is a direct sovereign maximum level for the exact product form; for a still soft drink it is the nearest applicable analog, and the tag follows the weaker of the two rather than the stronger. The sibling sports and energy drink row adopts the same anchor for the same still and carbonated mix and carries the same tag, so the two rows are consistent on their face. Three disclosures belong here. First, no other credible sovereign regulates this product form at all: the EU, Codex, FSANZ and Health Canada write no soft-drink lead cell, so 200 ug/kg is the whole of the applicable law and there is no stricter applicable value to select. Second, the stricter beverage cells that exist are inapplicable and were rejected as such rather than quietly ignored: the EU and Codex fruit-juice cells (30 ug/kg) are scoped to fruit juices, juices from concentrate and nectars, which a cola carrying a few percent juice is not, and the packaged-drinking-water quality standards (5 to 10 ug/kg) govern water sold as water. HMTc will not reach past an instrument's scope to publish a better-looking number. Third, HMTc does not pretend 200 ug/kg is a strong ceiling: this cell is a declared Standards Ratchet priority, and Governance Policy section 12 is the only route by which certified-lot evidence may lower it.

rows.basis: as_consumed
rows.rationale: Hexavalent chromium is not stable in a carbonated or still soft drink. At the pH of this product form (typically pH 2.4 to 3.5, with phosphoric, citric and carbonic acid and invert or high-fructose sugars present in the formulation) Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by the organic acids, sugars, ascorbate and polyphenols present in the matrix, so a positive Cr(VI) result is an artifact of the total-chromium determination rather than a species present in the beverage as consumed. The reference-method basis for this determination is the in-house species arbitration at data/workbench/standards/2026-07-31-chromium-formula-adjudication.md, which found that the superseded ion-exchange plus electrothermal-AAS methods that generated the historical Cr(VI) values in liquid food matrices are not reproduced by the modern reference method: saraiva2021 (species-specific isotope dilution HPLC-ICP-MS, limit of quantification 0.049 ug/kg) quantified no Cr(VI) in any milk or formula sample while resolving Cr(III) and total chromium at single-digit ug/kg. That adjudication was drawn on a near-neutral aqueous food matrix; the acidic beverage matrices in this row are a more strongly reducing environment still, so the artifact conclusion carries a fortiori. The health-relevant species is controlled through the total-chromium cell and the reflex rule below, and this determination is a method finding, not an occurrence-derived value: no number is taken from it.

rows.basis: read-across from strictest applicable principal-component Pb ML (as consumed)
rows.rationale: THE BINDING MOVED IN v1.2 BECAUSE THE DAIRY EXCLUSION DID NOT SURVIVE AUDIT, and it did not survive on this row in particular: the row's own component labels name bisque and chowder to justify the seafood anchor, and cream is a major-mass component of exactly those products, so calling dairy a minor formulation ingredient in cream-style variants contradicted the row's own text. The ruling and the rejected alternatives are stated in full in this row's scope_note; hk_cap132v_pb_milk_20 and hk_cap132v_pb_secondary-milk-products_20 are admitted and the ceiling is 20 ug/kg. CONSEQUENCE, STATED PLAINLY: a noodle soup (cereal lead 200) or a seafood chowder (fish 300) contains a component whose own sovereign ceiling is many times this composite ceiling and may measure above it; that does not loosen the ceiling, and a composite lot above 20 ug/kg lead is not certifiable on this row. The v1.1 ladder is retained and unchanged below the new binding: Cap. 132V sets lead at 50 ug/kg for fruiting vegetables (cucurbit and non-cucurbit) and for tomatoes preserved by heat treatment and hermetically sealed, and tomato soup is the flagship product of this row and is made from exactly that commodity. Two stricter Cap. 132V lead rows remain deliberately NOT adopted and are now equal to rather than stricter than the binding: cereal-based food (20 ug/kg) and ready-to-eat complementary food other than cereal-based (20 ug/kg), both scoped to persons under the age of 36 months; infant and toddler soups and purees route to HMTc Category 1 by the taxonomy boundary rule, and the Codex ready-to-eat meals for infants and young children ML (20 ug/kg) is dispositioned identically. Canned-vegetable (100) and leafy-vegetable (300) lead MLs are applicable but looser and are disclosed rather than adopted. BEVERAGE-COMMODITY RULING, applied once and consistently across every analyte on this row. Fruit and vegetable juices, nectars, rice-based drinks, and bottled and packaged waters are separately regulated ready-to-drink beverage commodities, consumed as the whole product, and they are NOT principal components of a prepared meal, soup, broth or stock. Where a formulation contains juice or juice concentrate it enters as a minor flavour, sweetener or acidulant fraction of a few percent, exactly like the cooking fat and the salt this row already dispositions as ingredient specifications rather than composite ceilings, and the vegetable commodity that a vegetable juice is pressed from is already in the ladder at its own maximum level (Cap. 132V fruiting vegetables and preserved tomatoes), so adopting the juice row as well would import the same commodity twice in a form this row does not sell. The rows dispositioned by this ruling, named by id so the choice is auditable: eu2024_ni_juice_250 (nickel 250, fruit/vegetable juices and nectars) and eu2024_ni_juice_listed_1000 (nickel 1000); fda2023_ias_apple_juice_10 (inorganic arsenic 10, apple juice), eu2023_ias_fruit_juice_20 (inorganic arsenic 20) and eu2023_ias_rice_drinks_30 (inorganic arsenic 30, non-alcoholic rice-based drinks); eu2023_pb_fruit_juice_other_30, hk_cap132v_pb_fruit-juices-other-than-fruit-juices-exclusively-from-b_30 and hk_cap132v_pb_grape-juice_40 (lead 30 to 40); and the packaged-drinking-water and natural-mineral-water parametric values dispositioned in the row scope note. THE RULING IS TESTED BY ITS CONSEQUENCE: if a juice were a principal component, the US apple-juice inorganic-arsenic action level of 10 ug/kg would become the ceiling for an entire prepared meal, which no sovereign anywhere has set and which would be an occurrence-free but nonsensical import. Adopting the nickel juice row at 250 while declining the inorganic-arsenic juice row at 10 is the asymmetry this remediation exists to remove, so both are declined under one stated rule. v1.2 REMOVES juice, nectar and drink from this row's audit_exclude_scope so these rows now surface in the compiler's stricter-unselected scan and in the publication gate's W1 warnings, where they are dispositioned by this paragraph rather than suppressed by a regex. Nothing else stricter is applicable: the by-hand scan of every credible live non-infant lead row below 20 ug/kg returns only drinking-water and bottled-water parametric values (5 to 10 ug/kg) and the EU 10/2011 plastics specific migration limit (10), both refused by this row's basis_guard. INGREDIENT-WATER RULING, and a correction to what the basis_guard can actually do. The Cap. 132V packaged-drinking-water and natural-mineral-water rows sit in the SAME basis string as Cap. 132V's food rows ('food as listed in Cap 132V Part 2 Schedule'), so this row's basis_guard does NOT filter them out even though it does filter the EU 2020/2184, US EPA, US 21 CFR 165.110 and Health Canada water instruments, whose basis strings are distinct. v1.2 corrects the earlier claim that the guard stops packaged-water values generally: the Cap. 132V water rows are excluded by DETERMINATION, not by the guard, and they are now named by id on every cell they could otherwise be read as binding. The determination: packaged drinking water and natural mineral water are a distinct beverage commodity, regulated as the sole daily hydration source and consumed by the litre, and formulation water is an INPUT SPECIFICATION rather than a principal component of the finished product. Certified lines are required to use potable water meeting the applicable national drinking-water standard, verified on the ingredient-water specification, rather than by re-deriving the composite ceiling from a water instrument. Applying a water parametric value as a food-content ceiling would hold a soup or a broth to a limit set for a product with a completely different daily intake, which no sovereign has done.

rows.basis: read-across from strictest applicable principal-component total-arsenic ML (as consumed)
rows.rationale: TOTAL ARSENIC IS PUBLISHED HERE AS A PROTECTIVE SOVEREIGN MAXIMUM LEVEL, NOT AS A SCREEN. v1.1 opened this substantiation with 'Total arsenic is a non-toxicological screen' while the cell emitted an ordinary numeric read-across with no screen flag, so the prose and the provenance disagreed about whether the published number was protective and any renderer that distinguishes the two would have contradicted the cell's own text. The disagreement is resolved in favour of what the cell in fact publishes: Cap. 132V regulates total arsenic as a per-commodity protective ceiling, 500 ug/kg is the strictest applicable sovereign total-arsenic maximum level for the components of this row, and it is published as such. Total arsenic is one of the eight mandatory HMTc totals and is never satisfied by its species. The screen mechanism (`screen: true` with a screen_note) is used on this config only for total chromium, where the published value genuinely is not protective as a standalone total-element ceiling; it is not available on a component_read_across cell in this compiler in any case. The toxicologically dominant arsenic species, inorganic arsenic, is separately and far more strictly controlled on the iAs cell at 50 ug/kg (EU 2025/1891 cephalopods), and the species-below-total relation holds (iAs 50 <= tAs 500). v1.1 tightens the cell from 1000 to 500 ug/kg on the Cap. 132V per-commodity total-arsenic MLs, and the v1.0 claim that cereal grains carry the only credible total-arsenic component ML is withdrawn. Rice is absent from Cap. 132V's total-arsenic schedule because rice is regulated on inorganic arsenic; congee and rice soups are therefore controlled through the iAs cell, never by substituting a species for a total. The Cap. 132V edible-fats-and-oils total-arsenic ML (100 ug/kg) and the food-grade-salt ML (500) are not adopted: cooking fat and salt are minor formulation ingredients rather than characterizing components, they certify under HMTc Categories 30 and 34 in their own bases, and importing either would set a whole-soup ceiling from a material that is a small percentage of the product. Packaged-drinking-water total arsenic (10 ug/kg) is dispositioned in the row scope note as an ingredient-water specification. Nothing else stricter is applicable: the by-hand scan of every credible live non-infant total-arsenic row below 500 ug/kg returns drinking-water and bottled-water parametric values (10) and the EU 10/2011 plastics specific migration limit (10), both refused by this row's basis_guard; and us_fda_21cfr73_73_520_tas_50 at 50, which is a colour-additive ingredient specification for soy leghemoglobin under 21 CFR 73.520, a purity specification for an additive as supplied rather than a contaminant ceiling for a food as sold, dispositioned in the same form as the edible-fats-and-oils and salt rows below. INGREDIENT-WATER RULING, and a correction to what the basis_guard can actually do. The Cap. 132V packaged-drinking-water and natural-mineral-water rows sit in the SAME basis string as Cap. 132V's food rows ('food as listed in Cap 132V Part 2 Schedule'), so this row's basis_guard does NOT filter them out even though it does filter the EU 2020/2184, US EPA, US 21 CFR 165.110 and Health Canada water instruments, whose basis strings are distinct. v1.2 corrects the earlier claim that the guard stops packaged-water values generally: the Cap. 132V water rows are excluded by DETERMINATION, not by the guard, and they are now named by id on every cell they could otherwise be read as binding. The determination: packaged drinking water and natural mineral water are a distinct beverage commodity, regulated as the sole daily hydration source and consumed by the litre, and formulation water is an INPUT SPECIFICATION rather than a principal component of the finished product. Certified lines are required to use potable water meeting the applicable national drinking-water standard, verified on the ingredient-water specification, rather than by re-deriving the composite ceiling from a water instrument. Applying a water parametric value as a food-content ceiling would hold a soup or a broth to a limit set for a product with a completely different daily intake, which no sovereign has done.

rows.basis: read-across from strictest applicable inorganic-arsenic component ML (as consumed)
rows.rationale: THE FULL EU 2025/1891 SEAFOOD INORGANIC-ARSENIC LADDER, disclosed because the row previously named one rung of it and carried no substantiation at all: cephalopods 50 (eu20251891_ias_cephalopods_50); muscle meat of fish other than the listed species 100 (eu20251891_ias_fish_other_100), crabs and crab-like crustaceans, prawns and shrimps 100 (eu20251891_ias_crabs_prawns_shrimps_100) and scallops 100 (eu20251891_ias_scallops_100), three equal-value applicable candidates; crustaceans other than those listed 200 (eu20251891_ias_crustaceans_other_200); muscle meat of anglerfish, monkfish and the other listed species 500 (eu20251891_ias_fish_listed_500) and bivalve molluscs other than scallops 500 (eu20251891_ias_bivalve_molluscs_other_500); and langoustine and rock lobster 1500 (eu20251891_ias_langoustine_rock_lobster_1500). CEPHALOPODS ARE ADOPTED and the published ceiling moves from 100 to 50 ug/kg. They are a principal seafood component of products this row certifies, and the row says so in its own voice elsewhere: the component label reads fish/seafood rather than fish, and the total-mercury substantiation names prawn stir-fry, clam chowder and lobster bisque as covered products, so aquatic invertebrates are plainly in scope and a squid or octopus component of a paella-style meal, a seafood fried rice, a seafood risotto or a seafood soup is characterizing rather than incidental. Ruling cephalopods a non-principal component while treating prawns and clams as in scope was not supportable. The stricter rung is adopted, the equal rungs are named, and the looser rungs are disclosed and not adopted. This cell carried NO substantiation field before v1.2, which is why the omission survived: it was the only numeric cell on either composite row with nothing written under it. BEVERAGE-COMMODITY RULING, applied once and consistently across every analyte on this row. Fruit and vegetable juices, nectars, rice-based drinks, and bottled and packaged waters are separately regulated ready-to-drink beverage commodities, consumed as the whole product, and they are NOT principal components of a prepared meal, soup, broth or stock. Where a formulation contains juice or juice concentrate it enters as a minor flavour, sweetener or acidulant fraction of a few percent, exactly like the cooking fat and the salt this row already dispositions as ingredient specifications rather than composite ceilings, and the vegetable commodity that a vegetable juice is pressed from is already in the ladder at its own maximum level (Cap. 132V fruiting vegetables and preserved tomatoes), so adopting the juice row as well would import the same commodity twice in a form this row does not sell. The rows dispositioned by this ruling, named by id so the choice is auditable: eu2024_ni_juice_250 (nickel 250, fruit/vegetable juices and nectars) and eu2024_ni_juice_listed_1000 (nickel 1000); fda2023_ias_apple_juice_10 (inorganic arsenic 10, apple juice), eu2023_ias_fruit_juice_20 (inorganic arsenic 20) and eu2023_ias_rice_drinks_30 (inorganic arsenic 30, non-alcoholic rice-based drinks); eu2023_pb_fruit_juice_other_30, hk_cap132v_pb_fruit-juices-other-than-fruit-juices-exclusively-from-b_30 and hk_cap132v_pb_grape-juice_40 (lead 30 to 40); and the packaged-drinking-water and natural-mineral-water parametric values dispositioned in the row scope note. THE RULING IS TESTED BY ITS CONSEQUENCE: if a juice were a principal component, the US apple-juice inorganic-arsenic action level of 10 ug/kg would become the ceiling for an entire prepared meal, which no sovereign anywhere has set and which would be an occurrence-free but nonsensical import. Adopting the nickel juice row at 250 while declining the inorganic-arsenic juice row at 10 is the asymmetry this remediation exists to remove, so both are declined under one stated rule. v1.2 REMOVES juice, nectar and drink from this row's audit_exclude_scope so these rows now surface in the compiler's stricter-unselected scan and in the publication gate's W1 warnings, where they are dispositioned by this paragraph rather than suppressed by a regex. Nothing else stricter is applicable: the by-hand scan of every credible live non-infant inorganic-arsenic row below 50 ug/kg returns only the beverage-commodity rows dispositioned above (apple juice 10, fruit juices 20, rice-based drinks 30) and the US EPA drinking-water maximum contaminant level (10), which is a water parametric value in a different basis family that this row's basis_guard refuses. rows.basis: as_consumed
rows.rationale: Inorganic tin is a tinplate migration pathway confined to the canned form, and three of the four forms this row certifies are not canned foods. The subcategory as scoped covers canned soups, dry soup mixes, bouillon cubes and powders, and ready-to-drink carton stocks and broths; the canned-foods tin maximum level reaches only the first. v1.1 published that ML as a row-wide firm ceiling of 250 mg/kg while its own label conceded that dry-mix, bouillon and carton-RTD forms have no tin migration pathway, so the compiled record asserted a 250 mg/kg tin ceiling for a carton broth that no instrument sets and the publication gate counted it as a firm protective limit. v1.2 converts the cell to the control + companion_ml pattern the other two rows of this category already use (mixed-meals-prepared-foods and bone-broth), so the canned form is verified against the ML while no ceiling is asserted for the forms the instrument does not reach. A form-split cell was considered and is not available in this compiler. A CANNED soup is verified against the canned-foods tin ML, on which three credible regulators converge at 250 mg/kg (250000 ug/kg): Codex CXS 193 (canned foods), FSANZ Schedule 19 (all canned foods) and HK Cap. 132V (canned food other than canned beverages), so the figure is not a single-jurisdiction artefact. The Cap. 132V canned-beverage row (150 mg/kg) is stricter but is not adopted: a ready-to-drink carton stock is not a canned beverage and has no tinplate contact, and a canned soup is a canned food under every one of these instruments. Instruments checked for the non-canned forms: EU 2023/915 (tin appears only as canned-food and canned-beverage MLs), Codex CXS 193, FSANZ Schedule 19, Cap. 132V, US FDA, Health Canada and UK dietary instruments; none sets a tin maximum level for a dry soup mix, a bouillon cube or a carton broth. THE STRICTEST APPLICABLE CANNED-FOOD TIN ML IS THE EU ROW AT 200 mg/kg, NOT THE 250 mg/kg FIGURE v1.1 NAMED. Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 sets tin at 200000 ug/kg (200 mg/kg) for canned foods other than canned beverages, except canned dried and canned powdered products (eu2023_sn_canned_foods_200000, basis product as placed on the market). It is stricter than the three rows v1.1 named as converging at 250 mg/kg (codex_cxs193_sn_canned_250000, aunz_sch19_sn_canned_250000, hk_cap132v_sn_canned-food-other-than-canned-beverages_250000), it is a credible-regulator maximum level in a basis this row accepts, and it was neither named nor dispositioned. This defect was found by hand during the v1.2 remediation and NOT by the compiler safety-net, because the soups row's audit_exclude_scope contained the term `beverage`, which matched the phrase 'canned beverages' inside the EU row's own scope string and suppressed it from every scan; the same class of regex self-defeat the v1.2 audit identified elsewhere. The term is removed. The canned form is verified against the EU value, and the EU instrument's own carve-out for canned dried and canned powdered products is independent confirmation that a tin maximum level does not reach a dry soup mix or a bouillon powder. Stricter still, and disclosed rather than adopted because they reach a different form: canned beverages at 100 mg/kg (eu2023_sn_canned_beverages_100000) and at 150 mg/kg (hk_cap132v_sn_canned-beverages_150000). Where a certified product is a canned drinkable broth presented as a beverage rather than a canned food, the canned-beverage value is the applicable one and the stricter of the two applicable rows governs; no single number is asserted across forms.
rows.limit_of_record: CONTROL: Inorganic tin is a tinplate migration pathway confined to the canned form, and three of the four forms this row certifies are not canned foods. The subcategory as scoped covers canned soups, dry soup mixes, bouillon cubes and powders, and ready-to-drink carton stocks and broths; the canned-foods tin maximum level reaches only the first. v1.1 published that ML as a row-wide firm ceiling of 250 mg/kg while its own label conceded that dry-mix, bouillon and carton-RTD forms have no tin migration pathway, so the compiled record asserted a 250 mg/kg tin ceiling for a carton broth that no instrument sets and the publication gate counted it as a firm protective limit. v1.2 converts the cell to the control + companion_ml pattern the other two rows of this category already use (mixed-meals-prepared-foods and bone-broth), so the canned form is verified against the ML while no ceiling is asserted for the forms the instrument does not reach. A form-split cell was considered and is not available in this compiler. A CANNED soup is verified against the canned-foods tin ML, on which three credible regulators converge at 250 mg/kg (250000 ug/kg): Codex CXS 193 (canned foods), FSANZ Schedule 19 (all canned foods) and HK Cap. 132V (canned food other than canned beverages), so the figure is not a single-jurisdiction artefact. The Cap. 132V canned-beverage row (150 mg/kg) is stricter but is not adopted: a ready-to-drink carton stock is not a canned beverage and has no tinplate contact, and a canned soup is a canned food under every one of these instruments. Instruments checked for the non-canned forms: EU 2023/915 (tin appears only as canned-food and canned-beverage MLs), Codex CXS 193, FSANZ Schedule 19, Cap. 132V, US FDA, Health Canada and UK dietary instruments; none sets a tin maximum level for a dry soup mix, a bouillon cube or a carton broth. THE STRICTEST APPLICABLE CANNED-FOOD TIN ML IS THE EU ROW AT 200 mg/kg, NOT THE 250 mg/kg FIGURE v1.1 NAMED. Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 sets tin at 200000 ug/kg (200 mg/kg) for canned foods other than canned beverages, except canned dried and canned powdered products (eu2023_sn_canned_foods_200000, basis product as placed on the market). It is stricter than the three rows v1.1 named as converging at 250 mg/kg (codex_cxs193_sn_canned_250000, aunz_sch19_sn_canned_250000, hk_cap132v_sn_canned-food-other-than-canned-beverages_250000), it is a credible-regulator maximum level in a basis this row accepts, and it was neither named nor dispositioned. This defect was found by hand during the v1.2 remediation and NOT by the compiler safety-net, because the soups row's audit_exclude_scope contained the term `beverage`, which matched the phrase 'canned beverages' inside the EU row's own scope string and suppressed it from every scan; the same class of regex self-defeat the v1.2 audit identified elsewhere. The term is removed. The canned form is verified against the EU value, and the EU instrument's own carve-out for canned dried and canned powdered products is independent confirmation that a tin maximum level does not reach a dry soup mix or a bouillon powder. Stricter still, and disclosed rather than adopted because they reach a different form: canned beverages at 100 mg/kg (eu2023_sn_canned_beverages_100000) and at 150 mg/kg (hk_cap132v_sn_canned-beverages_150000). Where a certified product is a canned drinkable broth presented as a beverage rather than a canned food, the canned-beverage value is the applicable one and the stricter of the two applicable rows governs; no single number is asserted across forms.

rows.basis: read-across from the sovereign total-chromium vegetable ML (Cap. 132V, food as sold, applied at face value to the as-consumed soup)
rows.rationale: v1.0 recorded this cell as a bare control on the statement that no credible regulator sets a total-chromium maximum level for soups or their components. That statement is false following Hong Kong's admission to the credible-regulator set on 2026-08-17: Cap. 132V Part 2 Schedule sets total chromium at 500 ug/kg for vegetables other than pulses and at 1000 ug/kg for pulses, cereals, meat of animal, meat of poultry and fish. The cell is therefore a disclosed read-across from the strictest applicable component rather than a control, published as a SCREEN because dietary chromium is overwhelmingly trivalent and the health-relevant hexavalent species is separately determined not material in a cooked wet matrix (Cr-VI cell, speciation-bounded). Total chromium remains mandatory on every lot; a result approaching the screen value is a stainless-steel equipment-leaching signal, which matters on this row because stock kettles have long hot contact times, not a toxicological finding. INGREDIENT-WATER RULING, and a correction to what the basis_guard can actually do. The Cap. 132V packaged-drinking-water and natural-mineral-water rows sit in the SAME basis string as Cap. 132V's food rows ('food as listed in Cap 132V Part 2 Schedule'), so this row's basis_guard does NOT filter them out even though it does filter the EU 2020/2184, US EPA, US 21 CFR 165.110 and Health Canada water instruments, whose basis strings are distinct. v1.2 corrects the earlier claim that the guard stops packaged-water values generally: the Cap. 132V water rows are excluded by DETERMINATION, not by the guard, and they are now named by id on every cell they could otherwise be read as binding. The determination: packaged drinking water and natural mineral water are a distinct beverage commodity, regulated as the sole daily hydration source and consumed by the litre, and formulation water is an INPUT SPECIFICATION rather than a principal component of the finished product. Certified lines are required to use potable water meeting the applicable national drinking-water standard, verified on the ingredient-water specification, rather than by re-deriving the composite ceiling from a water instrument. Applying a water parametric value as a food-content ceiling would hold a soup or a broth to a limit set for a product with a completely different daily intake, which no sovereign has done.

rows.basis: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
rows.rationale: Cadmium at 2 µg/L is the NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines health-based guideline value (0.002 mg/L, nhmrc2025_cd_drinking_water_2), the strictest cadmium value any government sets for water. It is published as a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS and not as a direct maximum for this product form, and the reason is stated rather than left to inference. The register records that instrument's product scope as 'drinking water' and its note describes it as a health-based guideline value; the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines are a non-statutory guideline for drinking-water supplies, and Australia regulates packaged water not under the ADWG but under the FSANZ Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code. No FSANZ packaged-water metals row exists in the register: of the AU, NZ and AU-NZ rows, the only water-scoped entries are the eight NHMRC drinking-water guideline values, and Schedule 19 is represented only by commodity rows (formula, cereals, fish, salt and the like). The Australian packaged-water cadmium cell is therefore absent from the register and is logged as a register gap, in the same way Commission Directive 2003/40/EC is logged on the mineral-water row. The category's two textual packaged-water bridges do not carry this instrument either: FDA 21 CFR 165.110(b)(4)(iii) incorporates the EPA maximum contaminant levels (cadmium 5 µg/L) and EU Directive 2020/2184's scope reaches water put into bottles or containers (cadmium 5 µg/L), and neither reaches an Australian guideline. Absence of a packaged-product carve-out is not affirmative scope, so the earlier regulatory-alignment tag overstated what this instrument does. WHAT THE INSTRUMENTS SET FOR THE EXACT CELL IS STATED OPENLY, because the read-across runs in the protective direction and nothing is served by concealing it: the strictest maximum level any government sets for cadmium in this exact packaged-water form is 3 µg/L, then 5 µg/L (EU Drinking Water Directive eu20202184_cd_drinking_water_5, FDA 21 CFR 165.110 fda21cfr165110_cd_bottled_water_5, EPA MCL epa2018_cd_drinking_water_5, California us_ca_swrcb_2024_cd_cadmium_mcl_5ugl), then 7 µg/L (Health Canada healthcanada2025_cd_drinking_water_7). HMTc publishes the stricter 2 µg/L: the substance and the basis are identical, HMTc does not relax a published limit toward a looser instrument, and the value is unchanged from the earlier compilation. Only the provenance tag is corrected, from regulatory-alignment to read-across, so that the record never claims a sovereign packaged-water maximum that no sovereign has written. The 3 µg/L tier for this exact form is Hong Kong Cap 132V (hk_cap132v_cd_bottled-or-packaged-drinking-waters-other-than-natural_3), Israel FCS 2016 (il_fcs2016_cd_17_bottled_drinking_water_and_mineral_water_3) and Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011 (vn_qcvn8_2_2011_cd_bottled-water_3), with the WHO guideline value (who2022_cd_drinking_water_3) at the same figure. Carbonation is not a cadmium pathway and no instrument writes a separate carbonated-water cadmium line.

rows.basis: as_consumed
rows.rationale: No sovereign sets a tin maximum for drinking water, bottled water or natural mineral water. The drinking-water instrument family carries no tin parameter at all (EU Directive 2020/2184 Annex I Parts B and C; US EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations; US FDA 21 CFR 165.110 standards of quality; Health Canada; NHMRC; WHO), and none of the national food-schedule packaged-water lines (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, India FSSAI 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Chile Decreto 977/1996, Fiji FSR 2009) carries a tin entry for water. A read-across is not supportable: the nearest sovereign tin maxima are the canned-food and canned-beverage maximum levels, which exist to bound dissolution of tin from a tinplate container wall into an acidic canned matrix, and the canned-beverage value (100 mg/kg inorganic tin) sits roughly four orders of magnitude above anything a packaged water can plausibly contain, so importing it would publish a ceiling that functions as no limit at all. The dominant packaging for this category (PET, HDPE, glass, aluminium) contains no tin. Unflavoured carbonated water is the one form in this category with a genuine canned presentation, so the canned-beverage instrument is recorded as a companion hard stop rather than ignored; the cans in ordinary use are aluminium or tin-free steel, which are not tin sources. Tin therefore remains a mandatory control cell; no number is invented.

rows.rationale: The exact cell is unregulated, and the record says so on its face rather than asserting a maximum no government has written for this product form. No jurisdiction in the register sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum for bottled water, packaged water or natural mineral water, and neither of the two textual packaged-water bridges this category relies on reaches the species: FDA 21 CFR 165.110(b)(4)(iii) incorporates the EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulation maximum contaminant levels and EPA sets no hexavalent-chromium MCL, and EU Directive 2020/2184 Annex I carries no hexavalent-chromium parameter. The nearest applicable sovereign value is therefore the California State Water Resources Control Board Title 22 section 64431 Table 64431-A maximum contaminant level of 10 µg/L (0.01 mg/L, us_ca_swrcb_2024_cr-vi_chromium-hexavalent_mcl_10ugl), re-adopted in 2024 after health-risk and feasibility analysis, and it is carried across as a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS. Two hops are disclosed rather than argued around. First, SCOPE: the register records that instrument's product scope as 'public water systems in California', which is utility-delivered tap water and not a packaged good; HMTc has not identified, and does not cite, any California provision applying Title 22 section 64431 maximum contaminant levels to bottled water sold in the state, so this cell must not be read as an assertion that California enforces 10 µg/L against a packaged product. Second, SOVEREIGNTY: California is a sub-national government. The only alternative anywhere in the register is the NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines statement that hexavalent chromium should not exceed 50 µg/L (nhmrc2025_crvi_drinking_water_50), which is five times looser and carries the same drinking-water scope hop; it is named here and not selected because the method takes the strictest applicable value. The value is unchanged from the earlier compilation at 10 µg/L; only the provenance tag is corrected, from regulatory-alignment to read-across. HMTc publishes Cr-VI as its own cell in addition to total chromium: a hexavalent result never satisfies the total-chromium cell and a total-chromium result never satisfies this one, and the total-chromium cell on this row is a direct sovereign maximum for the product form that bounds this species from above.

rows.basis: as_sold
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum level for any solid food in any jurisdiction. rows.rationale: The candidate set and why each alternative was rejected. The audit scan flags the whole juice and nectar lead family as stricter and unselected: the EU and Codex fruit-juice cells (30 ug/kg), the Codex and Hong Kong grape-juice cells (40 ug/kg), the EU and Hong Kong berry and small-fruit juice cells (50 ug/kg) and the US FDA Juice HACCP hazard-control level (50 ug/kg). The packaged-drinking-water quality standards (5 to 10 ug/kg) govern water sold as water and are inapplicable for the reason set out in the scope note. That leaves Hong Kong's carbonated-beverage cell as the only sovereign value written for a formulated packaged beverage, and it is adopted at face value. HMTc does not substitute a stricter but inapplicable instrument to make the number look better, and it does not soften the disclosure that 200 ug/kg is a weak ceiling: this cell is a declared Standards Ratchet priority, and Governance Policy section 12 is the only route by which certified-lot evidence may lower it.

rows.basis: as_consumed
rows.rationale: No credible sovereign sets an aluminium maximum level for a sports or energy drink. The only sovereign aluminium values in a dietary basis are the packaged-drinking-water quality standards (US 21 CFR 165.110 secondary allowable level 200 ug/kg, EU 2020/2184, Health Canada 2900 ug/kg), which govern water sold as water and are Category 8 instruments, and the FSANZ infant-formula aluminium limits, which are Category 1 and are excluded from this category's anchor set by the taxonomy boundary rule. In this form aluminium is a packaging and processing signal (aluminium cans and can linings, closures, filter aids, additive carry-over) rather than a raw-material contaminant. Aluminium is a live cell for this row because the dominant packaging format is the aluminium can and because acidulated formulations at low pH are the conditions under which a compromised can lining leaches, so the aluminium tripwire is a packaging-integrity control as well as an ingredient control.

rows.basis: as_consumed
rows.rationale: Hexavalent chromium is not stable in a formulated sports or energy beverage. At the pH of this product form (typically pH 2.5 to 3.8, with citric, phosphoric, malic and ascorbic acid present in the formulation) Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by the organic acids, sugars, ascorbate and polyphenols present in the matrix, so a positive Cr(VI) result is an artifact of the total-chromium determination rather than a species present in the beverage as consumed. The reference-method basis for this determination is the in-house species arbitration at data/workbench/standards/2026-07-31-chromium-formula-adjudication.md, which found that the superseded ion-exchange plus electrothermal-AAS methods that generated the historical Cr(VI) values in liquid food matrices are not reproduced by the modern reference method: saraiva2021 (species-specific isotope dilution HPLC-ICP-MS, limit of quantification 0.049 ug/kg) quantified no Cr(VI) in any milk or formula sample while resolving Cr(III) and total chromium at single-digit ug/kg. That adjudication was drawn on a near-neutral aqueous food matrix; the acidic beverage matrices in this row are a more strongly reducing environment still, so the artifact conclusion carries a fortiori. The health-relevant species is controlled through the total-chromium cell and the reflex rule below, and this determination is a method finding, not an occurrence-derived value: no number is taken from it.

rows.basis: total lead content of the accessible component, of the dried coating film and of any applied sticker or film (mg/kg)
rows.rationale: Five directly applicable total-content instruments are named and the strictest is taken. The US CPSIA s.101 children's-product substrate limit (100 mg/kg for any part of the product) and the 16 CFR 1303 surface-coating limit (90 mg/kg on the weight of the total non-volatile content of the dried paint film) both reach a stroller as a children's product; Canada SOR/2018-83 s.2(1) sets 90 mg/kg in each accessible part of consumer products for the sleep, relaxation, hygiene, carrying or transport of children under four; Canada SOR/2016-193 s.2(1) sets 90 mg/kg in a dried sample of surface coating material and s.6 sets 90 mg/kg in stickers, films and applied surface coatings on accessible parts of furniture and products for children. HMTc publishes 90 mg/kg and applies it to every accessible component, including the substrate whose own federal US limit is 100 mg/kg. The EU REACH Annex XVII entry 63 mouthable-article value (500 mg/kg) and the brass-alloy exception (5 000 mg/kg) are far looser and are not selected. A stroller is a children's product under CPSIA and is a product for the transport of a child under four under SOR/2018-83. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value.

rows.basis: total cadmium content of the component material (mg/kg of the homogenised component or of the dried coating film)
rows.rationale: All three candidates are TOTAL-CONTENT limits, so the strictest-of-components selection compares like with like. The EU REACH Annex XVII entry 23 plastic-material value (100 mg/kg) binds the article's moulded polymer components DIRECTLY; the EU painted-article value (1 000 mg/kg) binds its paint layer directly; the Australian coating value (75 mg/kg) is scoped to toys coated with a material and is therefore READ ACROSS to the coatings of a stroller or pram, which is not a toy but is a coated article for the same child, in the same mouthing and handling contact. Because the read-across value is the strictest of the three it becomes the published ceiling and is applied to every accessible component, including the polymer components whose own direct limit is 100 mg/kg — deliberate over-compliance, disclosed rather than silent. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value. COMPLIANCE OBLIGATION, stated so this record cannot be read as certifying a value the licensee cannot lawfully sell. The cadmium ceiling published on this row is 75 mg/kg, which sits ABOVE the Washington Children's Safe Product Act prohibition on cadmium exceeding 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component (register row wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b); the Act is codified in Washington's RCW chapter 70A.430). That Act's own definition of a children's product enumerates car seats, products designed to help a child sleep, relax or feed, and products worn as clothing by children, which reaches most of the forms certified on this row. A lot returning cadmium above 40 mg/kg would therefore conform to the HMTc ceiling and still be unlawful to sell in Washington. Any such result is escalated as a jurisdiction-specific regulatory hard stop under the HMTc legal-violation rule and is never certified without that qualification, pending scope-resolved re-ingest of the Washington row through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. The Minnesota cadmium value (75 mg/kg, register row mn_325e3892_2025_cd_covered_consumer_products_75ppm) equals the published ceiling rather than undercutting it, so a lot conforming here conforms there. Where the article incorporates a battery or a battery-powered module — a vibration unit, a sound or music module, a night light, a powered mobile or a powered rocker — the battery is a distinct regulated article with its own instrument, and its limits are not this row's. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 restricts cadmium in a portable battery whether or not incorporated into an appliance (register row eu_batteries_2023_cd_portable_batteries_20000, 20 mg/kg) and mercury in a battery (register row eu_batteries_2023_thg_batteries_5000, 5 mg/kg), both expressed on the weight of the battery. Both are stricter than the values published here and both are recorded as companion obligations on the battery in a battery-by-weight basis; the battery is never homogenised into an accessible-component sample and its instrument is never merged into this row's component-content ceiling.

rows.basis: total mercury content of the accessible component material and of the dried non-volatile coating film (mg/kg) — the sovereign value is written for surface coating material and is extended by disclosed read-across, not asserted as direct alignment
rows.rationale: The published value is 10 mg/kg, but it is reached by DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS and not by direct regulatory alignment, because the instrument's scope is narrower than the cell this row publishes. Canada SOR/2016-193 s.5 sets 10 mg/kg total mercury in a dried sample of SURFACE COATING MATERIAL; the register's product_scope for that row is 'surface coating material', which is the coating substance itself. The same instrument distinguishes that scope from the applied-coating scope — its s.6 reaches a sticker, film or surface coating material applied to accessible parts of furniture and products for children (register row ca_sor2016_193_pb_applied_stickers_films_coatings_90000) — and s.6 is lead-only, with no mercury analogue anywhere in the register. Publishing s.5 as a DIRECT sovereign ceiling for the homogenised wood, steel tube, moulded polymer, foam and textile of a stroller or pram would therefore over-read the instrument, which is the defect this cell was rebuilt to remove. HMTc reaches the value in two disclosed steps instead. Step one reads s.5 across from the coating material as such to the dried applied film on the finished article; the nearest sovereign instrument written in exactly that applied-coating scope is Canada Toys Regulations SOR/2011-17 s.23(1)(c) (register row ca_sor2011_17_thg_accessible_toy_coating_10), which sets the same 10 mg/kg for total mercury in surface coating materials applied to accessible parts of a child's article, so step one lands on a number a sovereign has already written for an applied coating on a children's product. Step two extends that same 10 mg/kg to every accessible component of a stroller or pram, which no sovereign requires and which HMTc adopts as deliberate over-compliance, disclosed here rather than applied silently. At 10 mg/kg the value is six times stricter than the Australian toy-coating mercury value (60 mg/kg, register row au_customs_1956_thg_toys_coating_60mgkg). The EN 71-3 Category III scraped-off-material total-mercury migration value (94 mg/kg, register row eu_2009_48_cat3_thg_toy_migration) measures transfer rather than content, is looser, and is excluded by this row's basis guard.

rows.basis: hexavalent chromium content on the total dry weight of the component (mg/kg) — leather, coating film, or plated and conversion-coated metal part
rows.rationale: This is the only hexavalent-chromium CONTENT limit in the register that reaches a skin-contact article, and it binds DIRECTLY wherever a stroller or pram carries a leather part in skin contact — a leather handlebar or bumper-bar wrap, a harness pad, a leather trim panel or a leather pull tab. For the article's non-leather Cr(VI) pathways — chromate-pigmented coatings, chromate conversion coatings and hexavalent chrome plating on metal parts — no sovereign sets a content maximum, so the 3 mg/kg value is READ ACROSS to them and applied article-wide. The read-across is disclosed and is argued from the material and the contact, not from convenience: it keeps the SAME analyte (Cr(VI) specifically, not total chromium) and the SAME basis (mg/kg of the component's dry mass), and crosses only a material boundary, from chrome-tanned leather to a chromate-pigmented or chromate-passivated surface. The hazard is identical (Cr(VI) skin sensitisation) and the route is identical (dermal transfer under sweat from a surface held against the child), which is exactly why entry 47 was written for skin-contact leather in the first place. Applying it article-wide is deliberate over-compliance and is the same rule this row applies to lead (90 mg/kg applied to a substrate whose own US limit is 100 mg/kg) and to cadmium (75 mg/kg applied to polymer components whose own EU limit is 100 mg/kg); declining to extend it to Cr(VI), the analyte where compliance costs a supplier a change of passivation chemistry, would be selective over-compliance and is not done. The EU RoHS 0.1 % homogeneous-material Cr(VI) value is scoped to electrical and electronic equipment and is over three hundred times more permissive, so it is not used as the read-across source. The EN 71-3 Category I and II Cr(VI) migration values are numerically lower but are leachate limits measuring transfer rather than content, and are excluded by this row's basis guard.

rows.basis: Finished cosmetic total content as placed on market (ug/kg of product as sold); technically-unavoidable-impurity basis. Not migration, not leachate, not dietary, not an ingredient purity specification.
rows.rationale: Korea MFDS is the ONLY authority in the register that publishes a nickel maximum for a finished cosmetic, and the instrument tiers it by product class: eye makeup 35000 ug/kg, colour makeup 30000, all other cosmetics 10000. Method step 4 requires the government's own product-form split to be preserved, so the applicable branch is selected rather than the strictest branch overall. Both register transpositions of the instrument (MFDS Notice 2024-9 and Notice 2025-63) are named and carry identical values, which is the cross-edition check. No other credible authority publishes a cosmetic nickel ceiling: the EU prohibits nickel compounds as intentional cosmetic ingredients under Regulation 1223/2009 Annex II without setting a numeric trace maximum, and Germany's BVL 2017 table covers only lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury and antimony. This row is neither an eye-makeup nor a colour-makeup product, so the 10000 ug/kg branch is the applicable cell and it binds. Where the mapping of an HMTc row onto the Korean product classes is not unambiguous, or where a row's forms straddle two branches, HMTc takes the stricter branch rather than claiming the looser one.

rows.basis: Finished cosmetic total content as placed on market (ug/kg of product as sold); technically-unavoidable-impurity basis. Not migration, not leachate, not dietary, not an ingredient purity specification.
rows.rationale: Applicable sovereign maxima surveyed for this exact form: Germany BVL 2017 general cosmetic orientation value, 2000 ug/kg; China NMPA 2015, 10000; Health Canada, 10000; Taiwan MOHW 2024, 10000; Korea MFDS Notice 2025-63, 20000; Singapore HSA 2024 and the ASEAN directive with its Indonesian and Malaysian transpositions, 20000; Kenya KS 2937:2021, 20000. Looser and therefore non-binding: the EAEU natural-raw-material tier (5000), the Korean clay-powder tier (50000), the India IS 3959:2004 skin-powder rows (20000 and 10000) and the Australian customs value (250000). The German value binds. Its own scope excludes the make-up categories the same table lists at 5000 ug/kg (make-up powder, rouge, eye shadow, eyeliner, kajal and theatrical make-up); none of those forms falls in this row, so the general branch is the applicable cell. The US FDA draft lead guidance for lip and externally applied cosmetics (10000) carries draft status in the register, is gated out by the compiler, and is looser in any case. No colour-additive or ingredient purity specification is used as an anchor: the US 21 CFR 73/74 cosmetic-use specifications (10000-20000 ug/kg), the India permitted-colour specification (20000), the Brazil ANVISA RDC 628/2022 organic-colorant specification (20000) and the New Zealand / Singapore carbon-black colourant profiles (10000) bound one raw material's purity rather than the finished product, they are refused by this row's basis guard, and every one of them is looser than the binding value in any event.

rows.basis: Finished cosmetic total content as placed on market (ug/kg of product as sold); technically-unavoidable-impurity basis. Not migration, not leachate, not dietary, not an ingredient purity specification.
rows.rationale: Korea MFDS is the ONLY authority in the register that publishes a nickel maximum for a finished cosmetic, and the instrument tiers it by product class: eye makeup 35000 ug/kg, colour makeup 30000, all other cosmetics 10000. Method step 4 requires the government's own product-form split to be preserved, so the applicable branch is selected rather than the strictest branch overall. Both register transpositions of the instrument (MFDS Notice 2024-9 and Notice 2025-63) are named and carry identical values, which is the cross-edition check. No other credible authority publishes a cosmetic nickel ceiling: the EU prohibits nickel compounds as intentional cosmetic ingredients under Regulation 1223/2009 Annex II without setting a numeric trace maximum, and Germany's BVL 2017 table covers only lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury and antimony. This row is neither an eye-makeup nor a colour-makeup product, so the 10000 ug/kg branch is the applicable cell and it binds. Where the mapping of an HMTc row onto the Korean product classes is not unambiguous, or where a row's forms straddle two branches, HMTc takes the stricter branch rather than claiming the looser one.

rows.basis: total lead content of the accessible component, of the dried coating film and of any applied sticker or film (mg/kg)
rows.rationale: Five directly applicable total-content instruments are named and the strictest is taken. The US CPSIA s.101 children's-product substrate limit (100 mg/kg for any part of the product) and the 16 CFR 1303 surface-coating limit (90 mg/kg on the weight of the total non-volatile content of the dried paint film) both reach an infant swing or bouncer as a children's product; Canada SOR/2018-83 s.2(1) sets 90 mg/kg in each accessible part of consumer products for the sleep, relaxation, hygiene, carrying or transport of children under four; Canada SOR/2016-193 s.2(1) sets 90 mg/kg in a dried sample of surface coating material and s.6 sets 90 mg/kg in stickers, films and applied surface coatings on accessible parts of furniture and products for children. HMTc publishes 90 mg/kg and applies it to every accessible component, including the substrate whose own federal US limit is 100 mg/kg. The EU REACH Annex XVII entry 63 mouthable-article value (500 mg/kg) and the brass-alloy exception (5 000 mg/kg) are far looser and are not selected. A swing or bouncer is a children's product under CPSIA and a product for the relaxation of a child under four under SOR/2018-83. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value.
