rows.basis: as sold, ug of element per kg of the emitting material (product as tested)
rows.rationale: No government anywhere sets a lead content maximum for an air freshener, plug-in evaporator, puff releaser, candle body, wax melt, oil or nebula diffuser, gel or reed diffuser, incense stick, potpourri, vacuum-cleaner fragrance additive or fragrance refill. The only sovereign heavy-metal instrument in any jurisdiction that names a product in this category is the United States CPSC prohibition on lead-cored candlewicks, 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13), mirrored by Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956; it restricts lead in the metal of a wick core and covers no other analyte and no other product form. The cell is therefore a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS, and it is taken on the axis the regulators themselves used: route of administration. Colorado's 2022 heavy-metal table and Maryland's Technical Authority Rev. 6.0 both publish a route LADDER over the same underlying matrices, with the inhalation row strictest, the oral row looser and the topical or cutaneous row looser still. The value is therefore a function of the route, not of the source matrix's chemistry, and Colorado scopes its strictest row in the instrument's own words to "inhaled product or audited product administered by metered-dose nasal spray", which describes a delivery mechanism this category shares. Maryland's own route gap is the sharpest available evidence for that reading: its inhalation-route total-chromium value is 600 ug/kg while its oral and cutaneous values for the same products are 1,100,000 ug/kg. A fines-fraction result at or above 100 ug/kg fails the lot independently of the bulk result, and the bulk result never averages the fines away. Where the fines fraction and the bulk result diverge by more than the combined expanded uncertainty of the two determinations, the lot is held, re-sampled after reconditioning to the declared particle-size distribution and re-tested, and a confirmed enrichment of mercury into the respirable fraction that the manufacturer cannot attribute to a controlled source blocks certification. The fines result is otherwise dispositioned under the control-and-escalation rule stated above. No emission-rate limit, per-actuation dose limit or indoor-air concentration limit is published for this row, because no credible sovereign government sets one for any product in this category and none is manufactured from an occupational or ambient-air value.

rows.basis: as sold, ug of element per kg of the emitting material (product as tested)
rows.rationale: No government anywhere sets a total chromium content maximum for an air freshener, plug-in evaporator, puff releaser, candle body, wax melt, oil or nebula diffuser, gel or reed diffuser, incense stick, potpourri, vacuum-cleaner fragrance additive or fragrance refill. The only sovereign heavy-metal instrument in any jurisdiction that names a product in this category is the United States CPSC prohibition on lead-cored candlewicks, 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13), mirrored by Australia's Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956; it restricts lead in the metal of a wick core and covers no other analyte and no other product form. The cell is therefore a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS, and it is taken on the axis the regulators themselves used: route of administration. Colorado's 2022 heavy-metal table and Maryland's Technical Authority Rev. 6.0 both publish a route LADDER over the same underlying matrices, with the inhalation row strictest, the oral row looser and the topical or cutaneous row looser still. The value is therefore a function of the route, not of the source matrix's chemistry, and Colorado scopes its strictest row in the instrument's own words to "inhaled product or audited product administered by metered-dose nasal spray", which describes a delivery mechanism this category shares. Maryland's own route gap is the sharpest available evidence for that reading: its inhalation-route total-chromium value is 600 ug/kg while its oral and cutaneous values for the same products are 1,100,000 ug/kg. Selected value 600 ug/kg, from Maryland (inhalation route). Maryland is the only regulator on the register that publishes a chromium value scoped to the inhalation route. The looser or route-unspecific values on the register are recorded and NOT selected: no other jurisdiction on the register publishes a chromium value for any inhaled product: California DCC section 15723, the Colorado route table, the Massachusetts protocol, the Nevada action levels and Israel IMC-GMP Procedure 152 all omit chromium entirely. Maryland's own oral-route and cutaneous-route chromium values for the same products, 1,100,000 ug/kg, are a different route scope and are deliberately not used. The basis is identical to this row's native basis, micrograms of element per kilogram of product as tested, so no basis conversion, no reconstitution and no dry-to-wet adjustment is performed. The read-across is published as `read-across` and never as `regulatory-alignment`, because no instrument regulates this exact cell. Adopting it tightens rather than relaxes the applicable regulatory position: it is three to four orders of magnitude stricter than every article-content instrument that actually binds these products (RoHS lead at 1,000,000 ug/kg of homogeneous material, the candlewick-core prohibition threshold at 600,000 ug/kg of wick-core metal, REACH cadmium in polymers at 100,000 ug/kg). No occurrence, percentile, feasibility or precautionary input touched the number in either direction. Determined on the additive as supplied, homogenised across the retail unit, with the friable fines fraction analysed separately by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS with collision/reaction-cell control of the interfered masses, with the article's non-emitting components digested and screened separately per this row's component plan. DISPOSITION OF THE ADDITIONAL ANALYSES THIS CELL MANDATES. This cell requires two analyses beyond the published test, and each carries a criterion and a lot consequence, so that no mandatory analysis on this row is an obligation without an outcome. COMPONENT RESULTS, THE FIRST ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS THIS CELL MANDATES. The published total-chromium screen of 600 ug/kg governs the emitting material and is NOT transferred to a component's bulk content: a mineral or zeolite carrier substrate, a metal-bearing dye or anti-caking agent, or a pigmented dispenser body is or may be substantially metal, metal-plated, metal-glazed or metal-pigmented by construction, and reading an emitting-material value against a structural component's bulk content would be exactly the basis conflation this row's basis guard exists to prevent, failing every compliant article for a metal that never enters the air. Every component result is instead dispositioned in three ordered branches, and no component result is left outside them. (a) WHERE A SOVEREIGN INSTRUMENT REACHES THE COMPONENT AND THIS ANALYTE, that instrument is the criterion. For total chromium and this row's components, branch (a) is EMPTY, and the instruments checked before saying so are named rather than waved at: EU RoHS 2011/65/EU restricts HEXAVALENT chromium in the homogeneous materials of electrical and electronic equipment (eu_rohs_2011_crvi_homogeneous_materials_1000000) and publishes no total-chromium value, so it reaches this row's hexavalent-chromium cell if a powered sub-assembly is ever present and never this total-chromium cell, because a species and its total-element parent are not interchangeable in either direction; Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 on batteries restricts mercury, cadmium and lead only and publishes no chromium value, and this row contains no battery in any event; REACH Annex XVII entry 63 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2015/628 (eu_2015_628_pb_mouthable_general_public_articles_0_05pct) reaches only articles supplied to the general public that may be placed in the mouth by children; Regulation (EU) 2018/1513 reaches consumer clothing and skin-contact textiles and does not reach a packaging, sachet or decorative textile that is not worn; the EU Toy Safety Directive 2009/48/EC with EN 71-3, the CPSIA surface-coating limit and the Canadian and Australian toy-coating limits reach accessible toy material and toy surface coatings, and none of these articles is a toy; 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13) reaches only the metal of a candlewick core and this row has no wick core; the food-contact ceramic, glassware and enamelware instruments reach only articles intended to come into contact with food. Every component result on this row therefore falls to branch (b) or branch (c), and neither leaves a result without a criterion or without a lot consequence. (b) WHERE THE COMPONENT IS IN THE EMISSION PATH (the carrier granule, bead, powder or pad substrate, and the sachet, disc backing or dispenser body through which the additive is drawn into the appliance airstream), the criterion is the published total-chromium SCREEN of 600 ug/kg, applied where its basis makes it meaningful: the test is performed on emitting material sampled from the finished, filled and assembled article rather than from a pre-fill bulk batch, at the end of the declared shelf life at the declared storage conditions, with the sample homogenised across the retail unit, so that any chromium transferred out of an emission-path component into the emitting material is carried into the published result rather than escaping it. The screen is a tripwire and never a pass/fail in its own right. An emitting-material total-chromium result reaching half the screen (300 ug/kg) orders reflex hexavalent-chromium speciation on that lot under the reference method published on this row's Cr-VI cell, and that cell's disposition then governs the lot: any hexavalent chromium quantifiable above the method limit of quantitation fails the lot. A rising component result while the emitting material stays below the reflex trigger does not by itself fail the lot and falls to branch (c). (c) OTHERWISE, for a component outside the emission path that no sovereign instrument reaches for total chromium, the component result is dispositioned under the HMTc control-and-escalation rule, in the same terms this row's control cells already use: the result is held to ALARA against the manufacturer's demonstrated process capability for that formulation and component set; a result outside that capability band, or an unexplained step change between lots, triggers CAPA and raw-material traceback to the carrier-substrate supplier, the fragrance house, the dye supplier, the anti-caking and fixative supplier and the sachet, backing or dispenser converter; a confirmed uncontrolled source blocks certification until it is removed or substituted; and the analyte goes onto priority surveillance for this row. No component ceiling is invented in branch (c), because no credible sovereign government publishes a total-chromium content maximum for these components in this product form, and an occupational exposure limit, an indoor-air guideline and an ambient-air standard are none of them converted into one. FRIABLE FINES FRACTION, THE SECOND ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS THIS CELL MANDATES. The friable fines fraction is not a separate matrix requiring a separate criterion: it is this row's emitting material in its most respirable form, and the published total-chromium screen of 600 ug/kg applies to it directly and on its own terms. A fines-fraction total-chromium result reaching half the screen (300 ug/kg) orders reflex hexavalent-chromium speciation on that lot under the reference method on this row's Cr-VI cell, and that cell's disposition governs: any hexavalent chromium quantifiable above the method limit of quantitation fails the lot. Where the fines fraction and the bulk result diverge by more than the combined expanded uncertainty of the two determinations, the lot is held, re-sampled after reconditioning to the declared particle-size distribution and re-tested, and a confirmed enrichment of chromium into the respirable fraction that the manufacturer cannot attribute to a controlled source blocks certification. The fines result is otherwise dispositioned under the control-and-escalation rule stated above. No emission-rate limit, per-actuation dose limit or indoor-air concentration limit is published for this row, because no credible sovereign government sets one for any product in this category and none is manufactured from an occupational or ambient-air value.

rows.basis: as_consumed
rows.rationale: Hexavalent chromium is not stable in a non-root vegetable juice. At the pH of this product form (typically pH 3.9 to 4.6 for tomato-based juices and mildly acidic for other non-root vegetable juices, with organic acids and ascorbate present) Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by the organic acids, sugars, ascorbate and polyphenols present in the matrix, so a positive Cr(VI) result is an artifact of the total-chromium determination rather than a species present in the beverage as consumed. The reference-method basis for this determination is the in-house species arbitration at data/workbench/standards/2026-07-31-chromium-formula-adjudication.md, which found that the superseded ion-exchange plus electrothermal-AAS methods that generated the historical Cr(VI) values in liquid food matrices are not reproduced by the modern reference method: saraiva2021 (species-specific isotope dilution HPLC-ICP-MS, limit of quantification 0.049 ug/kg) quantified no Cr(VI) in any milk or formula sample while resolving Cr(III) and total chromium at single-digit ug/kg. That adjudication was drawn on a near-neutral aqueous food matrix; the acidic beverage matrices in this row are a more strongly reducing environment still, so the artifact conclusion carries a fortiori. The health-relevant species is controlled through the total-chromium cell and the reflex rule below, and this determination is a method finding, not an occurrence-derived value: no number is taken from it.

The read-across is a form change (whole root to its juice), and the basis treatment is stated precisely rather than glossed. The two corroborating cells are recorded differently, Hong Kong Cap 132V as an as-sold Part 2 Schedule entry and FSANZ Schedule 19 as the portion ordinarily consumed, and each is compared to the single-strength juice at face value. rows.basis: total lead content of the accessible component, of the dried coating film and of any applied sticker or film (mg/kg)
rows.rationale: Five directly applicable total-content instruments are named and the strictest is taken. The US CPSIA s.101 children's-product substrate limit (100 mg/kg for any part of the product) and the 16 CFR 1303 surface-coating limit (90 mg/kg on the weight of the total non-volatile content of the dried paint film) both reach a walker as a children's product; Canada SOR/2018-83 s.2(1) sets 90 mg/kg in each accessible part of consumer products for the sleep, relaxation, hygiene, carrying or transport of children under four; Canada SOR/2016-193 s.2(1) sets 90 mg/kg in a dried sample of surface coating material and s.6 sets 90 mg/kg in stickers, films and applied surface coatings on accessible parts of furniture and products for children. HMTc publishes 90 mg/kg and applies it to every accessible component, including the substrate whose own federal US limit is 100 mg/kg. The EU REACH Annex XVII entry 63 mouthable-article value (500 mg/kg) and the brass-alloy exception (5 000 mg/kg) are far looser and are not selected. A walker is a children's product under CPSIA and a child learning and play product under SOR/2018-83. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value.

rows.basis: total cadmium content of the component material (mg/kg of the homogenised component or of the dried coating film)
rows.rationale: All three candidates are TOTAL-CONTENT limits, so the strictest-of-components selection compares like with like. The EU REACH Annex XVII entry 23 plastic-material value (100 mg/kg) binds the article's moulded polymer components DIRECTLY; the EU painted-article value (1 000 mg/kg) binds its paint layer directly; the Australian coating value (75 mg/kg) is scoped to toys coated with a material and is therefore READ ACROSS to the coatings of an infant walker or activity walker, which is not a toy but is a coated article for the same child, in the same mouthing and handling contact. Because the read-across value is the strictest of the three it becomes the published ceiling and is applied to every accessible component, including the polymer components whose own direct limit is 100 mg/kg — deliberate over-compliance, disclosed rather than silent. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value. COMPLIANCE OBLIGATION, stated so this record cannot be read as certifying a value the licensee cannot lawfully sell. The cadmium ceiling published on this row is 75 mg/kg, which sits ABOVE the Washington Children's Safe Product Act prohibition on cadmium exceeding 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component (register row wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b); the Act is codified in Washington's RCW chapter 70A.430). That Act's own definition of a children's product enumerates car seats, products designed to help a child sleep, relax or feed, and products worn as clothing by children, which reaches most of the forms certified on this row. A lot returning cadmium above 40 mg/kg would therefore conform to the HMTc ceiling and still be unlawful to sell in Washington. Any such result is escalated as a jurisdiction-specific regulatory hard stop under the HMTc legal-violation rule and is never certified without that qualification, pending scope-resolved re-ingest of the Washington row through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. The Minnesota cadmium value (75 mg/kg, register row mn_325e3892_2025_cd_covered_consumer_products_75ppm) equals the published ceiling rather than undercutting it, so a lot conforming here conforms there. Where the article incorporates a battery or a battery-powered module — a vibration unit, a sound or music module, a night light, a powered mobile or a powered rocker — the battery is a distinct regulated article with its own instrument, and its limits are not this row's. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 restricts cadmium in a portable battery whether or not incorporated into an appliance (register row eu_batteries_2023_cd_portable_batteries_20000, 20 mg/kg) and mercury in a battery (register row eu_batteries_2023_thg_batteries_5000, 5 mg/kg), both expressed on the weight of the battery. Both are stricter than the values published here and both are recorded as companion obligations on the battery in a battery-by-weight basis; the battery is never homogenised into an accessible-component sample and its instrument is never merged into this row's component-content ceiling.

rows.basis: total mercury content of the accessible component material and of the dried non-volatile coating film (mg/kg) — the sovereign value is written for surface coating material and is extended by disclosed read-across, not asserted as direct alignment
rows.rationale: The published value is 10 mg/kg, but it is reached by DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS and not by direct regulatory alignment, because the instrument's scope is narrower than the cell this row publishes. Canada SOR/2016-193 s.5 sets 10 mg/kg total mercury in a dried sample of SURFACE COATING MATERIAL; the register's product_scope for that row is 'surface coating material', which is the coating substance itself. The same instrument distinguishes that scope from the applied-coating scope — its s.6 reaches a sticker, film or surface coating material applied to accessible parts of furniture and products for children (register row ca_sor2016_193_pb_applied_stickers_films_coatings_90000) — and s.6 is lead-only, with no mercury analogue anywhere in the register. Publishing s.5 as a DIRECT sovereign ceiling for the homogenised wood, steel tube, moulded polymer, foam and textile of an infant walker or activity walker would therefore over-read the instrument, which is the defect this cell was rebuilt to remove. HMTc reaches the value in two disclosed steps instead. Step one reads s.5 across from the coating material as such to the dried applied film on the finished article; the nearest sovereign instrument written in exactly that applied-coating scope is Canada Toys Regulations SOR/2011-17 s.23(1)(c) (register row ca_sor2011_17_thg_accessible_toy_coating_10), which sets the same 10 mg/kg for total mercury in surface coating materials applied to accessible parts of a child's article, so step one lands on a number a sovereign has already written for an applied coating on a children's product. Step two extends that same 10 mg/kg to every accessible component of an infant walker or activity walker, which no sovereign requires and which HMTc adopts as deliberate over-compliance, disclosed here rather than applied silently. At 10 mg/kg the value is six times stricter than the Australian toy-coating mercury value (60 mg/kg, register row au_customs_1956_thg_toys_coating_60mgkg). The EN 71-3 Category III scraped-off-material total-mercury migration value (94 mg/kg, register row eu_2009_48_cat3_thg_toy_migration) measures transfer rather than content, is looser, and is excluded by this row's basis guard.

rows.basis: hexavalent chromium content on the total dry weight of the component (mg/kg) — leather, coating film, or plated and conversion-coated metal part
rows.rationale: This is the only hexavalent-chromium CONTENT limit in the register that reaches a skin-contact article, and it binds DIRECTLY wherever an infant walker or activity walker carries a leather part in skin contact — a leather handlebar or bumper-bar wrap, a harness pad, a leather trim panel or a leather pull tab. For the article's non-leather Cr(VI) pathways — chromate-pigmented coatings, chromate conversion coatings and hexavalent chrome plating on metal parts — no sovereign sets a content maximum, so the 3 mg/kg value is READ ACROSS to them and applied article-wide. The read-across is disclosed and is argued from the material and the contact, not from convenience: it keeps the SAME analyte (Cr(VI) specifically, not total chromium) and the SAME basis (mg/kg of the component's dry mass), and crosses only a material boundary, from chrome-tanned leather to a chromate-pigmented or chromate-passivated surface. The hazard is identical (Cr(VI) skin sensitisation) and the route is identical (dermal transfer under sweat from a surface held against the child), which is exactly why entry 47 was written for skin-contact leather in the first place. Applying it article-wide is deliberate over-compliance and is the same rule this row applies to lead (90 mg/kg applied to a substrate whose own US limit is 100 mg/kg) and to cadmium (75 mg/kg applied to polymer components whose own EU limit is 100 mg/kg); declining to extend it to Cr(VI), the analyte where compliance costs a supplier a change of passivation chemistry, would be selective over-compliance and is not done. The EU RoHS 0.1 % homogeneous-material Cr(VI) value is scoped to electrical and electronic equipment and is over three hundred times more permissive, so it is not used as the read-across source. The EN 71-3 Category I and II Cr(VI) migration values are numerically lower but are leachate limits measuring transfer rather than content, and are excluded by this row's basis guard.

rows.basis: finished oral-care product as placed on market (total nickel content, ug/kg as sold) — read across from the Korean residual finished-cosmetic nickel tier
rows.rationale: Nickel is a mucosal and contact sensitiser and reaches oral-care formulations through hydrated-silica and calcium-carbonate abrasives, mineral pigments, and stainless-steel process contact, so the cell must not be left without a ceiling where a sovereign anchor exists. The exact cell (nickel in a dentifrice, rinse, whitening system or denture-care product) is unregulated in every jurisdiction surveyed, which is why the value is published as a disclosed read-across tagged 'read-across' rather than as regulatory alignment; in Korea a dentifrice is a quasi-drug rather than a cosmetic, so the Korean cosmetic tier does not reach this form by its own terms. Two Korean notices state the same three-tier allowance at identical values: Notice 2024-9 Article 6(2) (kr_mfds2024_9_ni_other_cosmetics_10ugg) and the current Notice No. 2025-63 (the named anchor). The later notice is cited so that this standard and the Category 2 children's-dentifrice standard, which anchors the same cell, cite the same current instrument rather than splitting across two Korean notices for one number. The value is 10000 ug/kg under either notice, neither register row is flagged superseded, and the 2024-9 row remains inside this row's audit scan.

rows.basis: finished tooth-whitening product as placed on market (total content, ug/kg as sold)
rows.rationale: No jurisdiction sets a tin content limit for any oral-care or cosmetic product; the sovereign tin maximum levels in the register are canned-food and food-contact values written for tinplate migration into food and are a different basis entirely. Tin is additionally not a pure impurity in this category: stannous fluoride and stannous chloride are authorised anticaries and antigingivitis actives in dentifrices and mouthrinses, so a finished-product tin ceiling would be exceeded by design in a compliant stannous formulation and would be meaningless as a contaminant control. The cell is held under mandatory analytical control with a declaration reconciliation rather than declared not-material, because tin is unambiguously present at material levels in this category and an absence claim would be contradicted on its face.
